title: Ravens sign veteran OT Kendall Lamm following Hakeem Adeniji retirement
summary: The Baltimore Ravens signed veteran offensive tackle Kendall Lamm following a workout on Monday, per the NFL’s daily transaction report, filling the roster spot vacated by Hakeem Adeniji’s sudden retirement over the weekend. Lamm, 34, is entering his 12th NFL season. He spent the last four in Miami with 46 total appearances, including 15 starts […]
full_text: MIAMI GARDENS, FL - OCTOBER 30: Kendall Lamm #70 of the Miami Dolphins looks on from the sideline during the national anthem prior to an NFL football game against the Baltimore Ravens at Hard Rock Stadium on October 30, 2025 in Miami Gardens, Florida. (Photo by Cooper Neill/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Baltimore Ravens signed veteran offensive tackle Kendall Lamm following a workout on Monday, per the NFL’s daily transaction report, filling the roster spot vacated by Hakeem Adeniji’s sudden retirement over the weekend. Lamm, 34, is entering his 12th NFL season. He spent the last four in Miami with 46 total appearances, including 15 starts in 2023 and 2024. Last year, he appeared in 13 games, but played just seven snaps on offense and 52 on special teams. Most of Lamm’s pro experience came with the Texans between 2015 and 2018. He first signed in Houston as an undrafted free agent and made the 53-man roster as a rookie as the team’s swing tackle. He continued in that role for the subsequent two seasons before earning the right tackle job in 2018, his lone year as a full-time starter. After leaving Houston during the 2019 offseason, Lamm signed a two-year deal with the Browns, where he again served as the swing tackle, and spent the 2021 season in the same role in Tennessee. He has generally earned solid pass-blocking grades in his career from Pro Football Focus with a 5.9% pressure rate and a 96.5 pass blocking efficiency. (For context, Ronnie Stanley owns a 5.5% pressure rate and a 97.0 PBE, while Roger Rosengarten sits at 6.3% and 96.5 in each category.) The Ravens badly needed depth at offensive tackle following Hakeem Adeniji’s sudden retirement over the weekend. The 28-year-old just signed in Baltimore last week and participated in Saturday’s training camp practice at the University of Maryland’s SECU Stadium. Head coach Jesse Minter characterized Adeniji’s abrupt departure as a “personal situation” and said that the team would quickly fill his spot on the roster, indicating Lamm’s signing was already in the works. In addition to Lamm, the Ravens also worked out Jake Curhan and Nicholas Petit-Frere. Curhan, 28, started one game for the Panthers last season and two for the Bears in 2024; before that, he spent three years in Seattle, primarily playing right tackle. Petit-Frere was a Titans third-round pick out of Ohio State in 2022. He started 16 games at right tackle as a rookie but only appeared in three games the following year due to injury and a six-game gambling suspension. In 2024, he started 10 games with a 92.7 PBE that ranked 83rd out of 84 tackles with at least 300 snaps. He did not play last year. The Ravens have 2025 fifth-round pick Carson Vinson installed as their backup left tackle as he develops into a potential successor for Stanley. Offensive line coach Dwayne Ledford indicated on Monday that the team is hoping that 2024 third-rounder Emery Jones can provide depth at right guard and tackle this year, the latter being his college position at LSU. Lamm offers dedicated depth at right tackle as well as nearly 1,000 career snaps on the blind side, giving him a shot at earning a 53-man roster spot this summer.
author: Nikhil Mehta

title: Lamar Jackson’s narrative tax and how speculation becomes accepted fact
summary: Welcome back to Femi Ayanbadejo’s four-part series setting the record straight on Lamar Jackson. Part One reframed the debate surrounding his career. Part Two tested criticism of his play against the film and data. Part Three moves off the field to examine contracts, character allegations, and the media ecosystem that allows unsupported commentary to acquire […]
full_text: NEW YORK CITY, NY - DECEMBER 10: 2016 Heisman Trophy winner University of Louisville quarterback Lamar Jackson (4) with his mother Felicia Jones after winning the 81st Annual Heisman Trophy press conference on December 10, 2016, at the Marriott Marquis in New York City. (Photo by Rich Graessle/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Welcome back to Femi Ayanbadejo’s four-part series setting the record straight on Lamar Jackson. Part One reframed the debate surrounding his career. Part Two tested criticism of his play against the film and data. Part Three moves off the field to examine contracts, character allegations, and the media ecosystem that allows unsupported commentary to acquire the authority of fact. Certain athletes pay a price for existing outside the expected template. That price is not paid in dollars. It is paid in narrative: every decision questioned, every silence interpreted, every unconventional choice treated as evidence of a deeper flaw. Lamar Jackson has paid this tax consistently. The currency is unsupported commentary, repeated until speculation becomes accepted truth and zombie-like in its refusal to die. As Jackson begins another training camp, the discussion around his play has largely shifted back to football. Yet some of the longest-lasting narratives surrounding him were never about his performance at all. They were about his character, maturity, motives, and professionalism, claims that often became accepted without meeting the same evidentiary standard we expect elsewhere. Reporting vs. Speculating The most pointed example appeared in a Mike Preston commentary in The Baltimore Sun last December. Preston argued that the Ravens should trade Jackson for multiple first-round picks. That is opinion. He also wrote that Jackson, a South Florida native, would love to play in Miami or Las Vegas; described him as “an overgrown kid in an adult’s body”; alleged that he stayed up late playing video games and fell asleep in meetings; and suggested John Harbaugh had tired of him and the special treatment he received. Those are not all statements of the same kind. A proposed trade is a judgment, whereas claims about private work habits, relationships, motivations, and desired destinations are factual assertions capable of verification. Preston disclosed no source or direct evidence for them and later emphasized that he had written commentary rather than a sourced news report. Harbaugh publicly described his relationship with Jackson as an “A+.” Jackson denied sleeping in meetings and said he sits in the front row. Readers are free to decide whom they find credible. What responsible media cannot do is convert an unsupported character assertion into established fact merely because it appeared in a newspaper. The larger damage came through repetition. The allegations traveled nationally, separated from the limitations of the original commentary. Eric Mangini’s later reference to “many indications of immaturity” drew from a pool of claims that had never been publicly substantiated. That is how narrative laundering works: repetition creates familiarity, familiarity creates assumed credibility, and the original absence of evidence disappears. Calling this process out does not place Jackson beyond criticism. It protects the distinction between reporting and speculation. Opinion is legitimate. Inference is often necessary. Both must be labeled honestly. The Agent Narrative The suggestion that Jackson is disadvantaged by representing himself has been a recurring feature of his coverage, advanced most aggressively by Pro Football Talk’s Mike Florio. The argument is that without a traditional agent, Jackson lacks leverage, leaves money on the table, and navigates negotiations blindly. The description is incomplete. Jackson has used NFLPA resources, attorneys, a trusted inner circle, and his mother, Felicia Jones, who has been central to his business representation. His method is unconventional. The relevant question is whether the outcomes support the claim that it has damaged him. In 2023, Jackson signed a five-year, $260 million extension that briefly made him the NFL’s highest-paid player by annual value. He obtained substantial guarantees as well as no-trade and no-tag provisions. Reasonable people can debate whether a traditional agent might have changed the process or structure. They cannot simply declare that Jackson failed without reconciling that position with the contract he secured. His next negotiation will provide another measurable outcome. Based on the quarterback market and the projected salary cap, my forecast is a four-year extension near $300 million in new money, potentially including a signing bonus around $100 million. That is a projection, not a reported demand. The market will determine whether it is right. The Trade Request and the Cities He Never Named In March 2023, Jackson disclosed that he had requested a trade. The timing and eventual result strongly support the inference that the request functioned as a leverage-producing negotiation tactic after talks had stalled. No outside team produced an offer Baltimore declined to match. Hours before the first round of the 2023 draft, Jackson agreed to his record-setting extension. The trade request is verified fact. Its precise private motivation is inference. The destinations attached to it require a different label. Jackson never publicly said he wanted to be traded to Miami or Las Vegas. No person with direct knowledge has provided a verifiable account that he privately selected either city. Those destinations circulated as speculation and were later repeated with more authority than the underlying evidence justified. The distinction is simple: Jackson requested a trade. Commentators supplied the cities. The Broader Ecosystem Preston is the clearest case, but the pattern extends beyond one columnist. Colin Cowherd was an early Jackson skeptic who later revised his assessment. That intellectual flexibility deserves acknowledgment. Yet in the wake of Baltimore’s coaching transition and Jackson’s contract restructure, Cowherd returned to the word “mercurial,” a characterization that echoed earlier commentary without introducing new, verifiable evidence. Good-faith analysts can absorb a premise simply because it has circulated long enough. That is why sourcing matters most when the subject is character. Statistics can be corrected. A claim about maturity, effort, or loyalty attaches itself to a person long after the segment ends. Jackson responded to criticism in April 2026 with a brief public message: “Instead of trying to bring me down, ask GOD to bring you up.” We can verify the words. We should resist inventing the private emotion behind them. ​The standard is not complicated: critique the decision, analyze the performance, question the strategy. But when commentary asserts access to a player’s private habits, desires, or character, ask the fundamental question of journalism: How do you know?
author: Femi Ayanbadejo

title: Buffalo Bills 2026 scouting report: OLB Mike Danna
summary: The Buffalo Bills overhauled their defense this offseason, adding numerous players who have no connection to former head coach Sean McDermott. That might be a welcome sign for some of us who were growing tired of seeing familiar old faces like Shaq Lawson and Dane Jackson come back for second turns with the club. Am […]
full_text: ORCHARD PARK, NEW YORK - JUNE 9: Mike Danna #51 participates in drills during the Buffalo Bills mandatory minicamp at Kaleida Health Performance Center on June 9, 2026 in Orchard Park, New York. (Photo by Joe Hrycych/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Buffalo Bills overhauled their defense this offseason, adding numerous players who have no connection to former head coach Sean McDermott. That might be a welcome sign for some of us who were growing tired of seeing familiar old faces like Shaq Lawson and Dane Jackson come back for second turns with the club. Am I cherry-picking by leaving out Tre’Davious White and Jordan Poyer, whose second acts with the Bills were more successful? Yes, yes I am. The Bills even added a player from one of their great AFC rivals, poaching an edge rusher who was released in February. The last time the Bills added a player from that team, it was safety Mike Edwards, and it didn’t turn out well for either the team or the player. In today’s installment of “91 players in 91 days,” we discuss a veteran edge player who will have to prove himself worthy of remaining with the Bills through September. _____________________________________________________________________________ Name: Mike Danna Number: 51 Position: OLB Height/Weight: 6’2”, 261 pounds Age: 28 (29 on 21/1/2026) Experience/Draft: 6; selected by the Kansas City Chiefs in the fifth round (No. 177 overall) of the 2020 NFL Draft College: Central Michigan Acquired: Signed with Buffalo on 5/11/2026 Financial situation (per Spotrac): Danna’s one-year contract is worth $1,402,500 overall. Thanks to the veteran’s salary benefit, Buffalo’s cap hit if Danna makes the 53-roster counts slightly less than that, as it comes in at $1,262,500. That’s also the total guaranteed amount on the contract, so Buffalo will eat that figure as a dead-cap charge if Danna is released. 2025 Recap: Danna spent last season with the Chiefs, his sixth year with the club that drafted him. It was the second year of a three-year, $24 million extension he had signed with Kansas City in April 2024. Danna played 15 games last season, making 14 starts. He appeared on less than half of Kansas City’s defensive snaps for the first time since the 2021 season, and as a result, he had his worst year statistically. He tied career-lows with 25 tackles and three tackles for loss, and he set a new career low with just one sack. He did notch his first career interception, however, returning it for 10 yards against the Washington Commanders. The two games he missed were early in the season, Weeks 3 and 4, thanks to a quadriceps injury he suffered during Kansas City’s Week 2 loss to the Philadelphia Eagles. Positional outlook: Danna is one of eight players listed at outside linebacker on the current roster. T.J. Parker, Greg Rousseau, Bradley Chubb, Michael Hoecht, Javon Solomon, Andre Jones Jr., and Cade Denhoff are the others. 2026 Offseason: Danna is healthy and has participated in offseason work to date. 2026 Season outlook: Danna signed what essentially amounts to a fully guaranteed contract in May, so the Bills are going to eat his cap number whether he’s on the 53-man roster or not. The numbers crunch at OLB is tighter than it is at a lot of positions, though, as Buffalo will enter the season with Rousseau, Chubb, Parker, and Hoecht on the team barring some kind of injury or strange happenstance. That leaves room for one or two other edge players at most, and that may also depend on what the team decides to do at some other positions. Will new defensive coordinator Jim Leonhard be a bit more multiple with his fronts? If he is, the Bills might keep an extra defensive end type who might seem like he’d be better suited for a four-man front. That would benefit Danna, who played in such a defense under Steve Spagnuolo in Kansas City. In that scenario, Buffalo might also go a little lighter on players listed at defensive tackle, especially with those “tweener” types who might not have a clear home along the line. Between DTs and OLBs, I expect the Bills to keep 10 total players at most, and eight players at least. If we already have four locks in the players listed above, then we throw in clear roster locks at defensive tackle like Ed Oliver, Deone Walker, and T.J. Sanders, we’re already at seven players. I give Javon Solomon a leg up on the other outside linebackers thanks to his ability to play special teams at a high level combined with his untapped pass-rush upside. There’s eight right there, and we haven’t kept a backup down lineman or two. In short, while Danna’s contract might say that he’s a shoo-in for the roster, his positional group and his fit in Buffalo’s defense tell me he’s more of a bubble player than anything else. Barring injury, I don’t anticipate that he’ll be on the roster once the season starts, but a strong preseason combined with some other players suffering some dings could change that outlook.
author: Sean Murphy

title: Buffalo Bills S Sam Franklin Jr. starts for injured C.J. Gardner-Johnson on Monday
summary: When Buffalo Bills safety C.J. Gardner-Johnson picked up an injury during Saturday’s training camp practice, Bills Mafia held its collective breath. Gardner-Johnson has quickly won over Bills fans, and many believe he’s just what the doctor ordered on defense. Though we’re just into Week 2 of training camp, the thought of losing Gardner-Johnson left people […]
full_text: ORCHARD PARK, NEW YORK - SEPTEMBER 18: Sam Franklin Jr. #28 of the Buffalo Bills looks on during an NFL football game against the Miami Dolphins at Highmark Stadium on September 18, 2025 in Orchard Park, New York. (Photo by Michael Owens/Getty Images) | Getty Images When Buffalo Bills safety C.J. Gardner-Johnson picked up an injury during Saturday’s training camp practice , Bills Mafia held its collective breath. Gardner-Johnson has quickly won over Bills fans, and many believe he’s just what the doctor ordered on defense. Though we’re just into Week 2 of training camp, the thought of losing Gardner-Johnson left people concerned about the team’s depth. Of course, Gardner-Johnson’s injury turned out to be a lower leg strain , mercifully ending some fans’ doom-and-gloom “worst-case-its-his-Achilles” sessions. Yet that doesn’t necessarily mean Gardner-Johnson will be running at his typical full speed in the next week or perhaps a bit longer if the team is extra cautious. With Gardner-Johnson on the mend, it’s opened up opportunities for the other safeties behind Cole Bishop and CJGJ on Buffalo’s roster. In discussing the Bills’ potential depth chart for the 2026 NFL season, many saw rookie safety Jalon Kilgore as the one most likely to play the role of a first reserve. Kilgore came into the 2026 NFL Draft with a fair bit of hype where some projected him to be selected in Round 2. With that, fans as well analysts alike were enamored with Buffalo’s selection of Kilgore in Round 5 . Some are on record saying Kilgore could end up among the Bills’ most productive rookies from the 2026 class — this season and beyond — thanks to his freaky athletic traits and abilities and despite a large sampling of on-field tape . Then came Monday, August 3. Instead of Kilgore claiming those starting reps, veteran safety and special teams ace Sam Franklin Jr. was in to replace Gardner-Johnson. It’s an interesting development, to say the least, where a bigger-bodied safety known for special teams leaps over highly touted younger players and other steely vets — those many viewed as locks to see the field first. Recall, One Bills Drive did make Franklin a free-agent priority this past offseason, agreeing to terms with him on a three-year contract . It’s important to remember two things: 1 — it’s training camp (and it’s still early), and 2 — the defense is now led by an entirely new set of coaches. Where before certain players may have held favor in Sean McDermott’s court, now the board has reset itself. That means truly renewed opportunities for everyone at all defensive positions. Sure, the new coaches are going to have their guys, but there’s less written in pen these days on defense than in anytime over the prior nine seasons. For all we know, defensive coordinator Jim Leonhard could have someone different from the safeties room starting in place of Gardner-Johnson each day of practice. If Leonhard knows one thing it’s safety play, so his instincts should be given a fair bit of initial trust. If that holds true, allowing each of the safeties to get extra reps will likely benefit the depth of that room overall. While Franklin getting featured work at safety is indeed noteworthy, one can expect that his valuable but unsung role on special teams will keep him plenty busy during the season if all goes according to plan.
author: Matt Byham

title: Dion Dawkins explains why he’s fake panicking on some training camp reps
summary: Pittsford, N.Y. | Dion Dawkins has had a revolving door of left guards next to him in his first nine seasons as a member of the Buffalo Bills. After the past two seasons with veteran David Edwards next door at left guard, the 2026 campaign will mark another new teammate for Dawkins alongside him on […]
full_text: ROCHESTER, NEW YORK - JULY 29: Dion Dawkins #73 of the Buffalo Bills signs autographs for fans on the way to the field during training camp at St. John Fisher University on July 29, 2026 in Rochester, New York. (Photo by Joe Hrycych/Getty Images) | Getty Images Pittsford, N.Y. | Dion Dawkins has had a revolving door of left guards next to him in his first nine seasons as a member of the Buffalo Bills. After the past two seasons with veteran David Edwards next door at left guard, the 2026 campaign will mark another new teammate for Dawkins alongside him on Buffalo’s front protecting Josh Allen and paving lanes for James Cook. Following Monday’s training camp practice, Dawkins was asked about this orientation of sorts for whomever might win the left guard job out of camp. His answer began with what it’s like going from a familiar linemate to a new piece next to him: “My life as a left tackle, I live on an island… I finally get someone to come on the island, and stays with me on that island… I know exactly where him and his family are going to be.” “For 10 years, I’ve had a different guard next to me in almost every year of my career and still been one of the best left tackles in the NFL.” When speaking directly about Alec Anderson and Austin Corbett — the two strongest candidates to win the left-guard gig out of camp, Dawkins said: “I know who my guys are, but I don’t know who they are as a left guard consistently throughout the duration of a season. We are learning, I am learning who the guys are on a day in and day out basis.” Dawkins shedding light on what is typically an overlooked element of the cohesion across an offensive line was so enlightening. His words should serve as a reminder — even to yours truly — that there’s much more than simply plugging a new player the starting lineup. The star left tackle later went deeper about all the mental prep that goes into playing offensive line in the NFL — from knowing how different defensive fronts lead to different blocking responsibilities, inside zone vs. outside zone, and the communication needed on, say, a five-or-seven-step drop screen play. He noted that communication — particularly with the left guard — is vital, even if it’s just learning how frequently they need to talk and in which situations to do so. Fascinatingly, Dawkins ended his interview by saying during camp and at practice before the season, he will “fake” panic before a snap, checking with the left-guard candidates to see how they react if he’s walking to the line anxiously communicating he doesn’t know the protection or play call. That is an awesome Jedi mind trick from Dawkins, the wily vet, to aid the development of and rapport with whomever is the starting left guard next to him on the Bills offensive line this season.
author: Chris Trapasso

title: Bills Mafia share strong opinions about Buffalo’s current uniform options
summary: Rumblers, we asked, and you answered. With the Buffalo Bills’ recently revealing their alternate uniforms to great debate, we wanted to know what some of the team’s biggest fans had to say about the franchise’s current uniform options. Specifically, which current Bills uniform do you like best? We’re not here to solve any debate because, […]
full_text: ORCHARD PARK, NEW YORK - JANUARY 04: Buffalo Bills fans celebrate during the fourth quarter against the New York Jets at Highmark Stadium on January 04, 2026 in Orchard Park, New York. (Photo by Jason Miller/Getty Images) | Getty Images Rumblers, we asked, and you answered. With the Buffalo Bills’ recently revealing their alternate uniforms to great debate, we wanted to know what some of the team’s biggest fans had to say about the franchise’s current uniform options. Specifically, which current Bills uniform do you like best ? We’re not here to solve any debate because, well, when it comes to uniforms in professional sports conversation will never end. People can look past most companies’ uniform decisions without so much as an eyebrow lift, at least after a first glance. Not when it comes to one’s favorite team — the threads you’re most likely to pay handsomely for and wear in public. The results were a bit surprising, and may reveal a lot about the generational makeup of Rumblings readers. With that little spoiler shared, can you guess which uniforms won our poll? Let’s dive in… In a paradigm shift of sorts, we’ll start at the bottom and work our way to the top. Why? That’s were I believe the biggest surprise waits. How do you feel about the NFL | Nike Rivals uniform? Well, if these results are accurate, no one likes them. No one as in ZERO percent of the vote went to those uniforms. It’s fascinating, but perhaps the main reason is due to superstitions. See, the team is 0-1 in those threads (hardly a fair sample size, BTW). Yet, even quarterback Josh Allen was a bit harsh on them in claiming they haven’t won in them — while defending the new alternate uniforms. Despite the dislike, fans would do well to embrace them since the NFL has teams wearing those uniforms for at least three consecutive seasons once released. It makes sense from a rivalry standpoint with each team hosting three division rivals every season. That leaves the Bills left to face the Miami Dolphins and New York Jets in Rivals wear. Would you wager they have a great shot to go 2-1 in them against the AFC East? It’s impossible to beat zero percent, though Buffalo’s Color Rush (red combos, all versions), uniforms came close with just 2% of the vote. It’s another surprising result, considering the Bills haven’t lost a game in those uniforms since the 2019 season. Overall, Buffalo is 7-2 in their Color Rush hues. Last season saw the team modify that look, going with red jerseys and white pants. It was a sharp presentation, but had many people thinking “Patriots colors” from the moment they saw the combo. The other reason this specific result is so surprising has to do with the next uniforms in our discussion. Here they are, the brand-new Nickel City alternates with just 6% of the vote. Why is this surprising? Simply because it beat out the Rivals and Color Rush combination. I don’t know about you, but it sure seems like a lot of fans have purchased those Rivals and Color Rush jerseys in recent seasons. Will even more folks buy-in and wear the Nickel City jerseys in 2026 and beyond? Look, the gray/grey base color is a big departure for the Bills most folks know. But it is a color that’s been part of the franchise’s brand since Day 1. I’ve written at length about my desire to see the team properly pay homage to the Bills’ first uniforms (those borrowed from the Detroit Lions), and these offer the closest thing yet. That said, they’re still very much nowhere near those first uniforms, and there’s a complete left turn in the form of a blue helmet bathed in a logo that departs massively away from the bison. All that we get on the alternate helmet is a horn and the streak. Interestingly, the team had told us there actually is an eye in the horn’s form, but I still have to force myself to see the horn as a horn, with an eye socket just beyond and below the bottom “tip.” Who among us even sees that horn as a horn, truthfully? Come on, you know you see only a goofy looking eyeball. They’re not fooling anyone. So, overall, those three uniform options received just a combined 8% of the total vote. That’s… not great. Here’s where the decisions get a bit muddled. My personal favorite unis in all forms, the Bills’ standing bison helmet/throwbacks, come in third place with 26% of the vote. I will always love a well-executed classic look, and these are among the NFL’s best tribute threads. They pay tribute to two very important eras of Bills football, both their AFL Championship years and those first few seasons as the newest members of the reformulated NFL. Those who dislike the standing bison look tend to say they look a bit boring. That’s understandable with a logo that’s completely red. However, their actual AFL tribute forms of these uniforms are the ones I’d choose for them to wear every game. Next we get to the standard uniforms. They land in second place with 32% of the vote. Enough people weighed in saying that these uniforms can’t be beat, and it’s tough to find a better standard uniform in the NFL. It’s an updated look that manages to combine a lot of what made the ‘90s uniforms great by combining the jersey and pants colors with the same type of helmet and logo Buffalo used from the late ‘70s through the early ‘80s. If you didn’t know it yet, the reason they switched from a white to red helmet was due to the rest of the AFC East having white helmets, and quarterback Joe Ferguson sometimes finding it difficult to pick out targets in traffic. Speaking of ‘90s uniforms, Rumblers LOVE them! Well, at least 34% of voters in this poll say that uniform combo is the best among the Bills’ current inventory. In truth, that uniform is different from the standard only due to the red helmet. But it works as a tribute, even if the helmet is the only change. Bills Mafia loves the red helmet. If you’re of a certain generation (aka the Bills Country era) you understand well how important they are to the team’s history — but how they’re also synonymous with four incredibly heartbreaking final games. It’s clear that One Bills Drive understands their fans want more of that look, and they’re set to bring the helmets back in the 2026 NFL season. That’s right, the red helmets are expected to return for a Christmas Day road game against the Denver Broncos. Due to several factors, we’re willing to bet Bills Mafia will have that game circled on their calendars! Think you’ve got what it takes to make a play with the Buffalo Bills in 2026? title: Dion Dawkins refers to CJ Gardner-Johnson as another “Tazmanian devil”
summary: In the movie Step Brothers, the line “did we just become best friends?” occurs 21 minutes in, and it appears that’s how long it took for a Dale Doback and Brennan Huff esque bond to form between Dion Dawkins and CJ Gardner-Johnson. After training camp practice on Monday morning at St. John Fisher University, Dawkins […]
full_text: ROCHESTER, NEW YORK - JULY 29: C.J. Gardner-Johnson #22 of the Buffalo Bills signs autographs for fans at St. John Fisher University during training camp on July 29, 2026 in Rochester, New York. (Photo by Joe Hrycych/Getty Images) | Getty Images In the movie Step Brothers , the line “did we just become best friends?” occurs 21 minutes in, and it appears that’s how long it took for a Dale Doback and Brennan Huff esque bond to form between Dion Dawkins and CJ Gardner-Johnson. After training camp practice on Monday morning at St. John Fisher University, Dawkins took to the podium to explain his newfound buddy on the defensive side of the ball who’s only been a member of the Bills since mid March. When asked about Gardner-Johnson — remember, Dawkins was one of the first to comment on the defensive back’s injury on August 1, Buffalo’s left tackle said: “I love the guy… he’s literally one of the teammates I didn’t know that I needed… he unlocked a whole side of the me that I’m like, bro, you’re my guy.” Expanding further thanks to a follow-up question, Dawkins explained that while he’s always himself, there has been a more buttoned-up professional version of Dawkins. With Gardner-Johnson, he feels he can “just be Dion” all the time: “I’m going to put myself first instead of putting everyone else first in certain situations outside of ball.” And apparently Gardner-Johnson has helped him realize the importance of doing that, particularly as he enters the 10th year of his NFL career. Gardner-Johnson is an eight-year veteran. When explaining his new teammate having such a quick, positive impact on his mind space, Dawkins playfully referred to Gardner-Johnson as another “Tazmanian devil” who’s free and exactly himself at all times. Sometimes you just click with someone right away. That appears to be the case for new teammates Dawkins and Gardner-Johnson, two free spirits who happen to be darn good football players.

title: Josh Allen mostly sharp in rain-soaked fourth Buffalo Bills training camp practice
summary: Pittsford, N.Y. | Rain accompanied the start of the Buffalo Bills fourth training camp practice at St. John Fisher University in the immaculate town of Pittsford outside of Rochester, and it never stopped. The misty drizzle intensified to a steady rain near the end of practice, yet the elements hardly impacted the play of Josh […]
full_text: ROCHESTER, NEW YORK - JULY 29: Josh Allen #17 of the Buffalo Bills addresses the media following practice during training camp at St. John Fisher University on July 29, 2026 in Rochester, New York. (Photo by Joe Hrycych/Getty Images) | Getty Images Pittsford, N.Y. | Rain accompanied the start of the Buffalo Bills fourth training camp practice at St. John Fisher University in the immaculate town of Pittsford outside of Rochester, and it never stopped. The misty drizzle intensified to a steady rain near the end of practice, yet the elements hardly impacted the play of Josh Allen. Sure, a few balls slipped through the fingers of his targets — like rookie Skyler Bell, Dalton Kincaid, and Jackson Hawes in red-zone work. Heck, there was even a slightly wobbly, minimally under-thrown checkdown to James Cook in 11-on-11. Otherwise, Allen was surgical in slippery elements that were far from ideal. I’ll focus on Allen first before providing more notes from my observations at practice on Monday morning: Josh Allen Allen found Keon Coleman in the front corner of the end zone in 7-on-7 red-zone work. The throw was a tight-window laser, and Coleman gracefully toe-tapped for the score. After a pair of high-caliber pass breakups — of the diving then leaping variety — from Max Hairston and Cole Bishop, Allen rolled left in a scramble drill and somehow located Khalil Shakir among a sea of defenders for a touchdown. Interestingly, as the backup quarterbacks took their turns in red-zone work early in practice, I noticed Allen talking body movements — like giving route-running guidance and what he’s looking for — with Bell and DJ Moore. I’ve been at camp in all of Allen’s NFL seasons, and I don’t remember him getting that detailed with receivers after a session. Wasn’t contentious. Just thorough. Besides Kincaid’s easy drop during the heaviest rain of practice, he and Allen were locked in together — the veteran tight end snagged a laser through a microscopic window from Allen on a flag route in 11-on-11 red zone work that drew a major celebration from the rest of the offense. Dee Alford made the play of the day on defense, with a full extension diving pass breakup on an end-zone target that came after Allen rolled right out of the pocket. In what appeared to be calculated play-action work in the red zone, Allen found Bell over the middle for a touchdown. The running backs do seem somewhat more involved in the pass game, and through the rain, Allen delivered a bit of a wobbler to James Cook on a wheel that featured tremendous placement and concentration from the running back to collect the football and get his feet in bounds for six despite tight coverage. There was a vintage Allen moment late in practice when he pumped left, looked right, reversed his field back to the left — nearly taking out half the team watching the rep behind the play — before he found Moore standing all alone in the back left corner of the end zone. In what was Allen’s last throwing rep of the day, he faded away from a throw with Javon Solomon closing in from his left… and I thought it was a clear throwaway. The ball landed directly in the arms of Dion Dawkins for a score on the trick play. Miscellaneous notes & observations Tight ends coach Rob Boras got hands-on in the opening minutes of practice during a blocking drill, even giving tips to Dawson Knox on footwork. Kincaid did go down for a moment — but turns out it was not due to his knee at all: UPDATE: Dalton Kincaid’s knee is good. #BillsMafia @BuffaloPlus pic.twitter.com/vqVL47skNJ — Dan Fetes (@danfetes) August 3, 2026 Davison Igbinosun is skiiiinnnnny. I know the new trend at cornerback is lighter/faster. But in seeing IGB in person for the first time I was taken aback as to how narrow his midsection is. Cole Bishop was a blanket in coverage today — beyond his red-zone pass breakup. He made life difficult for all the tight ends when the ball was thrown their way. Phidarian Mathis made his presence felt in the run game on more than one occasion. Late in practice, he erupted through the line of scrimmage for what would’ve amounted to a tackle for loss and was pretty animated afterward. Justifiably so. I can’t believe Michael Hoecht tore his Achilles in early November 2025. He looks totally spry and there’s no hitch in his giddy-up whatsoever. He and Dawkins had quality battles all morning. Everyone is raving about Kaleb Elarms-Orr, from Bills staffers, to fellow media, to his teammates, and the common theme is that he does not act nor play like a rookie. Deone Walker was wearing his pads but did work off to the side, never taking part in individual or team drills. No injury update was given by the team. Keleki Latu took the opening 11-on-11 rep with the first team split out at wide receiver. That was his only snap I saw with the first team in the team session, but that development is noteworthy nonetheless. Sam Franklin Jr. was very active all morning — he took some first-team reps alongside Cole Bishop and was sprinkled in with the second team. He had a pass breakup on a Kyle Allen throw but was beaten on a few reps by Kincaid with the 1s. Jalon Kilgore’s strong start to camp continued. He knocked away a Kyle Allen pass near the goal line and primarily aligned at nickel. The Bills are expected to be in full pads tomorrow before a (closed to the public & media) walkthrough on Wednesday before two more SJFU practices ahead of the Return of the Blue & Red scrimmage on Saturday evening at the new Highmark Stadium.

title: Buffalo Bills 2026 scouting report: TE Jackson Hawes
summary: The Buffalo Bills were fantastic when they used three tight ends last season. In fact, only the Los Angeles Rams were better on offense when using heavy personnel groupings, as the Bills came in second in EPA per play out of 13 personnel at 15.7. They were also exceptional when using two tight ends, and […]
full_text: HOUSTON, TX - NOVEMBER 20: Jackson Hawes #85 of the Buffalo Bills runs a route during an NFL football game against the Houston Texans at NRG Stadium on November 20, 2025 in Houston, Texas. (Photo by Cooper Neill/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Buffalo Bills were fantastic when they used three tight ends last season. In fact, only the Los Angeles Rams were better on offense when using heavy personnel groupings, as the Bills came in second in EPA per play out of 13 personnel at 15.7. They were also exceptional when using two tight ends , and they did so more than any other team in football. An increase in usage for Buffalo’s tight ends means that the team has to carry multiple top-flight options at the position. Or, perhaps it’s because the Bills have multiple excellent options at tight end that the team chooses to forgo spread formations, using multiple tight ends instead. Coming into the 2025 season, the top two names on the tight end depth chart received most of the attention. As the season progressed, however, it became apparent that the third man on that chart was no slouch. In today’s edition of “91 players in 91 days,” we discuss one of the best blocking tight ends in the NFL. _____________________________________________________________________________ Name: Jackson Hawes Number: 85 Position: TE Height/Weight: 6’4”, 253 pounds Age: 25 (26 on 12/6/2026) Experience/Draft: 2; selected by Buffalo in the fifth round (No. 173 overall) of the 2025 NFL Draft College: Georgia Tech Acquired: Fifth-round draft choice Financial situation (per Spotrac): Hawes enters the second year of his rookie contract, a four-year pact worth $4,520,216 overall. For the 2026 season, Hawes’ cap hit is $1,085,054 if he makes the 53-man roster. Buffalo carries a dead-cap charge of $240,162 if he’s released. 2025 Recap: Hawes likely couldn’t have dreamed of having a better rookie season. He played 43% of the Bills’ snaps on offense during the regular season, and he even made eight starts in his first year in the NFL. With Dalton Kincaid once again missing time due to myriad injury woes, it opened up some additional opportunity for Hawes, and he thrived in his role. While offensive lineman Alec Anderson served as a frequent extra blocker during the 2024 season, he isn’t a threat to catch passes like Hawes is. And while Hawes might not be the same caliber receiver as Kincaid or Dawson Knox, defenses clearly have to pay more attention to him in the passing game than they would Anderson. Hawes caught 16 passes for 187 yards and three touchdowns on 19 targets, so he made the most of his opportunities. He played in both of Buffalo’s playoff games, as well, but he wasn’t targeted in either contest. Pro Football Focus called Hawes Buffalo’s “secret superstar,” and he earned an 83.1 overall grade, which was second among all rookies and second behind only Josh Allen on Buffalo’s entire offense, as well. Positional outlook: Hawes is once again joined by Kincaid and Knox at tight end. Shane Zylstra and Keleki Latu are also on the current roster. 2026 Offseason: Hawes is healthy, having participated in all offseason work, and now training camp. 2026 Season outlook: Initially, I assumed the Bills would let Dawson Knox go, save the cap space that would come from releasing him, and move forward with Hawes as their second tight end. However, after Buffalo and Knox agreed on a renegotiated contract, that thought became a moot point. Hawes is slated to go into the 2026 season in essentially the same role he had last season, as he’ll be the run-block tight end who likely replaces Kincaid in the Bills’ 22 personnel grouping. With the improvements Knox has made as an in-line blocker throughout his career, pairing him with a legit mauler like Hawes gives Buffalo a huge advantage in the run game. They can’t tip their hand by replacing Kincaid on every running play, however, so it’s not like Hawes won’t share the field with Buffalo’s TE1 at all. There’s even a chance that Hawes does some work out of the backfield in an H-Back or fullback alignment now that Reggie Gilliam is with the New England Patriots. Head coach Joe Brady and offensive coordinator Pete Carmichael have some options, and even if Hawes stays steady and plays around 40% of the offensive snaps again, I expect that he’ll be a big part of what the team wants to do. Might Hawes do some more as a receiver? It’s possible, but ideally, the Bills just have a healthy Kincaid available to see more targets, which would allow Hawes to continue doing what he does best — mauling would-be tacklers at the point of attack. There’s room for growth as a receiver, and Hawes already showed that he has reliable hands in a small sample size last year. Unless you play in a fantasy football league that rewards blockers, Jackson Hawes likely isn’t someone you should pick. However, if you were starting a real football team, Hawes is exactly the kind of tight end you want on your side. He’s a lock for the roster and his role is clear moving forward.

title: 2026 Season Opener Countdown: 40 Days Remaining
summary: Here at Cat Scratch Reader we have counted down the final 100 days leading up to the Carolina Panthers season opener by for at least the past ten years. We’ve always done this by highlighting the current player on the roster whose jersey number matches the day on the countdown. This year, we decided to […]
full_text: 8 Dec 1996: Linebacker Lamar Lathon of the Carolina Panthers celebrates during a game against the San Francisco 49ers at 3Com Park in San Francisco, California. The Panthers won the game, 30-24. | Getty Images Here at Cat Scratch Reader we have counted down the final 100 days leading up to the Carolina Panthers season opener by for at least the past ten years. We’ve always done this by highlighting the current player on the roster whose jersey number matches the day on the countdown. This year, we decided to change that up a bit by counting down our own list of the Top 100 Panthers of all time. This does not correspond to jersey number, does not need to be somebody who wore a jersey, and will in no way be controversial. #40. Lamar Lathon Lamar Lathon started his career as an off-ball linebacker out of the University of Houston. The hometown Houston Oilers selected Lathon 15th overall in the 1990 NFL Draft. After a rookie season that saw mostly backup and special teams duties, he took the starting role at strong side linebacker in his second season. That year just so happened to be his best year in Houston, logging 116 tackles, two sacks, three interceptions, and six forced fumbles. A couple years later, an injury and a coaching change cost him that starting role. During training camp in 1993, Lathon suffered a broken forearm. Newly hired defensive coordinator Buddy Ryan kept Joe Bowden as the starter even after Lathon was healthy. Lathon moved to more of an edge rusher role the following season, notching 8.5 sacks. Despite showing some pass rush promise, Houston released Lathon after the season. The Carolina Panthers had just come into existence in 1995 as Lathon hit the open market. Defensive coordinator Vic Fangio liked Lathon’s fit in his 3-4 as an outside linebacker, and the team signed Lathon. The team was rewarded with one of Lathon’s best seasons to that point. He then followed up that campaign with a 1996 season full of accolades. He combined with fellow edge rusher Kevin Greene to terrorize opposing quarterbacks. Lathon alone logged 77 tackles and 13.5 sacks (still good for fifth most in franchise history for a single season), leading to him being named to the Pro Bowl and All Pro Second Team. He even got seventh place in the Defensive Player of the Year voting, proving how dominant he truly was. After Kevin Greene left for San Francisco the following year, Lathon’s production took a huge hit, as did his health. He started the year with foot and ankle injuries and suffered a major knee injury in Week 3. Though he played through the injury for most of the rest of the season, the knee would need major reconstructive surgery during the offseason. Lathon tried to return the following season, but being 31 years old and coming off a major knee injury ultimately ended his career. Lamar Lathon showed incredible ability as both an off ball linebacker and edge rusher, essentially being a Micah Parsons or Abdul Carter before they were even born. His true home, like Parsons and Carter, was at edge. The “Salt and Pepper” combination of Greene and Lathon drove the Panthers defense to be second in points allowed, leading the team to a 12-4 record and a NFC Championship Game appearance. Though his time in Carolina was cut short, his dominance for the then expansion franchise helped catapult the Panthers into the hearts of the people of Charlotte. For this contribution, Lamar Lathon earned the No. 40 spot on our countdown.

title: 2026 Season Opener Countdown: 41 Days Remaining
summary: Here at Cat Scratch Reader we have counted down the final 100 days leading up to the Carolina Panthers season opener for at least the past ten years. We’ve always done this by highlighting the current player on the roster whose jersey number matches the day on the countdown. This year, we decided to change […]
full_text: Carolina Panthers center Jeff Mitchell sets to block against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers November 6, 2005 in Tampa. The Panthers defeated the Bucs 34 - 14. (Photo by Al Messerschmidt/Getty Images) | Getty Images Here at Cat Scratch Reader we have counted down the final 100 days leading up to the Carolina Panthers season opener for at least the past ten years. We’ve always done this by highlighting the current player on the roster whose jersey number matches the day on the countdown. This year, we decided to change that up a bit by counting down our own list of the Top 100 Panthers of all time. This does not correspond to jersey number, does not need to be somebody who wore a jersey, and will in no way be controversial. #41. Jeff Mitchell Panthers stats: 78 games, 78 starts Career stats: 119 games, 118 starts After a stellar college career at Florida, center Jeff Mitchell was a fifth-round pick by the Baltimore Ravens in 1997. His career got off to a slow start as he didn’t see the field in his rookie season, but that quickly changed. Over the next three seasons he started 40 games for the Ravens. In his final season with the Ravens in 2000, Baltimore won the Super Bowl with Mitchell starting throughout the regular season and playoffs. After winning the Super Bowl, Jeff Mitchell signed with the Carolina Panthers in 2001. And if you’re a Panthers historian, you’ll ruefully recall the Panthers went 1-15 that year. Immediately after hoisting the Lombardi Trophy, Mitchell was snapping the ball to Chris Weinke for the league’s worst team while trying to open holes for running backs Richard Huntley (165 carries), Nick Goings (66), and the immortal Tim Biakabutuka (53). Talk about the best of times and the worst of times. But things would get much better for Jeff Mitchell from there. Over the next four seasons from 2002-2005 Carolina went 36-28, including two 11-win seasons and a Super Bowl appearance in 2003. Stalwart players from the 2003 Super Bowl squad like Mitchell deserve a place of respect in the minds of Panthers fans, and that’s exactly what he’s getting today. Over five seasons with the Panthers he started all 78 regular season games in which he played, missing just two games over that stretch. While he never made the Pro Bowl in his career, he was a capable, steady, and solid at center. Good centers make the entire offensive line better and make life easier for their quarterbacks, and Mitchell was very good at that for half a decade in Carolina.

title: Will Patrick Jones II be the next man up?
summary: The Carolina Panthers signed Patrick Jones II during the 2025 free agency period to bolster a pass rushing unit that had been struggling for years. The plan was for him to have the opportunity to take the next step forward as a starter in the NFL while providing a strong veteran presence for the rookies […]
full_text: CHARLOTTE, NORTH CAROLINA - OCTOBER 5: Patrick Jones II #91 of the Carolina Panthers runs onto the field during player introductions prior to the game against the Miami Dolphins at Bank of America Stadium on October 5, 2025 in Charlotte, North Carolina. (Photo by Kara Durrette/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Carolina Panthers signed Patrick Jones II during the 2025 free agency period to bolster a pass rushing unit that had been struggling for years. The plan was for him to have the opportunity to take the next step forward as a starter in the NFL while providing a strong veteran presence for the rookies that the Panthers would ultimately select in the next month’s NFL Draft. Part of that plan held up to contact with the rest of the season. The Panthers drafted Nic Scourton and Princely Umanmielen with the 51st and 77th overall picks. Jones started four games for the Panthers before requiring a season ending back surgery. His absence allowed Scourton to flourish with an expanded role and develop into a fan favorite and potential star of the 2026 season. Scourton didn’t even make it out of training camp before suffering his own season ending injury this season. Panthers fans are now largely expecting Jones to step back into his starting role from last season and fill the gap until Scourton’s ultimate return. This is the obvious answer to the Reacts question we posed last week, but it is not an answer that is guaranteed to satisfy Panthers fans once the season actually starts. Jones only has nine starts and 13 sacks in his five years in the league, including his injury-shortened year with the Panthers. He had seven sacks in his contract year with the Minnesota Vikings, showing the potential that earned him his free agency contract with Carolina. But that potential is really all we have to work with right now when projecting Jones’ 2026 season. Until he or Umanmielen can capitalize on their potentials, it may well be that signing Jaelen Phillips and losing Scourton to injury may be another case of one step forward, one step back for defensive coordinator Ejiro Evero’s perennially hamstrung defense. title: Chicago Bears Question of the Day: What offseason narrative is most tired?
summary: It’s been a long offseason, but real football is back. In less than two weeks time the Bears will be taking the field against the Cleveland Browns to open the preseason. Already a handful of days into training camp and some players are already trying to reset narratives that have occurred throughout the summer break. […]
full_text: It’s been a long offseason, but real football is back. In less than two weeks time the Bears will be taking the field against the Cleveland Browns to open the preseason. Already a handful of days into training camp and some players are already trying to reset narratives that have occurred throughout the summer break. A few that I have seen pop up consistently since season’s end: Luther Burden will be the Bears #1 WR in 2026 and beyond Subtext, Rome Odunze will not be Dayo Odeyingbo and Grady Jarrett were flops Subtext, these two players will be minimal contributors in 2026 and will get cut next offseason Kyler Gordon’s soft tissue injuries are a major problem Subtext, the Bears are assessing replacements for him after the 2026 season at NB The Bears have problems at LT and C Subtext, Braxton Jones, Jedrick Wills, Garrett Bradbury, and Logan Jones will be worse than their 2025 starting counterparts The Bears will regress in 2026 Subtext, their defense, turnover differential, and 4th quarter comebacks are unsustainable and will lead to a regression to the mean There might be others, but these were some that I consistently gleaned from the media, other blogs, and even here at WCG. So which of these are the most tired? Which do we need to set straight and pull out of the offseason echo chamber? This is the basis of this week’s question: Which offseason Bears narrative is most tired? For me, it’s the conversation around Grady Jarrett and Dayo Odeyingbo. I get it — these two failed to live up to their lofty contracts in 2025. A reminder of each contract below: Grady Jarrett signed a 3 year, $42.75 million deal including cap hits of $18.9 and $16.8 million in 2026 and 2027 (but only $4 million in dead money in 2027) His annual average salary of $14.5 million ranks 24th in the NFL amongst IDL. Dayo Odeyingbo signed a 3 year, $48 million deal including cap hits of $20.5 and $19.5 million in 2026 and 2027 (but only $4.5 million in dead money in 2027) His average annual salary of $16 million ranks 29th in the NFL among Edge rushers. Neither of these are small cap hits, and one might argue that they kept the Bears from pursuing other defensive upgrades this offseason. I get it. But I think we are confusing sunken cost with a player that is no longer on the team. In case the offseason narrative has convinced you otherwise, Grady Jarrett and Dayo Odeyingbo are still members of the 2026 Chicago Bears — and I think they are both severely underrated for what they can do for the 2026 defense. Let’s start with the veteran, Grady Jarrett. Jarrett came in with a pedigree and something to prove after his long tenure with the Atlanta Falcons came to a close following a cut in March of 2025. Ryan Poles viewed him as the interior rusher and veteran presence that the Bears DL desperately needed. Unfortunately, in 14 games last season, Jarrett only tallied 1.5 sacks, 39 tackles, 1 TFL, 8 QB hits, and 3 PDs. Those numbers aren’t enough to justify his cost. But that’s not to say that Jarrett doesn’t have anything left in the tank. Jarrett himself has owned up to his 2025 season by saying: No, so we hear it, man. But it also comes with the job, you know, it comes with the job. And at the end of the day, we gotta really take it personal and get back to work. Even if sometimes your best ain’t good enough. So you gotta find out ‘Where can I be better at? Jarrett isn’t a stranger to down years, either. He also isn’t a stranger to bounce backs. In 2021, his age 28 season, Jarrett had a down year following two Pro Bowl seasons, where he only notched 1 sack, and 3 TFLs in 17 games. The next season, Jarrett responded with 6 sacks and 12 TFLs — a massive improvement that shows his ability to right the course. Additionally, he has noted being in better shape this offseason, after working through a knee injury that sidelined him for portions of 2025. So it should not be outlandish to expect a better Grady Jarrett in 2026, something that I have seen consistently discounted this offseason. As for Dayo Odeyingbo. It’s safe to say that Dayo has become the newest punching bag for Bears fans. Reports of a “Motivated Dayo” has become a sarcastic refrain for fans that expect him to be a non contributor in 2026. While I understand why people are questioning his impact, I think it is far too premature to write him off at this stage in his career. Dayo was but 26 years old with 3.5 seasons under his belt when he joined the Bears last offseason. Odeyingbo has draft pedigree and prototypical size for the position as a 2nd round pick that measures at 6’-5” and 282 lbs. While he still hasn’t put together a spectacular season in his career, he mustered 11 sacks, 16 TFLs, and 34 QB hits in his age 24 and 25 seasons combined — numbers that suggest a jump still may be warranted. Still, in his 8 starts in 2026, Odeyinbo struggled to string together strong performances and eventually ended with 1 sack and 2 TFLs — disappointing numbers that have led many to write him off. I think that’s a mistake. Odeyingbo had seen steady improvement under the tutelage of Gus Bradley, and found himself under a new defensive scheme for the first time in his career in 2025. When revisiting tape, I saw a player that frequently looked indecisive — which often led to him playing slower. I see an extra year under Allen, an offseason of good health, and more “motivation” as being key to a turnaround for Dayo. Will he ever be a 10 sack player? Unlikely. But to write him off would be a mistake. I think there is a very good chance of him tallying 6+ sacks and being a powerful counterpunch to Austin Booker’s speed/length. In total — I suppose my primary gripe is that we simply cannot write off two players after one season on a team and defense that feature a lot of new. I’ll eat my words if we continue to see the same issues 4-5 games into 2026. But until then, let’s give these two a chance to change the narrative. Now it’s your turn! Which offseason Bears narrative is most tired? Sound off in the comments!

summary: Welcome to SB Nation Reacts, a survey of fans across the NFL. Throughout the year we ask questions of the most plugged-in Bears fans and fans across the country. Heading into the offseason, three-fifths of the Chicago Bears’ offensive line were locked in. Left guard Joe Thuney, a 2025 Pro Bowler, All-Pro, and winner of […]
full_text: Jul 31, 2026; Lake Forest, IL, USA; Chicago Bears players practice during Training Camp at Halas Hall. Mandatory Credit: Kamil Krzaczynski-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect Welcome to SB Nation Reacts, a survey of fans across the NFL. Throughout the year we ask questions of the most plugged-in Bears fans and fans across the country. Heading into the offseason, three-fifths of the Chicago Bears’ offensive line were locked in. Left guard Joe Thuney, a 2025 Pro Bowler, All-Pro, and winner of the Protecter of the Year award, was recently named the best guard in the NFL by Pro Football Focus . Right tackle Darnell Wright is one of the best young tackles in the game and is coming off a second-team All-Pro nod. And right guard Jonah Jackson, a former Pro Bowler, bounced back in a huge way as he was reunited with Ben Johnson and was just named PFF’s 18th-best guard in the league. We’re now a week into training camp, and Chicago’s starting five is coming into focus. With Drew Dalamn retiring, center was up in the air, and after trading for Garrett Bradbury and drafting Logan Jones, it seemed like a camp battle was set up, but recent comments from Ben Johnson could allude to the battle being settled. On Saturday, tight end Cole Kmet said the transition from Dalman to Bradbury has been “flawless,” and Johnson was asked his take on that earlier today. “Yeah, he’s extremely impressive,” Johnson said . “He’s super smart. H’s played high-level football in a couple of places now, and he’s brought that here. I think what stands out the most is he’s got an elite level of communication. He is loud. He is decisive. He does a great job with seeing the defense… We’re cooking right now with him out there, so, really pleased.” But while Bradbury has received all the number one reps, left tackle has had a bit of a rotation during training camp. Braxton Jones got just about all the first-string left tackle reps in the offseason, but last week, the Bears gave Kiran Amegadjie and Jedrick Wills Jr. each a day with the ones. Jones was back with the starters today, but with pads finally on this week, I would not be surprised to see Amegadjie and Wills get some more work with the starting offense. Ben Johnson discussed what he wants to see from his left tackles this week. “It’s consistency for me,” he said. “We’re judging the ability to block these defensive ends one-on-one. And the ability to cut off on the backside of our wide zone scheme is huge for us. I think each one of those guys is probably a little bit stronger in certain areas than the other guy. And I think when we look at it, it’s who’s the most consistent player that we feel like is going to help us on a weekly basis.” Johnson was asked about Wills, who sat out last season, and he said that Wills has had a “good start” to camp. “Like I said, Braxton’s been great,” Ben continued. “Jed’s firmly in the mix. Kiran got some reps with the ones. I think Theo’s [Benedet] worth mentioning as well. I mean, I think we got a really good group of guys that continue to ascend and get better, so hopefully it’s a really difficult decision for us.” The Bears open their preseason slate on August 15 against the Cleveland Browns, and while Johnson was noncommittal on playing starters, those three preseason games and two joint practices will be a factor in who wins the left tackle job. title: Cash, Stash, or Slash: Rome Odunze
summary: As we continue our series of Cash, Stash, or Slash, we are going to look at Rome Odunze next, who I think you could argue is one of the most fascinating cases on the team. Odunze has had two good seasons at this point of his career, but there have been factors keeping him from […]
full_text: LAKE FOREST, ILLINOIS - JULY 29: Rome Odunze #15 of the Chicago Bears looks on during Chicago Bears Training Camp at Halas Hall on July 29, 2026 in Lake Forest, Illinois. (Photo by Geoff Stellfox/Getty Images) | Getty Images As we continue our series of Cash, Stash, or Slash, we are going to look at Rome Odunze next, who I think you could argue is one of the most fascinating cases on the team. Odunze has had two good seasons at this point of his career, but there have been factors keeping him from reaching the heights that the Bears fans thought he could reach when they drafted him in the top ten of the 210 NFL Draft. With Odunze, we know Slash isn’t one of the options to consider, but is this a man that the Bears should hammer down next offseason and make sure he’s locked into a contract? Let’s take a look at Odunze. Rome Odunze: Stash I think “wait and see” is a key aspect here for Odunze due to so many factors. Let’s look at all of them. One, if we are being honest, he hasn’t been as good as we all hoped. That doesn’t mean he’s been bad; he’s been a solid WR and one that Caleb Williams looks to often, but he hasn’t been an elite catcher of the football that can change a game. That’s what the Bears drafted, and he hasn’t been that. The injuries are also something to keep in mind. I know Odunze tried to clarify the situation with his foot and that it’s not some chronic disaster, but it did cost him 5 games last year, and he was compromised in other games he played. Will this be a lingering problem for him or will it be completely behind him? The Bears definitely would like to see a clean, fairly healthy season from Odunze. Three, how good does Luther Burden look this year? If Burden breaks out like many people think he could be, if he’s a true WR1 and an elite player, that’s going to impact how you want to treat Odunze moving forward. If Burden is inconsistent and shows flashes but doesn’t put it all together, that’s going to make Odunze more valuable to the franchise. Right now, there are simply too many factors to consider before the Bears can make a decision on what to do with Odunze. If Odunze breaks out and has a massive season with 1500 yards receiving and 15 touchdowns, then yes, sure, pay him next year and be excited he’s become the player you thought he could be. There are plenty of NFL analytic nerds that say that all the numbers are there for Odunze to break out and take several steps forward in 2026. Personally, I don’t see it. I think Odunze is a good player. I think Odunze is going to settle in as an excellent WR2, but I just don’t know if he has shown that he is going to step into that WR1 role. As always, I hope I’m wrong. I hope Odunze proves that he’s an elite receiver. I think he’s good to very good and makes him a great WR2 for the Bears or another team if the Bears do move on down the road. If I’m right and Odunze has another good season, but it isn’t an elite season, I think he’s still a “stash” a year from now. If I’m the Bears, and Odunze has a good year, I would pick up the 5th year option next year and let the 2027 season play out as well, and then you can decide if you want ot extend Odunze after the 2027 season before he heads into his 5th year in Chicago. A fifth-year option for Odunze in Chicago should fall somewhere between $18 and $24 million for that season. Right now, the range that Odunze could get paid is massive. If he breaks out and becomes an elite receiver, the value of his contract is going to be at least $30 million a year, if not $35 million. If Odunze continues to look like the solid, but not spectacular receiver he has looked like the first two seasons of his career and the Bears do want to keep him around as part of the team, Odunze’s salary should be somewhere between $15 and $20 million a year. That’s a $20 million gap in average yearly salary depending on how Odunze plays. With that kind of difference, I would like to have two more years of data before I decide what kind of contract to offer him. It’s also possible that if you wait two more seasons, Burden and Colston Loveland become an incredible duo and maybe even Jahdae Walker or Savion Thomas become reliable targets where Odunze becomes expendable. There are so many factors surrounding Odunze that trying to figure out his contract at this point is nearly impossible. Don’t just wait one season; wait two seasons. Get as much data on this offense with Burden, Loveland, Odunze, and the others, and figure out who the key pieces are that have to be around for years to come. Odunze is the most clear “Stash” on the team right now.

title: Ryan Poles and the NFL Draft: Is he good enough? Part 1
summary: Introduction One of the reasons I love the Windy City Gridiron community is because the members try to have engaged and thoughtful conversations in the comment threads, and the quality of discussion attempts objectivity and evidence-based reasoning even if all of us let our emotions come into play (we are, after all, fans). One question […]
full_text: Introduction One of the reasons I love the Windy City Gridiron community is because the members try to have engaged and thoughtful conversations in the comment threads, and the quality of discussion attempts objectivity and evidence-based reasoning even if all of us let our emotions come into play (we are, after all, fans). One question that has been asked in different forms repeatedly is how does Ryan Poles compare to prior Chicago general managers in terms of his skill at drafting? To answer this question, I needed not only to look at the draft records of Phil Emery and Ryan Pace, but I also needed external reference points who succeeded in steering a team to at least one championship. I chose Jason Licht’s first three years, who took his team to the Super Bowl after a long stretch to get there, and Howie Roseman (widely considered the exemplar of NFL general managers) beginning when he resumed personnel control in 2016. I chose them because like Poles (and also Pace), they drafted quarterbacks within the top two picks of the draft over their first three years and because they had idiosyncrasies that reminded me of Poles. Licht spent a high pick on a special teamer (Robert Aguayo with a second-round pick) and Roseman lacked a first-round pick in one of his first three years. Methodology This next section gets a little dense, and is mostly for my fellow football nerds. For each “general manager interval”, all the players drafted will be compared to all players drafted from 2011-2020 at their same position and draft round; because of the distinct advantage of the first eleven spots in the NFL Draft, however, that is considered its own separate round (Round 1A). The first five years of each player’s career will be compared on at least four data points–games played in the first five years, games started in the first five years, and at least two forms of production. For players who have not yet played for five years, their performance to date will be prorated to that level, cross-checked by the available data on how two-year markers develop into five-year outcomes, and then noted in the text with the potential error range discussed. In the event of ties (for example, the player has 45 starts, but so do four other players in his round and position), the player will be credited with the highest possible position. These will then be averaged for the player’s Value Percentile. The only exception is with punters and kickers, who are excluded from this component. Each GM class and interval will then have all of their Value Percentiles averaged together, weighted by Chase Stuart’s Expected Value draft chart. Stuart was chosen because conventional draft trade charts disproportionately scale off as the draft continues. Notably, for this component the value spent on punter or kicker is applied, which therefore penalizes GMs who spend draft capital on these players. That is not an oversight in the methodology but rather a deliberate element of design. Most importantly, though, this means that GMs are evaluated based on the typical performance of the picks they actually made, and they therefore are not penalized for picks that they did not have. Each draft class (GM+Year) will then have a rank 0-100 that indicates how well the GM drafted compared to the rest of the league when considering draft position and available resources, with 50 being average and 100 being perfect. Note that this methodology does not penalize GMs for unbalanced trades nor does it reward GMs for trading efficiency–it is purely about how well the GM actually drafted. Reference Points Jason Licht: Licht took over in 2014 and his first pick was Mike Evans. The rest of that class was poor with the exception of Kevin Pamphile, but he was able to get an elite wide receiver and a starting tackle, which was enough to score a 62 for this class (which again, just means that by weight of draft expectation, his class averaged a performance in the 62nd percentile. 2015 saw Licht draft Jameis Winston, Donovan Smith, Ali Marpet, and Kwon Alexander among others players who left less of an impact. This yielded a 78th percentile score. Then the sail came off the rigging a bit, and Vernon Hargreaves, Noah Spence, and Robert Aguayo dragged down some late round magic that found four players all in the 60s for their draft spot. Still, this class was a 38. Overall, though, when weighted across all twenty draft picks, Jason Licht’s first three years on the job netted him a score of 61. This was a solid start to his career, but there was fluctuation up and down. Howie Roseman: After assuming personnel authority and bringing in a new head coach, Roseman quickly took his team to a championship and strung together eight of ten winning seasons to date (including a second championship). Despite these accomplishments, his first year drafting on his own brought in modest returns (59), but notably every pick in that draft besides one of the three 7th-rounders was at least a little above average. 2017 was more up and down, and it came in at a 54. However, 2018 was a stunningly competent draft despite not having a first-round pick. Every selection was at the 79th percentile or higher, with an overall value of 82. Overall, Roseman was at a 61 in these three years, and it was a 61 powered by 16 of 21 picks being above average and 10 picks outside of first two rounds being above the 70th percentile. Just quality throughout. The man crushes the draft. Phil Emery: If I’m honest about my own biases, I have always thought of Phil Emery as a man who was decent at drafting but who was undone by one or two bad picks and a terrible selection at head coach. It turns out that I should have been more critical of his drafting. His first year was torpedoed by taking Shea McClellin, but the reality is that only Alshon Jeffrey was an above-average pick–this year was a 36. Most of 2013 was solid, but the back-to-back misses on Bostic (23rd percentile) and Green (25th percentile) meant that even Kyle Long could only drag the class up to a 52. Finally, he hit with Kyle Fuller but every other pick in 2014 was at or below the 40th percentile, and he ended with a score of 43. Notably, even Fuller took a few years to bloom. His overall value? Also a 43. Ryan Pace: Part of me simply wants to use Ryan Pace as another reference point in assessing the current GM in Chicago, and to that regard it’s easy to simply report the overall results–across his seven years, his average score works out to be that he drafted in the 52nd percentile, or completely average. Given what he gave up to get some of those picks he made, it’s simple to make the argument that his drafts weren’t worth the trade capital, and that a pair of bad GM decisions plus the quarterback selections undid him. That’s all true. However, it’s worth looking at how those results came to be, because they are informative on many levels, some of which have significance for the current state of the Chicago Bears. That will be a distinct article, however, so those people who are tired of reading about Ryan Pace can simply skip it. For now, though, it’s worth pointing out that while there was a general upward trend after Matt Nagy replaced John Fox, that trend was fragile. Percent “Good” here refers to what percentage of picks were at least at the 50th percentile. Notably, the curve is consistent between the two measures despite the disproportionate value given the top picks. Ryan Poles While it only takes three years to judge a draft class, the Draft Codex that powers this work uses five-year and two-year intervals, so there will be a certain amount of projection in this assessment. However, 30% of the draft picks made by Ryan Poles from 2022-2024 have not played a snap in the league since 2024, and so it’s probably safe enough to say that their performances are set. Another 20% are already such outliers at their position (for better or worse) that any movement is unlikely to change their relative…
