title: These are the most consistent winners at Cowboys camp
summary: There aren’t that many Sundays remaining this calendar year without Dallas Cowboys football at the forefront of our collective minds, but this past Sunday was one of them as the team was off from training camp practice. The next time the Cowboys take the field in Oxnard will ratchet up the intensity with a new […]
full_text: There aren’t that many Sundays remaining this calendar year without Dallas Cowboys football at the forefront of our collective minds, but this past Sunday was one of them as the team was off from training camp practice. The next time the Cowboys take the field in Oxnard will ratchet up the intensity with a new look as the pads will come on for the first time. Through three unpadded practices, there has been a flurry of takeaways that back up the way this team was positioned to go full speed ahead into nothing but football activities without any contract disputes or other drama lingering during the offseason. Rookies, veterans, and roster dark horses alike have all had standout moments. Still early enough in camp, now is a good time to remind fans that one of the best ways to carry any camp insights into anything actually meaningful for the regular season is to not get caught up in individual reps that show a player trending upwards or down, but rather be patient and wait to see the players that string together multiple reps, and then multiple practices, in a row. Let’s take a look at three players that have proven themselves in this regard, and what it means for not only them but the big picture of Brian Schottenheimer’s team in year two of his culture build. WR George Pickens If you were to ask yourself what single player anywhere on the Cowboys roster would benefit the most from having the type of reserved, locked-in on football offseason they have had, George Pickens would be a fantastic answer. Pickens was the source of the one contract related thing that played out, but it came and went without the Cowboys doing their usual thing of trying to drag down a players perception through the media. This turned out to be the right idea, because Pickens has been balling out at training camp, doing exactly what a player being asked to prove it on a franchise tag should be doing. Pickens has been so good that even some of the encouraging practice reports from Cowboys defensive backs have come with the asterisk that Pickens is still mostly getting the best of everyone in coverage. The Cowboys were forced to take a lot of shots down the field in the pass game last season from a trailing position thanks to their hapless defense. Even still in a lot of these moments, Pickens found a way to come down with highlight reel catches, and also had the juice in the short passing game to put up a career high in YAC. The thought of the Cowboys offense being on the field in a whole lot more neutral positions where defenses have to respect all levels of the passing game as well as the run (where Jaydon Blue and Phil Mafah would both be “honorable mentions” to make this consistency list) is a great one for Cowboys fans and scary one for defenses, especially with how dialed in Pickens has been from the first practice in Oxnard. 🔬 no other way for me to say this other than to say it: genuinely, through three practices, George Pickens is locked in every single rep — whether he gets the ball or not (decoy routes, blocking) and, when he does get the ball, you’d think he’s playing in a game TODAY.… — Patrik [No C] Walker (@VoiceOfTheStar) August 1, 2026 WR Ryan Flournoy Adding yet another layer to how dynamic the Dallas pass attack can be, the first inkling of this is that CeeDee Lamb is not even on this list despite his own strong start to camp, but rather a third-year player with the arrow pointing up that Lamb himself gave a recent endorsement to – saying he can be a 1,000 yard receiver in this offense. That would be none other than Ryan Flournoy, who impressed in the third WR role in a way the Cowboys have been lacking for some time. Having two top-dog type receivers that should leave plenty of room for a third to take advantage of coverage mismatches is an area the Cowboys have been good at roster building before, but actually getting that third target to establish himself in a way that keeps the whole offense humming is where they’ve fallen short. Not only did the duo of Lamb and Pickens show signs of turning a corner in this way from that top-dog standpoint, but Flournoy in the WR3 role did as well in the new scheme installed by Schottenheimer and Klayton Adams last season. Flournoy’s crispness as a route runner has stood out from the training camp highlight clips, giving the Cowboys a trio of players that can win all over the field. A lot of defenses around the league are preparing right now for how to play against heavy personnel and multiple tight ends on the field at the same time as a trend from last year expected to explode further in ‘26, but those on the Cowboys schedule better have answers for three legitimate threats at wide receiver first and foremost, before even considering any of their capable tight ends, too. Dak Prescott climbs up in the pocket and finds Ryan Flournoy for the touchdown. Flournoy just looks smooth so far this camp. pic.twitter.com/CFQ7uoZIgv — Joseph Hoyt (@JoeJHoyt) August 1, 2026 QB Dak Prescott When all three of your top wide receivers are standing out in camp, and the defense can’t actually hit anyone, naturally the reports on the quarterback play should be glowing as well. This has certainly been the case for Dak Prescott. What’s been particularly exciting about the glimpses we’ve seen from Prescott is the way the ball is coming out of his hands quickly, with confidence no matter where the ball is going. Be it the targets we’ve already discussed here like Lamb, Pickens, or Flournoy, or even a touchdown to UDFA TE Michael Trigg, the trust is there that if Dak puts the ball in the right spot his skill guys are going to come down with it. The extra touch of accuracy has been there from Prescott to make this point even stronger. The pressure the Cowboys offense was under to score every single time they were on the field in 2025 because of the defense was unlike anything a lot of fans have witnessed before. To have a defense that made the type of statistical season Prescott had an afterthought was malpractice, but now the question shifts back to Prescott in one important way too. Dak has not played a full season in consecutive years since his first four as a starter from 2016-2019. Based on just the little bit we’ve seen in Oxnard so far, Prescott is in full command of the offense at a level that will be nearly impossible for any QB2 to come in and replicate. The Cowboys will need their field general to stay healthy, and having as many answers as he’s found in the pass game at the start of camp is an exciting way to forecast a big season where he does stay healthy, the defense is at serviceable at worst, and the Cowboys improve on their 7-9-1 record as a result. Dak Prescott and Christian Parker sharing some laughs before practice pic.twitter.com/hF3xcVNy1d — Nick Harris (@NickHarrisFWST) July 30, 2026 What it all means Considering the fact the Cowboys pass offense has been a strength for years on end without any playoff success to show for it, but this time around has more depth popping up than usual, shows that even with an improved defense and the reliability of Javonte Williams at RB, this team will still flow through the passing game. We find ourselves saying repeatedly during the regular season that games in the NFL must be won and lost with your highest paid players on the field, which still favors the Cowboys offense and particularly Prescott. If one of the side effects of having a high-octane offense yet again is allowing the Dallas defense to disguise and mix things up more than they ever have before, thanks to Parker’s coaching and the new talent on that side of the ball, then that would be a welcome adjustment to give this team balance and find ways to win in all phases.

title: Cowboys 2026 roster rundown: The rest of the pack
summary: The Dallas Cowboys’ 2026 training camp began a week ago, with practice reports already rolling in for our ravenous consumption. As we shift to analyzing whatever nuggets we can get and speculating over decisions to come, we wanted to bring this rundown series to a close. Here are the players we didn’t get to, with […]
full_text: Jul 29, 2026; Oxnard, CA, USA; Dallas Cowboys receiver Traeshon Holden (80) catches the ball wearing a Guardian helmet cap at training camp at River Ridge Playing Fields. Mandatory Credit: Kirby Lee-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect The Dallas Cowboys’ 2026 training camp began a week ago, with practice reports already rolling in for our ravenous consumption. As we shift to analyzing whatever nuggets we can get and speculating over decisions to come, we wanted to bring this rundown series to a close. Here are the players we didn’t get to, with some brief thoughts on each of their prospects this summer. RB Dominic Richardson An undrafted rookie out of Tulsa, Richardson plays with power and aggression but lacks the speed and agility to make big plays. Also a willing pass blocker, he has traits that Klayton Adams likes and could help him compete for the bottom of the roster, especially if he can block and cover on special teams. But it will be tough overcoming this year’s competition, making the practice squad a more likely goal but still a big win if Richardson can get there. You can learn more about Richardson from his UDFA profile back in May. WRs Camden Brown, Traeshon Holden, Jaden Smith Brown and Smith are both new to Dallas. Brown is a UDFA out of Georgia Southern, who transferred there for his final college season after some slow years at Auburn. He’s got solid size and noted ball skills, but a lack of overall athleticism that helped him go undrafted last April. Smith is listed at 6’6”, so it’s not hard to guess why teams are interested. He went undrafted last season and signed with Tampa Bay, but spent the year on injured reserve. The Bucs waived him in early April, and he remained unemployed until Dallas signed him in June. If there’s an NFL player in that big body, Smith could move up the ladder quickly as a potential help for the redzone offense. Traeshon Holden is much closer to a roster spot than the other two, if last year means anything. One of the stars of the 2025 camp, Holden didn’t make the roster but spent the entire year on the practice squad. While most of last year’s WR cast is back, guys like Jonathan Mingo and KaVontae Turpin have looser grips on their offensive roles, with Mingo fighting for a spot in general. If Holden builds on last summer, he could be as competitive for the last WR spot as anyone. G/C Chris Glaser, G Nick Leverett Glaser and Leverett are both older prospects hoping that experience will help them find a way onto the roster, or at least the practice squad. Leverett was actually there for Dallas last season, signing in mid-November but never getting called up for a game. He does have 12 career starts, mostly with Tampa Bay in 2022. Glaser has less NFL experience, only starting one game for the Jets in 2023, but got more exposure this past spring in the UFL. Dallas signed Glaser shortly after backup center Matt Hennessy went to IR with an injury in OTAs, which may speak to Glaser’s intended role in 2026 or at least an area where he can compete. Both of these guys are longshots given the current interior line depth. T.J. Bass may be the primary backup at both guard and center, and Trevor Keegan was on last year’s roster before injury. With Nathan Thomas and Ajani Cornelius also offering some guard potential, Dallas is more likely to lean into their versatility so that they can go longer at offensive tackle. OTs Marcellus Johnson, Shiyazah Pete Speaking of tackles, these two prospects probably won’t benefit from an extra spot on the 53. If the Cowboys do go long there, it should be to facilitate having Thomas as the swing while Cornelius and Drew Shelton are protected on the roster for development. But at least with Pete, a 23-year-old UDFA who’s listed at a whopping 6’9”, you could see him worming his way into that developmental pipeline. Johnson, at 26 years old, would need to offer an immediate depth upgrade to find job security. DTs Kelvin Gilliam, Adedayo Odeleye Along with Tommy Dunn and Jay Toia, Gilliam and Odeleye are part of a young prospect pack trying to push for a final roster spot at defensive tackle. Gilliam and Dunn are both undrafted rookies, with Gilliam profiling as a stout run defender and surprisingly athletic for a near 300-pounder, though lacking much in the way of pass-rushing ability. He will likely be pushing for a similar role to what Jonathan Bullard and L.T. Overton will be serving in the scheme, with the practice squad his most likely destination. Odeleye is the Cowboys’ 91st player, coming from the International Player Pathway Program and giving the team a roster exemption for the offseason. He has been around professional football since 2021, when he played in the European League, and has since seen time in training camps and on practice squads for the Texans, Ravens, and, as of last year, the Cowboys. He turns 29 in October, so this summer may be the end of the line. LB Langston Patterson A starter and captain for most of the last three years at Vanderbilt, Patterson was the field general for the Commodores. He’s on the small side at a listed 6’0” and 229 lbs., and lacks any extra athleticism for it. But with high football IQ and leadership skills, plus experience playing the Mike, he could be competitive at what’s still a fairly thin ILB group for the Cowboys. CBs Trikwese Bridges, Ameer Speed Bridges and Speed are fighting for space in a crowded CB room. Bridges was a seventh-round pick last year by the Chargers, who Dallas claimed off waivers at final cuts. He appeared in 16 games and even started two due to injuries. Bridges had an interception in the Cowboys’ loss to the Broncos, but was otherwise not very notable in his playing time. Speed is new to Dallas but has been bouncing around the NFL since 2023, when he was a sixth-round pick by New England. He made the roster but was waived in late October, then claimed by the Colts. He also spent time on the Bears’ practice squad in 2024, when Matt Eberflus was their head coach. Eberflus had already been fired by the Cowboys months before they signed Speed in June. Both Bridges and Speed bring great size as corners, listed at 6’2” and 6’3” respectively. But with so many returning and new prospects for CB in camp this year, either will have to be a surprise this summer to move into the roster bubble. title: Depth and development have played key role in Broncos quick turnaround
summary: The Denver Broncos have swung big trades, reeled in top notch free agents, and drafted several quality contributors throughout the Sean Payton era. Boasting quality starters across the board, the Broncos have transformed from annual underperformers to touting the ability and talent to compete with any team in the National Football League. Securing back-to-back playoff […]
full_text: KANSAS CITY, MO - DECEMBER 25: Jahdae Barron #23 of the Denver Broncos runs out of the tunnel prior to an NFL football game against the Kansas City Chiefs at GEHA Field at Arrowhead Stadium on December 25, 2025 in Kansas City, Missouri. (Photo by Cooper Neill/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Denver Broncos have swung big trades, reeled in top notch free agents, and drafted several quality contributors throughout the Sean Payton era. Boasting quality starters across the board, the Broncos have transformed from annual underperformers to touting the ability and talent to compete with any team in the National Football League. Securing back-to-back playoff berths and their first division title in a decade, the Broncos’ outlook looks the brightest it has in ages. Overlooked, but equally as important, Payton and his staff have assembled a roaster loaded with depth in many areas. That has been critical for Denver’s three-year evolution and franchise turnaround. One position group in particular is the offensive line. Their success is a big reason why the Broncos can contend for a Super Bowl title. Early on, it appears that depth may be tested. In their first pads practice of camp, starting center Luke Wattenberg exited yesterday’s first pads practice session with an apparent arm injury and did not return. After practice, Payton expressed confidence Wattenberg wouldn’t miss much time. However, the extent of the injury and his timetable of return is unknown If he misses time, fourth year pro Alex Forsyth would take over. Forsyth was seventh-round draft selection out of Oregon and part of Payton’s first draft class with the team. A practice squad player for his rookie year, Forsyth has appeared in every game the past two seasons with six starts. Payton took a moment to praise the backup pivot’s intelligence and noted he was wise beyond his years. “Yes, he’s super savvy and smart. He’s one of the smarter guys in that room. You don’t feel a young player. You feel like, if you interviewed him, you’d feel like you’re talking to a seven-year vet,” stated Payton. “He’s a little bit of an old soul that way and much appreciated though. He’s really talented.” Speaking of talent, the Broncos defense has a lot of it. Especially in their secondary. Yesterday, reports acknowledged they were a key reason why the defense won the day against the offense. Sitting atop the depth of Broncos’ defensive backfield is second-year cornerback Jahdae Barron. With the high-profile trio of Patrick Surtain II, Riley Moss, and Ja’Quan McMillian scheduled to start once again, Barron is on the hunt for an increased role in 2026. Selected with their first-round pick in the 2025 NFL Draft, the former Jim Thorpe Award winner appeared in every game and notched five starts as a rookie. He posted 35 tackles, 7 pass breaks ups, 1 forced fumble, and 1 interception. Overall, he saw 334 snaps, roughly 30-percent of the defense’s total in ‘25. Some fans have been critical of Barron’s lack of immediate impact, but the former Longhorns standout fared well and made a positive impact in his snap share. During his post-practice presser, Payton dismissed rumors stating Barron had moved to safety and clarified his role with the defense. “He’s playing nickel, he’s playing corner and then when we get into dime, he replaces a linebacker. He’s doing really good. There’s been no position change.” Another spot where the competition is hot is wide receiver. The Broncos aerial attack is ready for liftoff. The have a batch of talented wideouts vying for the next big role after Courtland Sutton and Jaylen Waddle. Second-year wide receiver Pat Bryant is among them and has been turning heads at camp. A third-round pick alongside Barron in the ‘25 NFL Draft, Bryant’s physicality, run blocking, and ability to snag tough catches were a big part of his rookie campaign successes. He hauled in 31 receptions on 49 targets for 378 yards and 1 touchdown—22 of those catches resulting in first downs. Yesterday, Payton gave Bryant a glowing review for his efforts to date. It’s too early to tell who will earn the third spot battle at wideout, but the former Illini standout is making a tough run for it. “I think his weight is at a good spot. He has some of the better hands in traffic with his feet on the ground. He’s really good at run after the catch. I said this to you guys a year ago, he’s real smart. Someone that can move from ‘X’ to the slot. It’ll be easy creating his role.”

title: Horse Tracks: ‘Right pieces, right team,’ says Surtain
summary: Good morning, Broncos Country! It was inevitable someone would ask the “Super Bowl or bust?” question. Pat Surtain II didn’t take the bait. After all, it’s August. But he didn’t shy away from it, either. Because it’s August with some high expectations. “Our expectations are pretty high, but we are just going to take it […]
full_text: DENVER, CO - SEPTEMBER 7: Pat Surtain II (2), Ja'Quan McMillian (29) and Talanoa Hufanga (9) of the Denver Broncos prepare for Cam Ward (1) and the Tennessee Titans during the fourth quarter of the Broncos' 20-12 win at Empower Field at Mile High on Sunday, September 7, 2025. (Photo by AAron Ontiveroz/MediaNews Group/The Denver Post via Getty Images) Good morning, Broncos Country! It was inevitable someone would ask the “Super Bowl or bust?” question. Pat Surtain II didn’t take the bait. After all, it’s August. But he didn’t shy away from it, either. Because it’s August with some high expectations. “Our expectations are pretty high, but we are just going to take it week-by-week,” he said, as well-coached in PR as in coverage. “Obviously, that’s the main goal, but it starts right here in training camp and it starts early on in the season. Our main focus is to start out fast and start out hot early. That way we can prepare ourselves to get to that stage.” And the All-Pro corner believes the set-up is perfect for that. “We have all of the right pieces and the right team … the right guys with the right mentality to start things off the right way. This team is great all across the board.” Pat Surtain II “We have all of the right pieces and the right team,” Surtain said. “We have the right guys with the right mentality to start things off the right way. This team is great all across the board.” And a big part of that is the guy calling the defense. Having Vance Joseph back another year is not an insignificant piece of the Super Bowl puzzle. “It does a lot,” Surtain said. “Having ‘VJ’ on our side, a guy that’s been in this league for a long time and knows the ins and outs of this game. When you talk to him, everything about him speaks volumes, but he’s an even better person. Having a guy like that on the defensive side of the ball just translates to success.” Losing players like John Franklin Myers and PJ Locke means there is a void to fill, but Surtain is confident the coaches and veterans can bring the young guys along to do just that. “That’s part of the business, as they say,” Surtain noted about losing Myers and Locke. “Obviously when great players leave, you have to count on other guys to step up.” Between Sai’vion Jones and Eyioma Uwazurike working to replace Myers’ spot, or JL Skinner and Devon Key filling in for Locke, Surtain is not worried about that happening. There are always young guys stepping up. 🔒’d in at #BroncosCamp @R_moss5 x @PatSurtainll pic.twitter.com/KIop5m5aji — Denver Broncos (@Broncos) August 3, 2026 Ja’Quan McMillian, for example, is primed to be an impact player, says Surtain. “His mindset is off the charts. The way that he carries himself on and off the field and his work ethic… There are only a few that quite work like him,” he said. “Being undrafted and coming in, nobody knew about him. Now, he’s a hot commodity. It goes to show the work that he’s put in and how much he values and hones in on his craft. I’m excited for ‘J-Mac.’ He’s a big-time player.” And it was Riley Moss who stole the show yesterday when pads came on. It was cornerback Riley Moss, however, who stole the show with the play of the day. During the final 11-on-11 team period, Courtland Sutton appeared to catch the ball for a big gain, but Moss wrestled the ball away at the last second for the INT. “It’s fantastic,” Sean Payton said of the play. “… The ability to be able to catch it as a defensive back, it’s tough if you don’t have decent enough hands because they’ll just throw at you. So, it was a good play.” In fact, takeaways will be one major emphasis of improvement over last year’s success — something the defense struggled to get last season. “That’s true,” Surtain acknowledged. “We can do that when the ball is in the air, capitalize on more opportunities of taking the ball away. Obviously, those game-changing plays are very vital in NFL games. Taking the ball away and just doing that would definitely help us a lot, too.” But right now, in training camp, it’s mostly about trusting the process, and the wins will come, Surtain says. “I feel like every year, everyone has new goals. …I mentioned before starting out fast early on and not allowing anything to go by. I feel like that is our next step and just staying committed to the process,” Surtain added. “Trusting what ‘VJ’ has for us, and trusting us and our defense as a unit. We have the right pieces at the right places. It just feels right right now.” Even for the six-year veteran, training camp brings a new buzz for the upcoming season, and the buzz this year is good. “I mean, honestly man, it doesn’t even feel like Year 6. It feels like when I was a rookie just starting to come in, starting to come [out of] my shell, but yes, time is flying” he added. “Just seeing how far this team has come has been quite surreal honestly, to say the least. So yes, I’m excited to enter Year 6 and to get it going again.” But first training camp. “It’s going to be a fun camp,” Surtain added.

title: 2026 Denver Broncos Training Camp: Day 3 News and Notes
summary: The Broncos were back on the practice field today after a day off on Sunday, and for the first time this summer, they were in pads. Today’s practice was run-heavy, and the defense came out as the winner. Specifically, cornerback Riley Moss, who made multiple big plays, and the Broncos’ pass rush, including Jonah Elliss, […]
full_text: CENTENNIAL , CO - JULY 30: Riley Moss (21) of the Denver Broncos adjusts his hair as he stretches during practice at Broncos Park in Centennial, Colorado on Thursday, July 30, 2026. (Photo by AAron Ontiveroz/The Denver Post) The Broncos were back on the practice field today after a day off on Sunday, and for the first time this summer, they were in pads. Today’s practice was run-heavy, and the defense came out as the winner. Specifically, cornerback Riley Moss, who made multiple big plays, and the Broncos’ pass rush, including Jonah Elliss, who got after the quarterback today. We also had an injury scare with starting center Luke Wattenberg, but thankfully Sean Payton told reporters after practice that he believes he will be just fine. Pads 🔛, energy 🆙 pic.twitter.com/w5fdW3PuSp — Denver Broncos (@Broncos) August 3, 2026 In today’s piece, we have more on the Broncos defense and Riley Moss winning the day, Pat Bryant looking good, a positive update on Luke Wattenberg’s injury, injury updates, news and notes, tweets from camp, and more! Defense, pass rush, and Riley Moss win the day The pads came on today, and the Denver Broncos defense stepped up. Riley Moss was excellent in coverage and showed off his elite athleticism, making an incredible interception; the Broncos pass rush got after the quarterbacks while Jonah Elliss is beginning to look like an early training camp star. Riley Moss just won a 1-on-1 battle vs Sutton on a deep pass down the left sideline. Great coverage and fought for the ball for a McMillian-esque INT A couple plays later, Pat Bryant was able to adjust and high point it over Moss for 15+ yards — Ryan Edwards (@redwardsradio) August 3, 2026 Riley Moss stole the day with his Ja’Quan McMillian-ish interception in practice where he fought the ball away from veteran wide receiver Courtland Sutton. He showcased his athleticism throughout practice, and showed why he’s a very good number two cornerback in the NFL. After practice, Head Coach Sean Payton was asked how Moss has grown throughout his career, and he told reporters Moss competes his tail off and that he is moving around really well right now. He knows obviously what type of attention he’s going to get relative to the routes, the route tree. I think learning to play with his feet, really working on reducing some of those fouls. He competes his tail off. I love that about him. He has those traits where it’s a short mindset, short memory. He’s moving around really well right now.” He was later asked about his interception vs. Sutton during practice, and Payton told reporters it was “fantastic to watch”. “It’s fantastic to watch because look, there are two things that can happen. You’re either deflecting it, but the ability to be able to catch it as a defensive back, it’s tough if you don’t have decent enough hands because they’ll just throw at you. So it was a good play.” As we know, Moss is in the final year of his deal with the team, and we assume that the Broncos will need to decide who to re-sign between him and McMillian. So, it will be interesting to see how that goes, but it’s great to see he’s doing well in camp. As for Jonah Elliss, he continues to stand out. We’ll see what the future holds for Jonathon Cooper, but it appears that the team has an ascending player here in Elliss. Pat Bryant makes plays The Denver Broncos battle for the WR3 job and/or snaps/targets behind starters Jaylen Waddle and Courtland Sutton continues to be one of the top stories in camp. For the first few practices, Marvin Mims was the standout pass catcher who had multiple explosive plays, and today, second-year wide receiver Pat Bryant took his turn at being the standout wide receiver. Riley Moss and the Broncos defense stole the show, but with Moss in coverage, Bryant caught a beautiful back-shoulder 25-yard pass from quarterback Bo Nix. He followed that with a top-tapping catch from backup quarterback Jarrett Stidham. Sean Payton sees a clear path for Pat Bryant in Denver's offense “It’ll be easy to create his role” pic.twitter.com/f9LrAQD7yq — DNVR Broncos (@DNVR_Broncos) August 3, 2026 After practice, Payton was asked where he thinks Bryant can still grow in year two. He told reporters that Bryant has some of the better hands in traffic, he’s really smart, and can play all over the field, which will make it easy to create his role in this offense. “I think his weight’s at a good spot. He has some of the better hands in traffic with his feet on the ground, he’s really good [at] run after the catch. I said this to you guys a year ago, he’s real smart. So he’s someone that can move from ‘X’ to the slot. It’ll be easy creating his role.” Bryant is my favorite to win the WR3 job simply because of all the things he can do. We saw his role grow at the end of last year; he has great hands, runs good routes, can block, and simply made plays. I think he can thrive in this role, and I believe we see a second-year jump this season. Luke Wattenberg injury Early during today’s practice, Denver Broncos starting center Luke Wattenberg went down hard and was seen holding his arm and talking with trainers. He never returned to practice, and backup center Alex Forsyth handled the starting center duties for the rest of the practice. Sean Payton says they will evaluate Luke Wattenberg but thinks “he’ll be fine” @KOAColorado — Ryan Edwards (@redwardsradio) August 3, 2026 Thankfully, after practice, Denver Broncos head coach Sean Payton met with the media and told reporters that he believes starting center Luke Wattenberg will be just fine. “Yes, nothing now. We’ll go ahead and evaluate. I think he’ll be fine.” So, while we don’t know exactly, it’s good to hear that he thinks he will be fine. However, if he were to miss time, Alex Forsyth stepped in for him nicely at the end of last year, so I believe he can do that in the short-term. If he does miss time, hopefully it’s not for an extended period of time, and he can be ready for Week 1 vs. the Chiefs. title: Fans believe running backs super important to Broncos’ success this season
summary: Although this week’s poll results make the question seem a bit obvious, I believe it was tougher to decide than the answers may show. But it’s hard to argue that the running back position won’t be perhaps the most important room for this year’s team. And honestly, it’s been the most important position group for […]
full_text: DENVER, CO - JANUARY 25: Denver Broncos running back RJ Harvey (12) carries the ball in the fourth quarter against the New England Patriots the AFC Championship Game at Empower Field at Mile High on January 25, 2026 in Denver, Colorado. (Photo by Dustin Bradford/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Although this week’s poll results make the question seem a bit obvious, I believe it was tougher to decide than the answers may show. But it’s hard to argue that the running back position won’t be perhaps the most important room for this year’s team. And honestly, it’s been the most important position group for this offense the last many years. It just hasn’t been able to live up to its potential nor its need. After all, the absolute best thing an offense can be is multidimensional. But when the running game is so-so at best, a defense can do a lot to make the offense uncomfortable — and that’s all it takes to make it one dimensional. Thankfully Bo Nix has been able to use his legs to keep a defense honest, but that’s not really a sustainable philosophy. “It’s one of his superpowers. It’s hard to sack some quarterbacks; he’s one of them,” head coach Sean Payton said this week during training camp. “That was something you saw on college tape. In our league when you take a sack, you just do the analytics on what your points become in that drive, or likelihood to kick a field goal and it all drops dramatically. So it’s certainly one of his strengths.” And it’s a strength Nix is going to continue to use no matter what. “I think like any strength, it can be overutilized and it can be overused,” Nix said Sunday. “For me, it’s just about the balance. It’s making the plays when they’re there, but at the same time using that creativity and skill set when it’s not. I always feel like at every practice I’ve ever been in, there’s a time or two in practice that you have to move and escape and practice that dynamic play. Our guys are in tune with it, and those guys are moving around with me. It’s just all about the play’s never over and also being smart and just making plays.” #Broncos Training Camp Day 1 thoughts: -A lot of fireworks from the offense, attacking deep often -Big plays from Engram, Sutton, Mims, Butler, Franklin, Bandy -Waddle is ELITE off of the line -Nix looked very comfortable -Reid strip/fumble recovery -Moss/Austin PBUs — Ryan Edwards (@redwardsradio) July 31, 2026

title: PSLs ‘likely’ coming to Broncos Country
summary: According to Forbes, Rob Walton and family are worth $130.7 billion. To put that in perspective, let’s borrow the method described by author Bill Bryson in his book I’m a Stranger Here Myself. He imagined a fictitious room where unending stacks of $1 bills were piled high and a person inside is given a marker. […]
full_text: DENVER, COLORADO - JANUARY 25: Denver Broncos fans look on prior to the AFC Championship game against the New England Patriots at Empower Field At Mile High on January 25, 2026 in Denver, Colorado. (Photo by Lauren Leigh Bacho/Getty Images) | Getty Images According to Forbes, Rob Walton and family are worth $130.7 billion . To put that in perspective, let’s borrow the method described by author Bill Bryson in his book I’m a Stranger Here Myself . He imagined a fictitious room where unending stacks of $1 bills were piled high and a person inside is given a marker. We’ll pretend it’s the Broncos mascot, Miles. If [Miles] initialed one dollar per second, [he] would make $1,000 every seventeen minutes. After 12 days of nonstop effort [he] would acquire [his] first $1 million. Thus, it would take [him] 120 days to accumulate $10 million and 1,200 days— something over three years—to reach $100 million. After 31.7 years [Miles] would become a billionaire… Tasked with a sharpie and the chore above, it would take Miles just 4,141 years, 231 days, 4 hours and 40 minutes to count dollar-by-dollar, the Rob Walton & family fortune. No bathroom breaks. No sleep. No hype sessions on top of the scoreboard. …but they are going to claim they need your money via personal seat licenses to help offset the cost of building the new stadium. Per Damani Leech, PSLs at the new stadium are “pretty likely but we haven’t made any decisions on that” — Romi Bean (@Romi_Bean) August 1, 2026 Personal seat licenses are a one-time or recurring fee for season ticket holders to get the right to buy their season tickets. Shockingly enough, the Broncos have managed to survive 66-years of season ticket sales without them, but now they’re suddenly necessary? It’s a cash-grab scam done by other teams to gouge their fans out of even more money; a scam that casually lives right next to $220 jerseys, $45 hats, and $19 beers. Often touted as necessary to fund new stadiums, personal seat licenses are a junk fee that has been adopted by 21-teams in the NFL. The Broncos are not one of them. Leech’s statement, with it’s soft language – ‘likely’ – is little more than Leech sticking his naked toe into the water, trying to assess how such a needlessly greedy move would be received. I get it. A new stadium (that nobody is clamoring for) costs money. The Broncos current stadium was built for $400.9 million ($774 million in today’s money). The Waltons could easily build 168 Empower Fields at current values. Sure, but what about a modern stadium? They could finance the construction of 27 SoFi Stadiums at a cost of $5.5 billion each. What should be profoundly clear is that the new Broncos stadium can be comfortably built, multiple times over, without the need for personal seat licenses. Fans of the Denver Broncos are some of the most fiercely loyal in the NFL. We travel to games, we buy the gear, and we show up when it matters. There is no reason for new Broncos ownership to shake fans down for even more money with bogus fees to finance a stadium they could build with stacks of cash poor Miles couldn’t count by hand in a thousand lifetimes . Greed like this, even in the most gorgeous hues of orange and blue, is still greed and it has no place in Broncos Country.

title: Tracking the Detroit Lions’ defensive roster bubble: Arise, Ahmed Hassanein
summary: Every week, we are tracking the Detroit Lions players on the roster bubble, and offering our predictions for who is in and who is out. The Lions defensive roster bubble continues to grow with questions about injuries and a ton of moving parts in the secondary. Some situations are becoming a little clearer, while others […]
full_text: Detroit Lions edge Ahmed Hassanein(99) during OTAs at Meijer Performance Center in Allen Park on Friday, May 29, 2026. | Junfu Han / USA TODAY NETWORK via Imagn Images Every week, we are tracking the Detroit Lions players on the roster bubble, and offering our predictions for who is in and who is out. The Lions defensive roster bubble continues to grow with questions about injuries and a ton of moving parts in the secondary. Some situations are becoming a little clearer, while others only seem to be getting more confusing. Here are the Pride of Detroit’s staffs current predictions about the players on the defensive roster bubble. We’ll break down each position below the chart to explain why the shifts in the depth chart. View Link Defensive end : Assumed in: Aidan Hutchinson, DJ Wonnum, Derrick Moore Ahmed Hassanein: 10 “IN” votes (up 7) Payton Turner: 1 votes (down 5) Anthony Lucas: 0 votes Arise, Ahmed Hassanein believers. The love for Hassanein’s attitude and potential have come together this camp for a very, very strong early performance for the second-year edge defender. He’s making plays on special teams, and has worked his way up to consistent second-team defensive reps. This can’t be a bad look, either: Saw Brad Holmes and Ahmed Hassanein talking after practice today and asked Hassanein about it. “I’m gonna do whatever it takes to prove you right,” Hassanein said he told Holmes. “You prove me right by doing what you’re doing. You’re a football player,” Holmes said to him. https://t.co/1Nx0KxI5ov pic.twitter.com/vd5v6Vgb3L — Colton Pouncy (@colton_pouncy) August 4, 2026 And with Payton Turner struggling to shake his reputation as injury prone, this decision is starting to look easier and easier. Defensive tackle: Assumed in: Alim McNeill, Tyleik Williams, Levi Onwuzurike OFF BUBBLE WATCH: Jay Tufele (cut) Tyler Lacy: 11 “IN” votes (no change) Skyle Gill-Howard: 8 votes (down 1) Mekhi Wingo: 6 votes (up 3) Chris Smith: 4 vote (up 3) Tyre West: 0 votes (no change) Aidan Keanaaina: 0 votes (no change) Most of the movement here is in regards to the nose tackle position. Essentially, all of Jay Tufele’s votes prior to the start of training camp shifted to Chris Smith and Mekhi Wingo. Smith looks like the next guy up at nose tackle, but hasn’t stuck out early in camp. Wingo, however, continues to rep with the first and second team defenses when Alim McNeill needs a break. The fact that he is repping ahead of a guy like Levi Onwuzurike is notable, but we’re not yet ready to put Onwuzurike on the roster bubble. Linebacker: Assumed in: Jack Campbell, Derrick Barnes, Malcolm Rodriguez NEW TO ROSTER BUBBLE: Jimmy Rolder (injury) NEW TO ROSTER BUBBLE: Joe Bachie NEW TO ROSTER BUBBLE: Devin White (signed) Trevor Nowaske: 10 “IN” votes ( up 1) Damone Clark: 10 votes (up 1) Devin White: 6 votes Troy Reeder: 4 votes (up 4) Jimmy Rolder: 3 votes Erick Hunter: 1 vote (no change) The Jimmy Rolder injury has caused some massive shifts here. Campbell said the injury wasn’t significant, but he’ll be out for “a while.” Seems like the most likely scenario is he goes on injured reserve when the cutdowns start, meaning he’ll be OUT and miss at least the first four games. Still, three staffers are holding out hope he avoids IR. Rolder’s votes from last week have been spread across the room, with newly signed Devin White getting the biggest jump. About half of the staff thinks he’s in, but Troy Reeder and Damone Clark have a little more belief, as well. Cornerback: Assumed in: DJ Reed, Rock Ya-Sin, Ennis Rakestraw, Roger McCreary, Keith Abney Khalil Dorsey: 8 “IN” votes (down 2) Nick Whiteside: 6 votes (up 5) I’m dangerously close to putting Roger McCreary on the roster bubble due to the rise in Nick Whiteside. Whiteside’s play has been undeniable, but it’s really challenging to find a way to put him on the roster. Reed, Ya-Sin, Rakestraw, and Abney all feel pretty safe. Khalil Dorsey may be the best special teamer on the roster, which makes it hard to put Whiteside above him. Meanwhile, McCreary is on a one-year, minimum salary contract with just $800,000 guaranteed. I’ve still got him as an assumed in, but with the growing support around Whiteside, I think next week we may need to pull him down to the bubble. As Dan Campbell said on Monday, the cornerback room is about to get interesting. Safety Assumed in: Christian Izien NEW TO BUBBLE WATCH: Kerby Joseph NEW TO BUBBLE WATCH: Brian Branch Avonte Maddox: 11 “IN” votes (no change) Thomas Harper: 11 votes (no change) Chuck Clark: 11 votes (no change) Kerby Joseph: 4 votes Brian Branch: 4 votes Dan Jackson: 1 vote (up 1) Loren Strickland: 0 votes (no change) We are no longer assuming that Kerby Joseph is “IN” nor that Brian Branch is “OUT.” Dan Campbell dropped the bombshell last week that Branch could return to the practice field as early as the end of training camp, which would lead to him avoiding the PUP to start the season. But Campbell also said that they are not expecting Joseph to be ready by Week 1, which was just as big of a surprise. Detroit is going to face a very difficult decision with both players on whether they should start the season on PUP, and as you can see, the POD staff is split on what they’re going to do. Oddly, that hasn’t changed much about the rest of the room, as staffer have used the extra votes elsewhere on the roster. That said, Clark and Maddox are getting very close to moving off the roster bubble. Given that they’ve taken nearly every first-team rep in camp, it seems unlikely Detroit will change course. But we’ll see as camp continues.

title: Who will be in the Detroit Lions’ starting secondary in Week 1?
summary: Going into Detroit Lions training camp, one of the biggest questions was: how will the secondary shake itself out? There were—and still are—a ton of questions among the defensive backs that have left people both curious and concerned. The sudden fall of Terrion Arnold left the outside cornerback position thin and questionable. The unclear injury […]
full_text: Detroit Lions cornerback D.J. Reed (4), center, practices next to cornerback Rock Ya-Sin (23) and cornerback Ennis Rakestraw Jr. (2) during training camp at Meijer Performance Center in Allen Park on Thursday, July 30, 2026. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co Going into Detroit Lions training camp, one of the biggest questions was: how will the secondary shake itself out? There were—and still are—a ton of questions among the defensive backs that have left people both curious and concerned. The sudden fall of Terrion Arnold left the outside cornerback position thin and questionable. The unclear injury timelines for Brian Branch and Kerby Joseph made predicting the Week 1 starters challenging. Detroit also added a handful of new pieces—Roger McCreary, Keith Abney, Christian Izien, and Chuck Clark—who could all challenge for a significant role on this defense. But we now have about a week’s worth of information from training camp. Be it the play on the field or comments from coaches and players, we’ve got a somewhat better picture of what Detroit’s secondary may look like when they kick off the season against the New Orleans Saints. So today’s Question of the Day is: Who will be part of the Lions’ starting secondray in Week 1? My answer: Let’s start at the safety position. At this point, I think it’s fair to say that Brian Branch and Kerby Joseph are unlikely to be ready at the start of the season. Don’t get me wrong, there are seriously promising signs that Branch will return earlier than initially expected , and Joseph is going through some pretty intense workouts with trainers. However, coach Dan Campbell said they aren’t expecting Joseph to be out there in Week 1 , and he said Branch is on a very similar timeline. So while I think those players could be ready by Week 2-4, I remain doubtful for the season opener. In training camp, the Lions haven’t wavered in their replacements of the two. It’s been Chuck Clark and Avonte Maddox almost exclusively. It’s clear Detroit likes having experienced, trustworthy veterans on the backend, and defensive coordinator Kelvin Sheppard explained why: “As far as bringing in veteran guys, who understand what we’re looking for as far as disguising. That’s where we’re trying to get to now as a defense. I told them it’s time to go to the next level guys. The quarterbacks in thisleague are too good now. So, it’s all about lying to them. You have got to be liars on defense. You have got a lot of that guy with the green dot on offense. Pre-snap, he has to see something and then post-snap, that picture has to change or else you’re sitting duck. And, these guys have done these things. They understand the why behind it.” So, injuries pending, I think Clark and Maddox are the Lions’ starting safeties in Week 1. As for the cornerback situation, it’s a little more muddled. While I do think D.J. Reed and Rock Ya-Sin have separated themselves early in training camp, things get a lot more complicated when you start talking about the nickel spot. Ennis Rakestraw has seen plenty of first-team reps at outside corner and nickel, but I don’t think he’s exactly stood out yet. Roger McCreary has also gotten a ton of reps as the first-team nickel. But the wild card here is Christian Izien. He missed the first three practices, but then Campbell revealed the original plan was for him to start as the No. 1 nickel. He’s just now getting started in camp, and he’s already starting to command some first-team nickel reps. If he wins that job, do McCreary and/or Rakestraw move more predominantly to the outside corner position and contend for a starting job there? Of course, I can’t completely count out Nick Whiteside, either. He’s made more plays than anyone in training camp, albeit with the second and third-team defenses. He got extremely high praise from Dan Campbell on Monday, and Detroit has a history of being a meritocracy. Doesn’t matter when you were drafted. Doesn’t matter how much you’re getting paid. If you produce, you’ll play. And if Whiteside can continue this crazy start to camp—and do so against starting-level competition—he could win this job. Ultimately, though, I think the starting secondary looks like this in Week 1: CB1: D.J. Reed CB2: Rock Ya-Sin NB: Christian Izien S: Chuck Clark S: Avonte Maddox Now, it’s time for you to make your predictions. title: How Week 1 of training camp impacts Detroit Lions roster bubble: Offense
summary: The Detroit Lions aren’t even a full week into 2026 training camp, but we’ve already seen some surprises when it comes to the roster. The depth chart may not be exactly what we expected, and injuries have forced some roster reshuffling. For Week 2 of our Roster Bubble series, it’s not surprising that there have […]
full_text: Detroit Lions wide receiver Dominic Lovett (19) walks off the field after practice during training camp at Meijer Performance Center in Allen Park on Thursday, July 30, 2026. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co The Detroit Lions aren’t even a full week into 2026 training camp, but we’ve already seen some surprises when it comes to the roster. The depth chart may not be exactly what we expected, and injuries have forced some roster reshuffling. For Week 2 of our Roster Bubble series, it’s not surprising that there have been some significant shifts—although most are on defense. Today, let’s re-examine the players on the roster bubble on offense. View Link Quarterback: Assumed in: Jared Goff, Teddy Bridgewater Luke Altmyer: 0 “IN” vote ( down 1 ) I don’t think there’s anything in particular that has caused the one vote drop in Altmyer. Based on my personal observations, Altmyer has displayed a strong arm and decent accuracy. However, his progression and defense reading is taking time… like most rookies. That’s enough for him to keep the QB3 a conversation, but I think his camp will make or break with the preseason games. Running back: Assumed in: Jahmyr Gibbs, Isiah Pacheco, Sione Vaki Jacob Saylors: 9 “IN” votes ( no change ) No change for Saylors here, as he still needs to convince a couple of staffers that he’s worth keeping an RB4. Obviously, this outlook could change after Sione Vaki suffered an injury on Monday morning , but hopefully the poking of the eye isn’t too serious. Wide receiver: Assumed in: Amon-Ra St. Brown, Jameson Williams, Isaac TeSlaa, Greg Dortch Cedrick Wilson Jr.: 10 “IN” votes (up 2) Dominic Lovett: 2 votes (down 6) Tom Kennedy: 0 vote (down 1) Cedrick Wilson’s stock is reasonably up after a strong start to camp and some praise from Dan Campbell. “He just gets it. There’s nothing better than freaking vets, man, true pros that get it. They know how to go about their business, man. They come in here, they compete. They’re not entitled, they just go work, man and that’s what he does. And by the way, his special teams reps are pretty good, too. I mean, for a receiver, he can do some stuff and his tape says that too.” Wilson’s gain is Lovett’s pain. The second-year receiver had a sluggish start to camp, but he’s admittedly stacked a few good days here recently. Tight end: Assumed in: Sam LaPorta, Brock Wright OFF BUBBLE WATCH: Zach Horton (cut) NEW TO BUBBLE WATCH: Anthony Firkser (0 votes) Tyler Conklin: 11 “IN” votes (no change) Miles Kitselman: 2 votes (up 1) NOTE: SOME VOTES WERE MADE BEFORE NEWS THAT MILES KITSELMAN WILL BE OUT FOR “A WHILE.” Despite not playing yet due to injury, Conklin remains the unanimous pick for the TE3 spot. And with Conklin looking like he’s nearing a return that makes sense. Unfortunately for Detroit, the main competition keeps getting injured. Kitselman was getting a lot of early reps with the first and second team, but he’s now expected to miss serious time . Anthony Firkser came in and immediately put together two strong practices with some first-team reps sprinkled in, and now he suffered an injury on Monday that caused him to get carted off . It will be interesting to see if Jackson Meeks starts to get some early reps now and if he can rise to the occasion. Offensive tackle: Assumed in: Penei Sewell, Blake Miller, Larry Borom OFF BUBBLE WATCH: Giovanni Manu (injured) Colby Sorsdal: 0 votes Devin Cochran: 0 votes With Manu out an estimated three months , the tackle room just isn’t very interesting right now. Sorsdal and Cochran seem a far way from making a case for the 53-man roster. Plus, with Miles Frazier now taking a significant amount of reps at tackle, he could very well be the team’s OT4 going into the regular season without taking up an additional roster spot. Interior offensive line: Assumed in: Tate Ratledge, Cade Mays, Christian Mahogany, Miles Frazier Ben Bartch: 11 votes (no change) Juice Scruggs: 10 votes (down 1) Seth McLaughlin: 0 votes Michael Niese: 0 votes Bartch still has yet to see the field in any team drills, and his health appears to be heading in the wrong direction with two straight absences from practice. Nevertheless, the staff still has him in based on his strong reputation with Campbell. Additionally, there haven’t been a ton of standouts among the depth—although Scruggs still continues to get the majority of first-team reps with Christian Mahogany still being eased back in.

title: Detroit Lions 2026 training camp observations, Day 5: Offensive line shines in pads
summary: The Detroit Lions donned pads for the first time during their 2026 training camp, and while they spent a bit less time on the field than in previous practices, the intensity was ramped up. Monday’s practice was roughly only an hour and a half, but according to coach Dan Campbell, this was just a precursor […]
full_text: Detroit Lions center Cade Mays (64), left, talks to offensive tackle Penei Sewell (58) as they walk off the field after practice during training camp at Meijer Performance Center in Allen Park on Wednesday, July 29, 2026. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co The Detroit Lions donned pads for the first time during their 2026 training camp, and while they spent a bit less time on the field than in previous practices, the intensity was ramped up. Monday’s practice was roughly only an hour and a half, but according to coach Dan Campbell, this was just a precursor for what should be a week of intensity that will separate players between those hoping to make an NFL roster and the ones who are ready. “I told the players last night that by the end of this week, this roster will begin to separate itself. So, this is where we’ll find out. We’re about to get four really, really good days of pads. And this is day one just to kind of break them in for the other three.” Injury updates Campbell gave injury updates on rookies Blake Miller, Derrick Moore, Jimmy Rolder, and Miles Kitselman in his morning press conference, and then Jeremy Reisman followed up practice with a second update, including a participation report, along with notes on the three players who left practice on Monday . “Time will tell” Star running back Jahmyr Gibbs, who is still not participating in practices due to a presumed contract holdout, watched his teammates from the sideline of the practice field on Sunday and was back again on Monday. While he was able to avoid the media over the weekend, Gibbs walked through the media on Monday but did not shed any light on his situation. When he was asked when he expected to return to the field to practice, his response was simply: “Time will tell.” Campbell, at his morning presser, made sure to emphasize that Gibbs is in the building, attending meetings, getting some work inside the training facility, and is “still part of us; and the guys, our players, love him. We love him. And he’s a part of what we do.” Opening with 1 vs. 1, but with a twist As has become tradition under Campbell, the first practice in pads opens with a one-on-one tackling drill, where the team gathers in a large semi-circle, and two players square up in the middle. At the whistle, the player with the ball needs to get past the defender, while the defender needs to make a stop. While this drill is typically full go and a way to increase intensity, the Lions scaled back this year’s opening drill and eliminated the tackling portion, instead asking the defenders to two-hand touch the offensive player. The Lions have been criticized for their practices in the past, and this is the drill Ennis Rakestraw was injured in in 2025, so it appears as if the Lions are being more cautious with their players this year. However, as Campbell mentioned previously, this practice is part of the ramp-up period, so it’s possible this drill could add tackling back in the coming days. As for the drill itself, the defense got the majority of the wins (two-hand touch certainly helps them), but I did award some offensive wins: RB Jabari Small was the only player to earn two wins, utilizing a cutback on the first and a speed-to-the-edge move on the second. WR Dominic Lovett got past his defender on a slick cutback. WR Lawrence Keys used a hesitation move to catch his defender throttling down. WR Tay Martin won with speed-to-the-edge. DB Aamaris Brown switched to offense for a snap and executed a juke move on his defender Offensive linemen impress in pads Whether in team drills or one-on-ones with defensive linemen, the offensive line showed fans a lot of optimism on Monday. On Monday, the Lions offense spent a fair amount of time working on their rushing offense, and that meant a variety of blocking schemes on display. While it can be challenging to sift through the bodies to see which individual players are standing out in the trenches, it gets much easier when they end up out in space, either by pulling or running their blocks out of the play. We saw Cade Mays and Christian Mahogany stand out on pulls during this practice, with the center walling off a hole for the back to run through, while Mahogany—fresh off returning from injury—pulled from his left guard spot and overpowered Aidan Hutchinson, a difficult thing to do. Mahogany’s power has been evident since his return, and now that he has flashed on pulls the last few days, it’s easy to see why I believe he’ll fit into Drew Petzing’s blocking scheme. The most impressive offensive lineman in camp has to be second-year utility lineman Miles Frazier, who continues to not only show off ridiculous range and endurance, but also execute at a strong level. After starting camp in the battle for the left guard position, he’s since shifted to right tackle on the second unit, while also contributing on the third team at both guard spots and sometimes left tackle as well. The offensive line also showed well on 1-0n-1s with the defensive line, showing nice patience and the ability to anchor versus power. OL vs. DL 1 vs. 1 recap: Starters Penei Sewell and Hutchinson split their two reps Mahogany bested Alim McNeill twice Tyleik Williams overpowered Mays, but Mays rebounded by taking down Chris Smith Tate Ratledge got wins against Mekhi Wingo and Levi Onwuzurike Blake Miller took care of Tyler Lacy, but DJ Wonnum caught him with a snatch-and-pull Reserves Larry Borom beat Wonnum and Ahmed Hassanein Miles Frazier (at RT) stallmated with Anthony Lucas, beat Eric O’Neill, then shifted inside to RG and beat Wingo Juice Scruggs locked down Skyler Gill-Howard, but lost to Lacy Melvin Priestly beat Gill-Howard and Tyre West Seth McLaughlin beat Myles Adams and Aidan Keanaaina Jacob Saylors stepping up With Gibbs holding out and Sion Vaki leaving practice early after getting poked in the eye, Jacob Saylors stepped into a larger role behind Isiah Pacheco. Saylors made the most of his opportunity, bursting through a right side gap for a 20+ yard gain during 11-on-11s, then closing out practice with a 40+ yard wheel route that he took untouched for a touchdown. Saylors has quietly had a solid camp, and depending on Gibbs and Vaki’s situations, could suddenly be in line for more touches and a chance to prove his worth. The Christian Izien domino effect Christian Izien has worked past the flu bug that kept him from practicing the first three days of camp, and while he returned to the field on Sunday, Monday was a truer representation of how his presence can create a domino effect on the secondary depth chart. At practice, Izien opened as the starting nickelback, working inside of D.J. Reed and Rock Ya-Sin or Ennis Rakestraw. However, when the second team took the field, Izien shifted back to safety alongside Thomas Harper. As a result of Izien’s presence, Roger McCreary shifted to the second team, operating on the outside opposite Khalil Dorsey when only two corners were on the field, then kicking inside when they went to nickel. When Izien took a breather from second-team safety, it was UDFA rookie Aamaris Brown who stepped in as his replacement, who appears to have possibly jumped Dan Jackson and Loren Strickland on the depth chart. With McCreary on the second team, rookie Keith Abney was bumped to the third team. Like McCreary, Abney worked as an outside corner in two CB sets (opposite Nick Whiteside), then kicking inside in nickel sets. Quick hitters The Tyler Lacy hype looks deserved and is gaining momentum. On Monday, during 11-on-11s at big end, he burst into the backfield and forced Jared Goff to throw the ball away. A few plays later, he kicked inside to defensive tackle and overpowered a second-team guard right into Teddy Bridgewater. DJ Wonnum sets a mean edge. Ahmed Hassanein delivered a powerful double-swipe and swim move to beat Colby Sorsdal in 1-on-1s. Hassanein’s intensity is ramping up on the field. After beating Thomas Gordon on a special teams drill, he stared…

title: Detroit Lions training camp Day 5 injury news: Optimism for Brian Branch’s return
summary: While the Detroit Lions’ injury list continues to grow, there is some potential good news on the horizon. It begins with Brian Branch and Kerby Joseph, who continue to show signs of progress toward returning to the field, but there are also a few players whose injuries may not be as serious as they look. […]
full_text: Detroit Lions safety Brian Branch (32) walks off the field after practice during training camp at Meijer Performance Center in Allen Park on Wednesday, July 29, 2026. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co While the Detroit Lions’ injury list continues to grow, there is some potential good news on the horizon. It begins with Brian Branch and Kerby Joseph, who continue to show signs of progress toward returning to the field, but there are also a few players whose injuries may not be as serious as they look. We break it all down below with our Day 5 training camp injury report. Note: All injury designations are unofficial based on my own observations unless otherwise stated. Returned to practice: RT Blake Miller (unknown) Miller didn’t miss Sunday’s practice, but he was limited to individual drills. Dan Campbell said on Monday that they were being precautious and he would be a full go during Monday’s practice. He was taking every visible right tackle first-team rep during the first padded practice of camp. While the job seems safely his over veteran Larry Borom, Campbell continued to preach caution until we see everyone in pads. “We like where Blake (is), we feel like has gotten a little bit better every day, and that’s a good thing,” Campbell said Monday. “Larry’s played in this league. But now here we go, now it’s real. So, we can talk about how good somebody looks, how much better they get without pads on. Well, now the pads are on. So yeah, anybody’s got a shot. So, we’ll see what it looks like. My gut tells me that Blake’s going to continue to grow, but we’ll see.” Not practicing: RB Jahmyr Gibbs ( not-injury related ) TE Milles Kitselman (leg) OT Giovanni Manu (NFI) EDGE Derrick Moore (groin) EDGE Payton Turner (back) LB Jimmy Rolder (leg) Campbell gave full injury updates on Miles Kitselman and Derrick Moore . Kitselman is expected to miss significant time, while Moore’s timetable is more optimistic with a minor strain that should sideline him 7-10 days. Still no sign of Payton Turner, who only lasted a day in training camp before a back injury. It’s worth noting, at the time, Campbell did not believe it was serious. “He’s got a little bit of a stiff back, so just got that, but we don’t think that’ll be anything serious,” Campbell said last Thursay. Out, but working with trainers G Ben Bartch (undisclosed) TE Tyler Conklin (PUP, calf) S Kerby Joseph (PUP, knee) S Brian Branch (PUP, Achilles) Conklin continues to put in serious work with trainers and appears to be one of the players closer to returning from injury. Bartch missed a second straight day of practice with an undisclosed injury. But the significant news here comes from Brian Branch getting his first on-field work during training camp. It was just a relatively short session with a trainer (15-20 minutes, by my estimate), but he was moving at a good speed and doing some change of direction things. Remember that early in camp, Campbell broke the news that Branch could return to practice as soon as the end of training camp. “Branch is doing well. His will be—obviously PUP, there’s no setbacks,” Campbell said. “Take it as it comes and we’ll see. I’m sure late training camp, maybe early September he can start practicing. We’ll see.” If he returns to practice and avoids the regular season PUP, it would mean he would not have to sit the first four games of the season, although it still seems unlikely he’ll be ready for Week 1. Kerby Joseph’s trainer work lasted significantly longer than Branch’s, and he continues to work up a good sweat. Left practice early RB Sione Vaki (eye) TE Anthony Firkser (leg) WR Lawrence Keys (leg) On the second play of full team padded practice, Vaki took a carry and stayed down for a considerable amount of time, forcing the team to move further down field to continue the drills. Eventually, he exited the field and did not return to practice. The team reported that he got poked in the eye. Jacob Saylors bumped to RB2 for the rest of the day with Gibbs and Vaki out. On the final play of an early 11-on-11 session, Firkser limped off the field with a leg injury. He was not able to make his way to the building on his own, so he was carted inside the facility. I did not see Lawrence Keys’ injury and can only go off the team report of a “leg” injury.

title: 9 standouts from Day 4 of Detroit Lions training camp
summary: After an off day on Saturday, the Lions returned to the practice field Sunday for their first training camp session in front of fans. Despite a threatening forecast, the rain held off, allowing Detroit to put together a lengthy, fast-paced, and competitive practice in shells. The defense set the tone on the final day before […]
full_text: ALLEN PARK, MICHIGAN - JULY 29: Malcolm Rodriguez #44 of the Detroit Lions looks on during Detroit Lions Training Camp at Detroit Lions Meijer Performance Center on July 29, 2026 in Allen Park, Michigan. (Photo by Nic Antaya/Getty Images) | Getty Images After an off day on Saturday, the Lions returned to the practice field Sunday for their first training camp session in front of fans. Despite a threatening forecast, the rain held off, allowing Detroit to put together a lengthy, fast-paced, and competitive practice in shells. The defense set the tone on the final day before the pads come on, turning in one of its strongest practices of camp while several players continued making their case for larger roles and roster spots. Below are my nine biggest standouts from the day. Keep in mind that the Lions held two individual competition periods, where I primarily observed the offensive and defensive line one-on-one pass-rush drills alongside Erik Schlitt. When necessary, I’ve also incorporated additional observations from Jeremy Reisman on the one-on-one coverage and seven-on-seven periods. Offensive line depth — Miles Frazier & Larry Borom With Blake Miller limited to individual drills, Penei Sewell receiving periodic rest, and Christian Mahogany still working his way back up to speed with the second team, Sunday served as another reminder of just how important quality depth and versatility are along the offensive line. Miles Frazier went from working almost exclusively at left guard early in camp to taking reps at left tackle, left guard, right guard, and right tackle during Sunday’s practice. It was a nonstop exercise in recalibrating his footwork and technique, yet he rarely looked out of place. Frazier appeared promisingly comfortable at tackle, even rotating in with the first team at right tackle while Larry Borom handled the sixth offensive lineman role. He also turned in one of the more impressive performances during one-on-one pass rush drills going 7-1 in a team-high eight reps. On one red-zone rep, after taking second-team reps at right tackle, Frazier immediately rotated in with the third team at right guard and snow-plowed Aidan Keanaaina out of the gap. His endurance and stamina stood out throughout the afternoon while further reinforcing his value as a versatile reserve and likely the team’s fourth tackle option. Borom continued to show why the Lions value him, seamlessly rotating between left tackle, right tackle, and the sixth offensive lineman role. He also finished a perfect 4-0 during one-on-one pass rush drills. Both players served as another reminder that Detroit has built enough depth and versatility to keep the offensive line from becoming a liability as the season progresses. Linebackers — Malcolm Rodriguez & Joe Bachie Malcolm Rodriguez continued to receive an abundance of work with the first-team defense at WILL linebacker, including a handful of red zone nickel reps, while also mixing in with the second team at MIKE linebacker. He was particularly sharp in coverage, highlighted by a step-for-step pass breakup against Sam LaPorta on a fourth-down goal-line corner route. Rodriguez also flashed against the run, recording a tackle for loss on an Isaiah Pacheco run off the right side. Overall, he looks noticeably more comfortable and decisive than the rusty version returning from injury last season. Joe Bachie followed suit with an impressive string of red-zone and goal-line reps that showcased why the coaching staff might be starting to trust the veteran. Rotating in for Rodriguez as the second-team MIKE linebacker during the first red-zone series, Bachie helped stonewall the run after Christian Izien had already blown up the previous play for a tackle for loss. Then came the goal-line period. On three consecutive plays, Bachie recorded a tackle for loss on first-and-goal, blanketed a tight end on a quick post route without drawing a target on second down, and finished the series by breaking up a Luke Altmeyer pass on third down. A Bachie barrage like that, after already starting to quietly put together a strong camp and, if Jimmy Rolder misses time, could have the inside track for the sixth linebacker spot. Defensive line depth – Ahmed Hassanein & Levi Onwuzurike The arrow continues pointing up for a bulked-up Ahmed Hassanein. His energy and trademark war cries echoing throughout practice remain impossible to miss. More importantly, the production is beginning to match the enthusiasm. Hassanein crashed down the backside to disrupt a run near the goal line, was the first defender to surge through on the lone kickoff during the end-of-game scenario with the first-team units, and later generated a pressure during that final four-minute drill. Lined up next to Alim McNeill, Hassanein looped inside on a stunt, with McNeill crashing in front, and beat Cade Mays cleanly, and forced a pressure, although Jared Goff answered with a strike to Jameson Williams. His versatility continues to stand out, and he looks increasingly capable of providing interior pass-rush juice while contributing on special teams. While Levi Onwuzurike is still working behind Tyler Lacy at big end and seeing most of his snaps with the second-team defense, it’s encouraging to see him beginning to rev his engine. During one-on-one pass rush drills, Onwuzurike gave Juice Scruggs the business with a powerful bull rush before following it up with a physical rep against Tate Ratledge. He carried that momentum into team drills,where he had an overwhelming pressure inside to force Teddy Bridgewater to dirt a ball. Later, during red-zone work, Onwuzurike crossed Miles Frazier’s face and quickly penetrated into Luke Altmeyer’s lap, forcing a hurried throw that nearly resulted in an interception. If Detroit’s defensive front is going to take another step forward this season, reclaiming the disruptive version of Onwuzurike will be a significant piece of that equation. Cornerbacks — Rock Ya-Sin & Keith Abney II Before practice, defensive coordinator Kelvin Sheppard expressed confidence in his secondary, emphasizing the value of having cerebral veterans in the defensive backfield. “The quarterbacks in this league are too good now. So, it’s all about lying to them,” Sheppard said. “You have got to be liars on defense. You have got a lot of that guy with the green dot on offense. Pre-snap, he has to see something and then post-snap, that picture has to change or else you’re sitting duck. And, these guys have done these things. They understand the why behind it.” Rock Ya-Sin backed up those comments with another encouraging day as he continued battling for a starting role. During one-on-one and seven-on-seven periods, Jeremy Reisman shared that Ya-Sin was fantastic against Isaac TeSlaa, forcing two incompletions in his pair of reps against the second-year wide receiver. He carried that momentum into full-team red-zone drills, opening the period by breaking up a pass intended for TeSlaa on a post in the end zone that Jared Goff launched up to TeSlaa from roughly the 20-yard line. A few plays later, Goff went back to TeSlaa on a fade near the goal line, Ya-Sin once again broke up the pass as it was reaching TeSlaa’s massive catch radius. The veteran cornerback consistently outmatched TeSlaa’s size and physicality throughout practice, refusing to give ground. Keith Abney II also had an encouraging afternoon. Still working primarily with the third-team defense, Abney nearly came away with two interceptions in the red zone. First, he dove in front of a seam route intended for Tarik Black in the end zone before nearly jumping a goal-line slant on fourth down while aligned at outside cornerback. For a rookie starting to find his footing, getting his hands on the football twice in high-leverage situations was another promising step in his development. Tight end — Anthony Firkser The Lions’ decision to bring Anthony Firkser back for a third stint with the organization already looks…
