title: Discussion: Which linebackers will make the Detroit Lions 53-man roster?
summary: The Detroit Lions’ linebacker group has quietly turned into a logjam. Between making an impact on defense and an impact on special teams, the Lions’ coaching staff will have some difficult decisions to make when roster cuts roll around. The Lions are lucky to have one of the league’s best in Jack Campbell, but the […]
full_text: CHICAGO, ILLINOIS - JANUARY 4: Trevor Nowaske #53 of the Detroit Lions lines up during the first half of the NFL football game against the Chicago Bears at Solider Field on January 4, 2026 in Chicago, Illinois. (Photo by Todd Rosenberg/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Detroit Lions’ linebacker group has quietly turned into a logjam. Between making an impact on defense and an impact on special teams, the Lions’ coaching staff will have some difficult decisions to make when roster cuts roll around. The Lions are lucky to have one of the league’s best in Jack Campbell, but the rest of the depth chart has a lot to prove. Can Derrick Barnes have a rebound season to justify his expensive contract extension? Can Malcolm Rodriguez show that a subpar 2025 campaign was just rust from a prior ACL injury? Which of their depth players can stake a claim on a coveted roster spot? With more training camp and preseason still to come, we can hope for some clarity, but we could just as easily be left with a tough decision: whom to keep and whom to cut? Today’s Question of the Day is: Which linebackers will make the Detroit Lions 53-man roster? My answer: My current guess is six: Jack Campbell, Derrick Barnes, Malcolm Rodriguez, Damone Clark, Trevor Nowaske, and Troy Reeder. The first three names on that list are obvious and require no explanation. The back half of the linebacker room is where the discussion starts. In the past, the Lions have liked to keep six linebackers in total. In 2025, the team kept six linebackers despite an initial roster of just 50 players. The same can be said about 2024 and 2023—that is three seasons in a row with six linebackers on the Week 1 roster. We can use 2025 as a template for what the Lions like: they have typically kept three starting-caliber players (Campbell, Barnes, and Alex Anzalone), one backup with defensive capabilities (Zach Cunningham), and two backups with special teams roles (Grant Stuard and Nowaske). As it stands, the Lions currently have 10 linebackers on the 90-man roster and you could make a genuine case for all of them. Starting trio of Campbell, Barnes, and Rodriguez aside, you have rookie Jimmy Rolder, a player that would undoubtedly be a roster lock if not for an injury with an as-of-yet unknown timeline . Then there is Clark, a veteran with a mix of defensive experience, special teams experience, and youth. Trevor Nowaske returns for yet another season in Detroit as a player that has grown into a valued special teamer with SAM potential on defense. These three are my favorite bubble players to make the roster, pending Rolder’s injury status. Joining the group are three veterans in Devin White, Joe Bachie, and Reeder. White is the newest of the signings and is coming off a 174-tackle season, albeit to poor performance grades . Bachie has bounced around the league, starting the occasional game but largely being a special teams contributor. Reeder, meanwhile, had been a frequent starter for the Los Angeles Rams since 2019, but 2025 was the first year in which he was largely relegated to special teams duties. Rounding out the linebacker room is undrafted rookie Erick Hunter, a player with an intriguing athletic profile and a strong developmental ceiling. Because Rolder’s status is presently up in the air and it prompted the Lions to sign White immediately, I think there is a decent chance he starts the season on the Injured Reserve. This would cause him to miss at least four games, an unfortunate circumstance but not a career-altering one. Odds are the Lions will not need Rolder in the early part of the season, especially if he is unable to play during training camp and preseason. That leaves me at five linebackers (Campbell, Barnes, Rodriguez, Clark, and Nowaske) and despite the Lions shifting away from three-linebacker sets, I still think they will want to keep six. I give my early nod to Reeder. Because Clark could realistically be a solid LB4 on defense and a solid contributor on special teams, I think the value of keeping a defense-only option like White is greatly reduced. That increases the value of Reeder, who could step into a role on defense or special teams when called upon. It is also worth remembering that the Lions only signed White after Rolder’s injury, whereas Reeder was signed at the start of training camp—sure, this is only a difference of a few days, but White’s signing was reactionary, while Reeder’s was not, perhaps hinting at Reeder being a more coveted option. How will the Lions’ crowded linebacker room shake out? Let us know in the comments below.
author: John Whiticar

title: Green Bay Packers to re-sign McCallan Castles
summary: The Green Bay Packers’ tight end room is extremely banged up right now. Beyond not having Tucker Kraft, who is still ramping back up in practice after suffering a season-ending ACL tear in 2025, the Packers were also down Luke Musgrave (neck) and R.J. Maryland (hamstring) going into practice on Monday. The Athletic’s Matt Schneidman […]
full_text: COLUMBIA, MO - NOVEMBER 11: Tennessee Volunteers tight end McCallan Castles (34) during a SEC conference game between the Tennessee Volunteers and the Missouri Tigers held on Saturday Nov 11, 2023 at Faurot Field at Memorial Stadium in Columbia MO. (Photo by Rick Ulreich/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The Green Bay Packers’ tight end room is extremely banged up right now. Beyond not having Tucker Kraft, who is still ramping back up in practice after suffering a season-ending ACL tear in 2025, the Packers were also down Luke Musgrave (neck) and R.J. Maryland (hamstring) going into practice on Monday . The Athletic’s Matt Schneidman noticed that Luke Lachey, who was signed by the Packers in mid-June after initially failing his physical due to a hamstring issue, was also in a boot and on a scooter post-practice. How many healthy bodies did that leave Green Bay with at the tight end position? Josh Whyle Drake Dabney Messiah Swinson Thomas Yassmin That’s it! And Yassmin, an Aussie, is an international exemption player, so he doesn’t even count against the team’s 90-man roster. In order to correct their numbers problem, the Packers will be re-signing McCallan Castles, according to Sports Illustrated’s Bill Huber . Castles was first signed by Green Bay last November, after a series of injuries at the position led to Whyle being called up from the practice squad. On January 1st, Castles was placed on the team’s practice squad injury list, which essentially functions as the practice squad’s injured reserve. After the season, he signed a reserve/futures deal with the Packers, but was waived by the team before the 2026 draft. Castles worked out with Green Bay last week , along with six other tight ends, including Yassmin, who was eventually signed by the team. McCallan Castles is a TE prospect in the 2024 draft class. He scored a 8.59 #RAS out of a possible 10.00. This ranked 170 out of 1199 TE from 1987 to 2024. https://t.co/nSogMXrQ5U pic.twitter.com/Y8yH5UrGZa — RAS.football (@MathBomb) April 18, 2024 Castles has yet to play in an NFL regular-season game and hasn’t even played for the Packers in the preseason, but there’s a chance he’ll get that shot in 2026. At the college level, he began his career at Cal, where he posted one reception for 15 yards over two seasons before dropping down to the FCS level at UC-Davis. With UC-Davis, he recorded 69 receptions for 928 yards and nine touchdowns over three years before making the jump back up to the FBS, where he played his final year at Tennessee (22 receptions for 283 yards and five touchdowns). He went undrafted in the 2024 class and had stints with the Philadelphia Eagles, Los Angeles Chargers and Los Angeles Rams before coming to Green Bay. Back in 2024, Castles was ranked as The Athletic’s Dane Brugler’s #19 tight end (14 were given draftable grades) and received a priority free agent grade. Here is what Brugler had to say about the non-combine invite: SUMMARY: McCallan (mick-CAL-un) Castles grew up north of Denver with his father (Thomas), who ran track at UC Riverside, and mother (Alison), who played basketball at Idaho State. Castles played football, baseball, basketball and ran track in high school, initiall y at Berthoud High (Colo.) and then at South Lake Tahoe. He was an All-State tight end and League MVP in basketball. A three-star recruit, Castles signed with Cal but left two games into his second season. After three seasons at UC Davis, he transferred to Tennessee. Primarily an inline blocker at UC Davis, Castles worked out of the slot in Knoxville and had uneven results blocking in space and consistently getting open. Overall, Castles needs to improve his special-teams resume and blocking consistency to stick, but his basketball background is evident. The Packers’ roster is currently full, which means that Green Bay will need to make a corresponding roster move to allow for Castles to join the roster before tomorrow’s practice. Keep an eye on the team releasing a player early on Tuesday.

title: What Matthew Golden playing the X position could mean for the Packers
summary: Over the weekend, as the Green Bay Packers started to settle into the groove of training camp, quarterback Jordan Love raised a bit of a hubbub during an interview with NFL Network’s Stacey Dales when he said that receiver Matthew Golden was “locked down over there at X.” I’m sure the vast majority of you […]
full_text: Over the weekend, as the Green Bay Packers started to settle into the groove of training camp, quarterback Jordan Love raised a bit of a hubbub during an interview with NFL Network’s Stacey Dales when he said that receiver Matthew Golden was “locked down over there at X.” "It's not our first rodeo together" 🤠 @packers QB Jordan Love excited to get to work with his offensive weapons @StaceyDales | @jordan3love pic.twitter.com/HJAvkjFswJ — NFL Network (@nflnetwork) August 2, 2026 I’m sure the vast majority of you already have a picture in your head of an X receiver, but we’ll spend a minute with that first. Traditionally, the prototypical X receiver has been someone like Andre Johnson or DeAndre Hopkins: a big-bodied, sure-handed receiver who is good in contested-catch situations. On the other side would be the Z receiver, who would be someone like DeSean Jackson. In his excellent book The New Thinking Man’s Guide to Pro Football , Paul Zimmerman (aka Dr. Z) bucketed them in two categories: “possession” and “flyers”. That feels right. Your X receiver is your on-the-ball, isolated receiver who is asked to win one-on-ones. While football has changed and evolved over the years, those tags – X and Z – are still used, and, in the minds of many, those classifications are still gospel. They can still hold true to a certain extent, but they’re not hard-and-fast rules. In this Packers offense in the LaFleur era, you can think of Romeo Doubs in that X role. Going back a little earlier in his tenure, it was Davante Adams. With that in mind, we’re going to view Matthew Golden through the lens of some pages from the 2019 Packers Playbook (I know, I know. It’s pretty outdated by now from a play perspective, but it still outlines the core philosophy and formations that are still very much in use.) We’ll start with a definition of skill positions: As is laid out here, the Y (Tight End) determines the strength of the formation, while the X is “Predominantly the Weak Side Receiver”. That is to say, aligned on the other side of the formation from the Tight End. You can likely see this in your head when the Packers go into a 3×1 or Quads formation; there was Romeo Doubs or Dontayvion Wicks as the X, all alone on the backside. There’s a term that’s been floating out there over the past couple of years of “the sacrificial X”. I truly despise the term, but if you look at formations like this, I get it. Out of a formation like this, you could have the “concept” side and the “one-on-one” side. To me, this diagram is a perfect example of what that kind of thing would look like. This is a concept called All Go that was a big part of their playbook when Davante Adams was at X. It’s a flood concept to the right side, while the X receiver is isolated backside. The QB would read the coverage over the X, then read the concept. It would be a pre-snap & immediate post-snap read. If the coverage was favorable for the X, it’s an immediate throw. If there’s nothing there, the QB barely gives him a glance before moving to the concept. When the idea of an X receiver comes up, this is what tends to spring to mind. That’s certainly part of the role, but it’s not the entire role. Defining a WR as an X, Z or F doesn’t mean they’re always doing the same thing. Here’s Bin RT, a bunch formation. There is the X, once again, all alone on the weakside. Just below Bin RT, we’ll find Box RT. It’s the same bunch formation, with a key difference: the X is now part of the bunch. You’ll find some of this in their 2×2 formations as well. Deuce RT finds the X as the outside receiver on the weak side. Just below that, you’ll find Dixie RT, where X is the slot. Motion, of course, changes the picture and further blurs the lines. Here’s Coco Bow out of Bunch RT Tight. The X starts as the isolated receiver in a 3×1 formation, but the motion turns it into a 2×2 set with the X running a corner route. If you want an even clearer look, here is a page from the Tree concept. There are four versions of it. In the top two versions, the X is running the Basic from the top of a two-man stack. In the third diagram, he’s the under man in the stack, running the Shallow Cross and working as the Hot receiver in a blitz situation. In the fourth diagram, the concept has been flipped, and he’s the run-off Alert receiver, running a go route. Picture this page and the call, and then imagine what it’s like if you’re swapping receiver tags. Say Golden is the X in the top right diagram, but the Z in the bottom right. Think of the additional mental processing that would likely occur. Having defined receiver tags doesn’t mean that receiver is always going to be doing the same thing. In this offense, you want the X to be able to win off the line and have sure hands, but that’s not the only thing he’s going to be asked to do. He likely won’t be the guy called on to be the insert blocker the majority of the time (that will likely be Christian Watson as the Z), but there are times that’s exactly what he’ll be asked to do. By paring down the receiver room this offseason, it has allowed for clarity in receiver roles, which should allow for a smoother operation. It doesn’t mean boxing yourself in: it means more clarity in communication, which is never a bad thing. title: Packers Training Camp Recap: Trey Smack is starting shaky
summary: We’re here to recap the last two days of the Green Bay Packers’ training camp, which included the team wearing full pads for the first time. On Sunday, the team was in shells, as head coach Matt LaFleur stated that the team worked through rules of engagement (he didn’t seem too happy about the pass-rushers […]
full_text: ASHWAUBENON, WISCONSIN - JULY 31: Trey Smack #28 of the Green Bay Packers works out during the Green Bay Packers training camp at Ray Nitschke Field on July 31, 2026 in Ashwaubenon, Wisconsin. (Photo by Patrick McDermott/Getty Images) | Getty Images We’re here to recap the last two days of the Green Bay Packers’ training camp, which included the team wearing full pads for the first time. On Sunday, the team was in shells, as head coach Matt LaFleur stated that the team worked through rules of engagement (he didn’t seem too happy about the pass-rushers swiping at his quarterbacks), and Monday is when the team’s leg pads came on. This is also your reminder that the Packers’ Family Night practice, the team’s annual scrimmage at Lambeau Field, will be held on Friday. The Hall of Fame Game will be played on Thursday on NBC. Football games are right around the corner! Injuries Most of the news on the injury front has been positive the last two days. Cornerback Kamal Hadden and offensive tackle Brant Banks have been taken off the physically unable to perform list and are back in practice, even though Hadden’s return on Sunday did lead to a new injury: a dislocated pinky finger. Offensive lineman Jager Burton, who injured his hamstring earlier in camp, is also back out on the field. The team has suffered two new injuries, though: hamstring injuries to both cornerback Carrington Valentine and tight end RJ Maryland. No Packer has suffered a major injury in camp yet, but those pesky hamstrings have certainly been an issue. The following players still remain on Green Bay’s injury lists (either PUP or NFI): RB Chris Brooks (hamstring) TE Luke Musgrave (neck) EDGE Micah Parsons (ACL) DL Javon Hargrave (knee) DL Jordon Riley (Achilles) LS Matt Orzech (calf) Offense One interesting note in camp is that 2025 draft pick John Williams, who missed his rookie season with a back injury, has been playing all three offensive line spots in camp so far. He’s had to bounce all over with the second-team unit, as the team continues to keep Aaron Banks and Zach Bako-Bewele (formerly Tom) out of team drills. Overall, the team has been pretty conservative with returning their players to team periods following an injury. Jordan Love confirms Matthew Golden will be mostly playing X. Essentially replacing Romeo Doubs in the offense. Golden X Watson Z Reed F Whats really cool is all 3 guys have played all 3 spots at some point and can be moved around. The Packers 2026 Offense about to be 🔥… — Packerfan Total Access- Clayton (@packers_access) August 2, 2026 If you missed it, quarterback Jordan Love stated on Sunday after practice that second-year first-round pick Matthew Golden will be playing the X position, which was previously played by Davante Adams and Romeo Doubs, in the team’s offense moving forward. Just something to pay attention to. Speaking of Love, it finally happened. It took five practices, but the quarterback finally threw an interception. Safety Xavier McKinney got the better of him when Love tested the All-Pro. Defense With Valentine out and Devonte Wyatt still being held out of team periods, along with Javon Hargrave on the PUP list, we aren’t getting too many answers on how the two biggest camp battles are going right now. On paper, the starting roles most up for grabs going into 2026 are the second cornerback position and the third interior defensive lineman for the Packers. Because of injuries, though, it’s tough to get a gauge on Green Bay’s preferred rotation and how much their opinion is changing day-to-day. Matt said DDS has flashed so far (with caveat that pads aren't on yet) and that he's handled them asking to play inside and outside well, while praising his versatility. — Andy Herman (@AndyHermanNFL) August 2, 2026 One player who got a shoutout from LaFleur earlier this week was rookie fourth-round pick Dani Dennis-Sutton, who general manager Brian Gutekunst stated the team tried to trade up for on Day 2 of the draft. The rookie has been kicking inside a good bit in practice, potentially a role he can hold down in obvious passing situations until Micah Parsons returns to the lineup. DT Anthony Campbell has batted down like 3 passes at LOS in first four practices — weston hodkiewicz (@WesHod) August 2, 2026 Another player who is turning heads is defensive lineman Anthony Campbell, a 2025 undrafted free agent who had a stint with the Seattle Seahawks before joining the Packers in-season last year. The 6’6” defensive lineman has been batting passes down left and right and is up to four PBUs in five practices after Monday. The sixth defensive line spot on the 53-man roster is potentially up for grabs, depending on if there’s an injury or if Nazir Stackhouse does/doesn’t take the next step this preseason. For what it’s worth, second-year fourth-round pick Barryn Sorrell has consistently been the “starter” opposite of Lukas Van Ness throughout camp, even if the position has been rotated heavily. Rookie second-round pick Brandon Cisse was the starting cornerback today opposite Keisean Nixon with Valentine, who has generally gotten the nod, out with an injury. Special Teams The practice long snapping video you didn’t know you needed. pic.twitter.com/rZME6hW7on — Rob Demovsky (@RobDemovsky) August 2, 2026 The Packers worked receivers Skyy Moore, Jayden Reed, Matthew Golden and Will Sheppard (along with running back Jaden Nixon) as punt returners on Monday. Players who have gotten looks as punt gunners have been safety Kitan Oladapo, receiver Bo Melton, cornerback Brandon Cisse, safety Mark Perry, receiver J. Michael Sturdivant, receiver Kaden Prather and receiver Isaiah Neyor. Contributing on punts (or punt returns) is a way to make the 53-man roster (and 47-player unit active on game days). With the injury to Matt Orzech, the Packers didn’t begin kicking in training camp until Sunday. Rookie draft pick Trey Smack went three of five on Sunday and went five of eight on Monday, including a doink off the upright. 8 of 13 doesn’t look great on paper, but this time last year Brandon McManus was on a heater and looked like he couldn’t miss a kick, so how much can we really take from training camp kicks at this point?

title: The Josh Sweat hold-in continues, but the timing just isn’t right
summary: While everything in Green Bay Packers camp has run mostly smoothly thus far- no holdouts, extensions for budding star players, and returns for key players- not everyone is so lucky. Arizona Cardinals edge rusher Josh Sweat appears to be engaging in something of a hold-in. While officially Sweat is on PUP with what is being […]
full_text: GLENDALE, ARIZONA - NOVEMBER 23: Josh Sweat #10 of the Arizona Cardinals looks on from the line in the game against the Jacksonville Jaguars at State Farm Stadium on November 23, 2025 in Glendale, Arizona. (Photo by Norm Hall/Getty Images) | Getty Images While everything in Green Bay Packers camp has run mostly smoothly thus far- no holdouts, extensions for budding star players, and returns for key players- not everyone is so lucky. Arizona Cardinals edge rusher Josh Sweat appears to be engaging in something of a hold-in. While officially Sweat is on PUP with what is being categorized as “knee maintenance,” I was not born yesterday. It was known that Sweat had submitted a trade request to the organization in the off-season, but more reporting from below highlights that Sweat actually went to the team the day current Packers defensive coordinator Jonathan Gannon was fired. "Josh Sweat asked to be traded the day Jonathan Gannon got fired… "He came to Arizona because of JG, and he's had the best seasons of his career because of JG." @JohnnyVenerable explains what's going on with Josh Sweat, who is on the PUP list with "knee maintenance." https://t.co/GnPdewtbTQ pic.twitter.com/om8RSOI024 — Ari Meirov (@MySportsUpdate) August 3, 2026 The relationship between Sweat and Gannon has been well-documented already, and the Packers’ need for an additional pass rusher in the short-term is glaring until Micah Parsons returns sometime between Weeks 5 and 8-ish. Beyond that point, it would give Green Bay a strong threesome of edge rushers with Parsons, Sweat, and Lukas Van Ness, who, despite injuries, started to look like a player Green Bay was hoping for in the last few weeks of 2025. Per Easton Butler, who has been on top of multiple trades over the past few years, Green Bay did engage in discussions with Arizona around Sweat earlier in the off-season. Yes, the Cowboys did call on Sweat yesterday, but were turned away. TB sent an offer of a 4th, but were denied. Sweat wants Green Bay, and if that fizzles out, the Eagles are his #2. — Easton Butler (@Easton__Butler) June 2, 2026 Green Bay’s offer, however, has not reached the threshold Arizona is looking for. Since @bigpackers4x got 10k, here's a little info. The Packers HAVE called about Vita Vea. (I will not go into more detail about GB on it.) Hearing likely a contract ploy, but IF traded it'll be to a west coast team. Josh Sweat talks are currently "dead" right now. No new info,… pic.twitter.com/s3OgAPm9C8 — Easton Butler (@Easton__Butler) July 30, 2026 I don’t think Green Bay’s alleged offer here is off-base, nor do I think Arizona is necessarily wrong for holding out for more. The problem arises with the timing for both teams. Green Bay needs Sweat early in the season, while Micah Parsons finishes up his rehab from his ACL tear. The Arizona Cardinals are in no particular rush to move him before the trade deadline, which won’t be until November 10th, between weeks nine and ten. Sweat can continue his hold-in, erm, completely legitimate injury rehab, but that still doesn’t really alter the market for his services. If everyone knows he’s really fine, it’s not going to ding his market, and Arizona, even despite the complete delusion the NFL provides teams, is probably quite clear-eyed about their 2026 outlook, and will be prioritizing getting the most compensation for him rather than trying to make sure he’s out of the building. As much as I would like to see Josh Sweat in Green and Gold, it’s tough to thread the needle. His value to Green Bay is highest now, and by the time Arizona will be prompted to move, Green Bay’s offer may be even worse than it is now and other teams will enter the fray. And with Sweat’s contract entirely made up of non-guaranteed money from this point forward, there’s a great deal of malleability financially that would be of use not just to Green Bay, but to any contender. Expect Green Bay to be involved in discussions to the end, but perhaps the return of Parsons and the hopeful ascendence of Van Ness make it unnecessary by November.

title: Zach Bako-Bewele’s name change is awesome
summary: The Packers have a new right tackle, same as the old right tackle. Zach Tom is gone. Hello Zach Bako-Bewele. The fourth-year Bako-Bewele formalized a name change over the weekend, combining his grandparents’ surnames to create a new, hyphenated last name with the intent of one day passing it on to his kids. “I want […]
full_text: GREEN BAY, WISCONSIN - NOVEMBER 23: Zach Tom #50 of the Green Bay Packers takes the field prior to an NFL football game against the Minnesota Vikings at Lambeau Field on November 23, 2025 in Green Bay, Wisconsin. (Photo by Todd Rosenberg/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Packers have a new right tackle, same as the old right tackle. Zach Tom is gone. Hello Zach Bako-Bewele. The fourth-year Bako-Bewele formalized a name change over the weekend, combining his grandparents’ surnames to create a new, hyphenated last name with the intent of one day passing it on to his kids. “I want to have a name I can pass down where it represents where they came from, where I came from,” he said. “I just feel like people will see that name and have a good understanding of who I am, where I come from.” Tom’s grandparents are Nigerian immigrants and the new name represents that heritage. And frankly, it rules. First, it’s an awesome name. It’s satisfying to say, and it’ll eventually look great on a jersey. It’s going to take some time to get used to typing, I’ll say that, but considering Bako-Bewele himself still has to go through the process of changing his social security card and driver license, that feels like a pretty small hurdle. The wheels of local government bureaucracy turn slowly, and having helped my wife through the process of getting her name changed (including getting a new passport in the middle of the pandemic), I can sympathize with the impending headache. But the name itself is cool, and lends itself to a bunch of nicknames. Here are a few: Z-Bak, ZBB, Zeebs, Double B, Killer Bs, and so on. Take your pick or grow your own. I’m sure we’ll land on something for him organically. But second, and more importantly, I love it on the grounds of self-determination. I don’t think it’s an overtly political statement to say there’s a lot that could be improved about our immigration process in America, and historically it wasn’t much better. Look into the history of how many names were changed (or erased entirely) at Ellis Island, or forgotten due to (ahem) other forms of immigration, at least one of which particularly affected people of Bako-Bewele’s heritage. As a human being, I can’t help but root for a guy planting a flag and saying “This is what I’m about. This is who I am. This is the history I’m choosing to honor, and this is the future I want to build.” Yes, it some senses, it’s just a name. Zach Bako-Bewele is still the same person as Zach Tom. But names matter, too. There’s power in a name, and history. Case in point: I’m from a small town in Wisconsin called Cedar Grove, about an hour south of Green Bay. My ancestors moved there in the back half of the 1800s, around 1864 if my memory serves. The first of my family in the area, a man named Gerrit Hendrik Meerdink, built a house on farmland he cleared himself. And on the front of that house he put his initials in giant iron letters: GHM. You can still go to the house and see those letters today. The history is still there, and it’s still going. I’m living proof, and my children will carry the name their many-times-great grandfather brought to America with little else more than 150 years ago. Now, Zach Bako-Bewele gets to start a similar legacy. He’s getting to decide a little bit of what his future is going to look like right now, and we get to root for him as his story begins to play out. How can you not love that?

title: Green Bay Packers News: Time to put the pads on
summary: The first week of an NFL team’s training camp is a nice ramp-up period for everyone. The coaches are getting used to running drills and calling plays again, the training staff is back into the swing of things, and of course, the players need time to readjust to the pace of practices. But once the […]
full_text: Green Bay Packers offensive linemen Karsen Barnhart (61), Zach Tom (50), Josh Gesky (76) and Anthony Belton (71) run through a drill during the second day of training camp Thursday, July 30, 2026, at the Don Hutson Center in Ashwaubenon, Wisconsin. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co The first week of an NFL team’s training camp is a nice ramp-up period for everyone. The coaches are getting used to running drills and calling plays again, the training staff is back into the swing of things, and of course, the players need time to readjust to the pace of practices. But once the first handful of practices are over and the pads come on, it’s a different ballgame. For the Green Bay Packers, that day is today. After four practices over the last five days in shorts, today is when the real work begins, as the team will don full pads for the first time this season. It’s a big change, and one that often brings some surprises, both positive and negative. It’s not uncommon for a player to go relatively unnoticed early in training camp, only to look like a totally different player when the contact ramps up. This year, it would be great if the Packers could find a couple of those players starting today, particularly among their deep but young group of pass rushers and their not-so-deep (but still young) tight end room. This week’s practices will build towards Family Night on Friday evening, after which the focus begins to shift to preseason games starting a week later. For now, let’s enjoy the sounds and sights of the first padded practice period of the summer. title: Groupthink: Texans writers discuss their opinions on Clowney’s return to Houston
summary: All roads lead to Rome for veteran defensive end Jadeveon Clowney. It was announced yesterday that he’d be returning to the team who selected him first overall back in 2014. He joins an extremely talented defensive end room to bolster the depth and provide veteran experience on a team hoping to make a deep playoff […]
full_text: HOUSTON, TEXAS - DECEMBER 02: Jadeveon Clowney #90 of the Houston Texans is introduced to the crowd before playing the Cleveland Browns at NRG Stadium on December 02, 2018 in Houston, Texas. (Photo by Bob Levey/Getty Images) | Getty Images All roads lead to Rome for veteran defensive end Jadeveon Clowney. It was announced yesterday that he’d be returning to the team who selected him first overall back in 2014. He joins an extremely talented defensive end room to bolster the depth and provide veteran experience on a team hoping to make a deep playoff run. With this breaking news, I urgently asked the other writers to provide their thoughts on Clowney playing in Houston one last time. Jadeveon Clowney has re-signed with the Houston Texans. Give me your immediate reaction, are you excited for his return, and how much of an impact will he have? Patrick H. Honestly, I’m way more on board with this than I thought I would be. He provides much needed depth at defensive end. He fills in for Derek Barnett’s absence, and received rave reviews from his coaching staff in Arlington. Last season he was one sack short of his career season high while playing in only 13 games. To add him makes this defense much more terrifying and puts that much more pressure on the offense to un[kitten] themselves and lead us to the promised land. VBallRetired I wrote a Value of Things (VOT) earlier this spring on possibly adding a defensive end. He was one of those guys. Essentially, when Houston lost Autry and other depth pieces, it opened the door for this kind of move. Ostensibly, Houston needed backup for Anderson and Hunter. For one, it allows them to take some plays off, to be fresh in the fourth quarter, and to step in case of injury. I like the move. Clowney is a starting quality end when motivated and it sounds like he is. Fizzy Joe I agree with Patrick and VBall, I think this is a great move made that much better as it’s a reunion between Jadeveon Clowney and his first team. Houston’s consistent success during the DeMeco Ryans era has allowed them to quickly shake off the rust and baggage of the Bill O’Brien era. Signing Clowney after all of these years is another reminder of how far we’ve come. He left via a trade surrounded by controversy and frustration across the fanbase. Now, he returns as another weapon in an already loaded defensive arsenal. As for the player, I still think Clowney is one of the most underrated DEs in the modern NFL. He’s one of the best run-defenders along the defensive line who was still a free agent. He immediately fills in the hole left by Derek Barnett and Denico Autry (even thought I’d still like Autry back, even for just his field goal blocking abilities) as a rotational edge rusher that can take the load off of Will Anderson or Danielle Hunter. Clowney’s speed when setting the edge makes him a starting-caliber player on many other teams. He’ll get plenty of playing time this year, and he’s going to feed off of being on the same line as Anderson/Hunter, Sheldon Rankins, and Kayden McDonald. He adds another layer of swarm to the defensive line, with the ceiling of being a real impact player on a weekly basis. So…yeah I’m kinda excited about Clowney coming back lol Still…wish they’ve would’ve got Calais Campbell when they had the chance… L4Blitzer I like the move. Clowney is a rotational player at this point, but that hasn’t hurt him that much. Clowney did give Dallas 8.5 sacks, and he didn’t play the entire year for a really-not-good Cowboy D. He also gave Cleveland and Baltimore solid play over the last few seasons. On a 1 yr/$8M-type deal, this won’t hurt the team much if it goes south. If Clowney can offer the type of play he showed in his last couple of stops, this is a huge bonus for the Texans. Granted, if Hunter or Anderson miss significant time, Clowney isn’t going to fully replace them. Overall, great depth signing. Kenneth L. I too anticipated Clowney, among other former Texans veterans , to re-sign this training camp. I mentioned that “out of all the names on this list, Clowney might be the best fit. He’s no longer a full‑time starter, but he plays with remarkable endurance and understands his role. Houston needs an edge‑setter with real pass‑rush juice, and Clowney delivered exactly that for the Cowboys last season”. Where I like Clowney the most is on third-down packages where he can move inside next to Anderson or Hunter and rush the passer from the DT spot. That will open up a myriad of opportunities for Houston. Not only is he savvy against the run, but his strength and length pair well with the type of pass rush responsibilities DeMeco Ryans prefers. Do I still wish they drafted a second-round DE instead of TE “Sideline” Marlin Klein, absolutely, but this is a fantastic short-term stop-gap. Oh, and the Texans re-signed Mario Edwards. This defense is going to be absurd.

title: Is Colts’ Chris Ballard on ‘borrowed time’ serving as team’s longtime GM?
summary: Last week to kickoff team training camp, Indianapolis Colts longtime general manager Chris Ballard indicated that if offered a contract extension, he won’t accept it because his built roster needs to win—entering ‘Year 10.’ Now chivalry may not in fact be dead, but on the other hand, there doesn’t appear to be any contract extension […]
full_text: Jul 30, 2026; Westfield, IN, USA; Indianapolis Colts GM Chris Ballard is seen on day two of training camp at Grand Park Sports Campus. Mandatory Credit: Robert Goddin-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect Last week to kickoff team training camp, Indianapolis Colts longtime general manager Chris Ballard indicated that if offered a contract extension, he won’t accept it because his built roster needs to win—entering ‘Year 10.’ Now chivalry may not in fact be dead, but on the other hand, there doesn’t appear to be any contract extension forthcoming from Colts team owner and CEO Carlie Irsay-Gordon. If there had been, despite the public posturing, Ballard would’ve already accepted a lucrative NFL general manager’s salary for the next few years. Ballard’s lengthy tenure as Colts general manager from 2017-2025 speaks for itself, overall win-loss record of 70-78-1, no division titles, and two playoff appearances with 1 win—and never advancing past the AFC Divisional Round approaching a decade on the job for Indianapolis. Despite proclaiming upon his arrival that it would never be about one guy, the Colts have struggled replacing and finding any sort of stability since former franchise quarterback Andrew Luck shockingly retired just ahead of the 2019 season—with the starting quarterback position continuing to be a turnstile. While a re-signed Daniel Jones may solidify the QB1 position, if he can regain his first half 2025 form, he still has to stay healthy for an entire season coming off a late year season-ending torn Achilles and even a lack of prior durability with the Giants. It figures to be ‘playoffs or pack your papers’ in Indianapolis, as the Colts have to obtain meaningful success in 2026—and that’s at least a playoff appearance one would reasonably think. The problem for Ballard and the Colts right now though is that it’s a fair question of whether Indianapolis is anymore than the 3rd best team in the AFC South, especially since current head coach Shane Steichen has gone a combined 2-10 against both the Houston Texans and Jacksonville Jaguars over his first three seasons in Indy. The Colts’ top divisional rivals are only continuing to improve too, as the Texans just re-signed their former #1 overall pick, veteran edge Jadeveon Clowney, who had 8.5 sacks last year as a rotational defensive end to what’s already a loaded positional group and stacked Houston defense collectively. It’s a fair question of whether Clowney would be an upgrade to anyone the Colts could start opposite Laiatu Latu along their d-line right now. It’s not just at defensive end where the Colts surprisingly didn’t reinforce the position with more higher-end talent, as the wide receiver spot on the outside opposite currently hobbled Alec Pierce continues to be a major question mark: One week into Colts training camp and I STILL remain convinced they are living on the edge at WR. With Alec Pierce (ankle) still out, the depth chart is essentially 1) Josh Downs 2-4) Ashton Dulin, Laquon Treadwell, Nick Westbrook-Ikhine (in some order). Gotta make a move IMO. — Stephen Holder (@HolderStephen) August 3, 2026 It seems like every offseason, Colts fans have this same typical frustration with Ballard, where there’s at least a starting position or two that looks visibly weak on paper, but Indy had some flexibility to do more. It’s been at wide receiver, left tackle, cornerback, tight end, linebacker, and safety before in years past, and with the exception of safety (where Nick Cross did emerge two years ago to be fair), it seems to have worked out less often than it’s ultimately gone right on Ballard’s intuition and seemingly ‘liking his guys.’ Perhaps Arden Key will be a solidifying veteran edge or 2nd-year pro Jaylahn Tuimoloau will take a major leap forward, and Ashton Dulin will continue to work his tail off and ascend as a suitable WR2, but it seems like Ballard and Co. are taking a major gamble, with their margin of error being small at premium NFL positions. I’m not rooting for the Colts to lose by any means. I hope they win and win consistently at that—and snap their playoff drought of five seasons dating back to 2020—and finally win at Jacksonville, snapping another woeful franchise streak in the process. By winning games, the Colts are more fun to discuss and analyze, our viewership is better across the board, and it’s more fun to write exciting articles filled with hope and serious title aspirations than somber summaries. The hope has to be that with Jones fully healthy, the Colts can replicate their first half of 2025 form, especially with former All-Pro cornerback Sauce Gardner anchoring their secondary for a full season. That being said, looking at the Colts roster as a whole, particularly with the arguable remaining key deficiencies at both Edge2 and WR2, and I’m not sure how anyone can feel super confident that it stacks up better than either the Texans or Jaguars right now—and finishing 3rd place in the AFC South simply won’t cut it again. More than likely, that means the Colts winning 7-9 games, falling just short of the playoff sticks again, and without even a 2027 first round pick to make the Horseshoe faithful even feel slightly better about it with more favorable early draft positioning. That’s what we call staying in NFL purgatory. However, I’d love to be proven wrong, and in order to do so, Ballard must firmly silence his critics and meaningfully win again, because his continued job security (*and perhaps Steichen’s too) seemingly depends on it.

(Photo by John Rivera/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images On Monday, the Indianapolis Colts announced that they waived-injured cornerback Cameron Mitchell and signed fellow corner Mekhi Rodgers in a corresponding roster move. Mitchell was injured during last Friday’s training camp practice and seemingly suffered a shoulder injury while being tended to by members of the Colts medical training staff. If unclaimed, he will revert to the Colts injured reserve. Mitchell appeared in 8 games (1 start) for the Colts last season, recording 18 tackles (14 solo), 2 tackles for loss, and 4 passes defensed. He was fighting for a cornerback spot lower on Indianapolis’ positional depth chart. Meanwhile, Rodgers is a 6,’1”, 197 pound cornerback who recently participated in the Colts 2026 rookie minicamp on a tryout basis and worked out for the club on Monday. He played in 13 games (1 start) for James Madison last year, making 8 tackles and 1 pass defensed. Along with Rodgers on Monday, the Colts also reportedly worked out former Wisconsin cornerback Ricardo Hallman, Green Bay Packers wide receiver Jakobie Keeney-James, and Philadelphia Eagles/Jacksonville Jaguars cornerback Zech McPhearson.

title: Top 3 Position Groups The Colts Quietly Need to Produce This Year
summary: When you think of the storylines surrounding the Colts this year of course the big names like Daniel Jones, Josh Downs, and Sauce Gardner come to mind. After all, the Colts need their best players to have good seasons in order to be successful. But for the sake of this exercise, I’m not going to […]
full_text: When you think of the storylines surrounding the Colts this year of course the big names like Daniel Jones, Josh Downs, and Sauce Gardner come to mind. After all, the Colts need their best players to have good seasons in order to be successful. But for the sake of this exercise, I’m not going to include them. DEFENSIVE END: Michael Clemons/Jaylahn Tuimoloau People forget the Colts signed Clemons to a sizable deal for a 4th round pick that never put it together in New York. The Colts DE depth is thin as it is and they’re asking Laiatu Latu to carry the burden of a group of players with very little pedigree or stature in the league. 3-year $17.5M isn’t the type of contract that will cause long term financial damage, but it’s enough to demand production when DL depth was the Colts biggest need heading into the spring, and Clemons was one of the few moves the Colts made to address it. I’m combining Clemons with Jaylahn Tuimoloau because they go hand-in-hand. The Colts simply cannot afford to have a third straight 2nd round pick fail to pan out for them. In my opinion, the storyline’s around the DL are too focused around Laiatu Latu becoming a stud pass rusher, when it really should be about the resources Chris Ballard surrounded the room with. Obviously Laiatu Latu needs to take the next step as a pass rusher, but if Latu is ever unavailable, this is the worst defensive end room in the league. After some thinking, I've arrived at this conclusion: If both Jaylahn Tuimoloau and Michael Clemons don't produce this year, it would be completely unacceptable regardless of how the overall defense preforms. In my mind there's a lot riding on how those two preform this year. — Colts Film Room (@ColtsFilmRoom) August 2, 2026 BACKUP RUNNING BACK: DJ Giddens, Seth McGowan The backup RB spot was an afterthought for the Colts in 2026 given how special Jonathan Taylor was playing (Outside of some quality Ameer Abdullah reps). While JT will continue to get the bulk of the carries, and deservedly so, I often think about the 2023 season and the role Zack Moss had. While JT has done an incredible job staying on the field, he’s headed for his third contract. RB longevity is scarce, and while JT is a rare breed an exception to the rule, I think the Colts would be wise to manage some of his carries to make sure he’s available when it matters. Additionally last year he regressed as the season wore on in pass protection and teams like the Chiefs and Steelers set the blueprint for how to take advantage of that. The Colts seemed excited aboutDJ Giddens , yet only Abdullah seemed to crack the starting roster. The Colts staff values trust (sometimes to a fault), and Giddens has yet to earn that. I don’t think there’s enough of a sample size of publicly available snaps to say whether Giddens can pan out for the Colts yet, but I did like the pick at the time. Seth McGowan is another interesting pick that I think offers the Colts some upside. I think McGowan has the better chance of the two to make an impact for the Colts. Giddens had the opportunity to emerge last year, but Ameer Abdullah won Shane Steichen over and became. the de facto 2nd RB. Nonetheless, it all comes down to whether or not the Colts want to manage JT’s snap count. It’s hard to see what he does every Sunday and take him off the field, but it would feel a lot easier if one of two backs emerged. RIGHT SIDE OF THE OL: Matt Goncalves, Jalen Farmer, Jalen Travis We’ve lived in a Chris Ballard world where the OL has rarely been the concern of the Colts. It’s one of the few benefits that I think Colts fans probably take for granted. With Braden Smith departing in free agency and the Colts drafting Jalen Farmer to push Goncalves in year 2 at guard, I think there’s some fair question marks. While I have very little doubt that Tony Sparano Jr. won’t find a proper solution, but it’s crucial that the right side of the OL holds up this year. Daniel Jones obviously needs proper protection as someone who has historically struggled under pressure and struggled to stay healthy, but also because the Colts have a diverse run game that needs versatile lineman in order to execute.

title: Ground game takes center stage in Colts first padded practice
summary: WESTFIELD, Ind. — The thud of shoulder pads popped and echoed across Droplight Grand Park Sports Campus for the first time as the Indianapolis Colts held their first fully padded practice.  Day 5 of training camp featured the physicality of football, culminating in a live tackling period for reserve players that brought an extra level […]
full_text: WESTFIELD, IN - AUGUST 3: Indianapolis Colts running back Jonathan Taylor (28) runs through a drill during the Indianapolis Colts training camp practice on August 3, 2026 at the Grand Park Sports Campus in Westfield, IN. (Photo by Zach Bolinger/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images WESTFIELD, Ind. — The thud of shoulder pads popped and echoed across Droplight Grand Park Sports Campus for the first time as the Indianapolis Colts held their first fully padded practice. Day 5 of training camp featured the physicality of football, culminating in a live tackling period for reserve players that brought an extra level of intensity before the final team session of practice. As expected, head coach Shane Steichen shifted the focus toward establishing the run game in the trenches and emphasizing proper tackling angles for the young defensive unit. Quarterback Daniel Jones completed just 5-of-7 passes across three team periods, while none of his attempts were thrown further than 10 yards downfield. His best deep shot started off the 7-on-7 drills as he dropped a perfectly placed slot fade into Ashton Dulin’s hands, but the veteran receiver couldn’t finish the catch after cornerback Justin Walley contested it. Without receiver Alec Pierce on the field, Indianapolis lacks any vertical element of its offense, which allowed the defense to tighten coverage underneath. Cornerback Sauce Gardner opened team drills by breaking up a slant intended for Dulin. In fact, all three quarterbacks had a pass broken up by a defensive back in the initial team period. Cornerback Jonathan Edwards recognized the run-pass-option to knock away a slant from Anthony Richardson Sr., then safety Daniel Scott added another pass breakup in the flat against Riley Leonard. While the passing game stayed quiet, the rushing attack found plenty of success. Star running back Jonathan Taylor looked every bit like the reigning NFL leader in total touchdowns (20), displaying his burst throughout Monday’s practice that was centered around the ground game. It was evidenced best on a slick screen pass that Taylor took for an explosive play during one of the final team sessions. Taylor is entering the final year of his three-year, $42 million extension with the Colts. 𝐉ust ₂₈ doin his 𝐓hing pic.twitter.com/sWdSN4B6Um — Indianapolis Colts (@Colts) August 3, 2026 Rookie running back Seth McGowan also continued to shine in his impressive first camp. The seventh-round draft pick ripped off consecutive productive runs during the opening 11-on-11 period. First, McGowan found daylight on a counter play behind the first-team offensive line, then immediately followed it with another strong run the opposite way while staying on the field with the second unit. McGowan later took a swing pass past midfield for a gain of more than 20 yards. New additions on the defense also made their presence known as rookie linebacker Bryce Boettcher continued receiving significant first-team reps alongside Akeem Davis-Gaither. First round draft pick C.J. Allen and third-round safety A.J. Haulcy also continued to ramp up their involvement within the starting defense. Rookie edge rushers George Gumbs Jr. and Caden Curry also created their share of disruptions in the backfield. Gumbs exploded through an interior blocker for what likely would have resulted in a sack, while Curry secured a tackle for loss and added another run stop after a minimal gain. Kicker Blake Grupe connected on all six of his field goal attempts from distances of 26, 33, 39, 45, 51 and 57 yards out. His flawless performance throughout training camp shows he may be the favorite heading into the 2026 season. Grupe made all 11 of his field goal attempts during the final five games of the 2025 season after being picked up off waivers by Indianapolis in December. Real football is officially back as the Colts’ fifth open practice featured collisions for the first time this summer. The Colts have just five more practices and 10 days to sharpen their execution before opening their first preseason game against the reigning AFC-champion New England Patriots in Foxborough.

title: Jaguars Reacts Survey: How many takeaways will the defense have in 2026?
summary: Welcome to SB Nation Reacts, a survey of fans across the NFL. Throughout the year we ask questions of the most plugged-in Jaguars fans and fans across the country. The Jacksonville Jaguars’ turnover luck on defense finally flipped last season. After generating the NFL’s third-fewest turnovers from 2020-24 (89), including the fewest in the league […]
full_text: JACKSONVILLE, FL - JULY 31: Jacksonville Jaguars cornerback Jourdan Lewis (2) and Jacksonville Jaguars cornerback Keni-H Lovely (31) work on a drill during training camp on July 31, 2026 at the Miller Electric Center in Jacksonville, Fl. (Photo by David Rosenblum/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Welcome to SB Nation Reacts, a survey of fans across the NFL. Throughout the year we ask questions of the most plugged-in Jaguars fans and fans across the country. The Jacksonville Jaguars’ turnover luck on defense finally flipped last season. After generating the NFL’s third-fewest turnovers from 2020-24 (89), including the fewest in the league in 2024 (9), the Jags ranked second with 31 forced turnovers in 2025. The secondary adopted the moniker “Strapsonville” about halfway through the season. It was quite the debut for defensive coordinator Anthony Campanile and his staff. “We’re being coached to take the ball away,” cornerback Jourdan Lewis said after Monday’s training camp practice . “High pointing the ball, making sure that the receiver can’t make a catch, make a play on the ball in the air. We’re being coached to do that. Everything that you see, all the turnovers, everything that we’re doing, being ball hungry, that’s getting coached.” “And we have the talent to go out there and do it every single week, as you saw last year. When we came out here at OTAs last year, I knew, like, ‘Wow, we got some guys that can go take the ball away.’ Just like this year. OTAs and training camp, we just have to fine-tune some of our detailed things, but we have the talent to take the ball away.” While I don’t disagree with anything Lewis said, it’s hard to imagine Jacksonville forcing 30+ turnovers for a second straight season. Linebacker Devin Lloyd accounted for nearly a fifth of the 2025 production with 5 interceptions and 1 fumble recovery; he’s now a Carolina Panther. The defense will gain playmaking ability via Travis Hunter, sure, but a 15.6% clip of turnovers per drive will still be difficult to carry over. Such rates tend to fluctuate from year to year . Here’s some added context on the Jaguars from clevanalytics . The defense finished 5th in the NFL by EPA but when you eliminate turnovers, they ranked 11th, the 2nd largest drop in the NFL behind the Bears defense. They also faced the single easiest schedule of opposing QBs by EPA, with 54% of snaps coming from either a backup QB or a QB ranked 30th or worse by EPA. When adjusting for opposing QB and using success rate instead of EPA, which can be heavily skewed by turnovers, the Jags pass defense was right around league average. Those turnovers also really helped benefit the Jags as no offense in the NFL saw more short fields than Jacksonville (28) and no team saw a higher percentage of their season points come from short fields (25.3%). If only evaluating offenses by drives that started in their own territory, the Jags offense ranks just league average on a points per drive basis. Again — I don’t disagree with Lewis’ points about having good coaching and talent. That should keep Jacksonville from pulling a sharp U-turn back into the pits of turnover rankings. But will they get enough bounces of the ball to have another massive season in the turnover department? How many turnovers do you think the defense will force in 2026? Sign up here to participate in the weekly emailed surveys: Let us know your thoughts in the comments below!

title: Chris Rodriguez Jr. brings the boom to Jaguars’ first padded practice of 2026 training camp
summary: The pads came on today at the Miller Electric Center for Day 5 of Jacksonville Jaguars training camp. Real football is rapidly approaching. “I thought those guys did a nice job of getting some work in while protecting each other,” head coach Liam Coen said post-practice. “I thought we got some good quality work. Good […]
full_text: JACKSONVILLE, FL - AUGUST 02: Jacksonville Jaguars running back Chris Rodriguez Jr. (24) during training camp on August 2, 2026 at the Miller Electric Center in Jacksonville, Fl. (Photo by David Rosenblum/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The pads came on today at the Miller Electric Center for Day 5 of Jacksonville Jaguars training camp. Real football is rapidly approaching. “I thought those guys did a nice job of getting some work in while protecting each other,” head coach Liam Coen said post-practice. “I thought we got some good quality work. Good to see some of those guys make some plays one-on-one in those situations.” Cornerback Jourdan Lewis was a bit more hesitant to praise the team’s first padded practice of the 2026 season. “It felt like we were overthinking. We were overthinking about it. Just some of the detailed things that we did over the last few days kind of slipped—especially me. A lot of times I’m talking from my perspective, as a leader. It just slipped today. You can see that going through all of the guys from the younger to the older guys. I got to bring that discipline, that intentionality to our practices. It was just, ‘Oh, we got pads on, let’s go hit, let’s go get our hands on them’ instead of just being on our details.” There was definitely a little more excitement in the air this morning. The first day of pads is an unofficial celebration for every NFL club. And the player whom Coen seemed most excited to see in pads did not disappoint. Running back Chris Rodriguez Jr. has been brought along slowly in offseason training programs after undergoing foot surgery . The free agent pickup only participated in individual drills for the first three days of training camp, but Rodriguez Jr. saw his first rep in team drills on Sunday, and he left a mark on Monday. On his first of a handful of carries on the day, the 5’11”, 224-pound bowling ball weaved through a rushing lane before unleashing his momentum upon a defensive back, making him look like a rack of pins hurling backward. The slobberknocker brought a chorus of “oohs” and ”aahs” from the peanut gallery. Jaguars fans gave Rodriguez Jr. a standing O as former Jaguars legends nodded in appreciation from the sideline. I joked to one ex-player, “That run was like a cup of coffee, huh?” He replied with a straight face: “I like seeing that shit.” It was, like, an 8-yard run. In the beginning of August. Without referees, or scoreboards, or announcers, or TV timeouts. It’d be easy to say it doesn’t matter much. But anyone who witnessed the play might say it set the tone not just for this morning, but for this season. “Yeah, I mean, he did kind of what you think he’s going to do in a way,” Coen said of Rodriguez Jr., whom he coached at Kentucky in 2021. “I mean, I don’t think he meant to necessarily—I don’t think he even really lowered his shoulder on Caleb [Ransaw]. It was just one of those hits.” “I think he was feeling better. He’s continuously getting better, and we’re just trying to be smart with, all right, getting him to work, getting him acclimated while not trying to aggravate it, knowing that we’re so early on. And I know he was excited about getting the pads on.” Notes & Quotes I came away from OL/DL 1-vs-1 drills with two major impressions. 1: When Anton Harrison is on, he looks like one of the best offensive tackles in all of football. His foot speed and general smoothness have always stood out, but ‘Ton is also shining when it comes to hand usage and finishing plays. Today, he cross-trained at left tackle without missing a beat. Harrison didn’t let up any ground against Josh-Hines Allen, and he made Danny Striggow (who did play well in team drills) look like it was you or me out there. “He was dominant,” linebackers coach Mark Duffner told 1010XL . “I think he’s done a nice job,” said Coen. “It’s part of what we’ve done, moving those guys around and seeing what sticks. And if that ends up sticking, hopefully that’s a good thing for us.” 2: Ruke Orhororo is another trench player who’s flashing. He came to Jacksonville via an April trade with Atlanta and already looks ready to contribute. A sudden swipe move during 1-vs-1 drills led to a quick whistle from a coach and an approving roar from the fans. “Nice to see him flash,” Coen said. “It’s always a little bit more realistic when you get the pads on. I mean, pass pro sucks with no pads on. It just does. So, it’s nice to see him win when you’re expecting the pass rush to maybe be a little less than it’s been because of the pads being on.” Beyond the baptism by Rodriguez Jr., the play of the day came from Brian Thomas Jr. on a one-handed catch deep down the sideline. His reception came against Montaric Brown, a.k.a. “Buster, a.k.a “our number one [cornerback]” according to Lewis. It was notably the first time that Thomas Jr. and Trevor Lawrence connected on a long ball during team drills in training camp. Coen said, “When you can throw the ball over somebody’s head, it’s a threat, man. And it’s something that we need. We need not just him to be able to do that but win on some of the other reps. He’s run a lot of routes out here that maybe weren’t getting targeted to him that he’s won as well that I’ve been pleased with. So, I think it brings everybody up. It elevates everybody’s game when BT is playing at his highest level.” Coming at ya! 💥 @Dream_Finders | #DUUUVAL pic.twitter.com/9itZkDOPFW — Jacksonville Jaguars (@Jaguars) August 3, 2026 This morning’s rainy conditions did lead to some issues for the offense. A few snaps were fumbled, a handoff was nearly botched, and Lawrence missed two downfield throws to Parker Washington that seemed to be partly tied to the weather. But Coen was glad to have had the opportunity to play with a wet ball. “Like, it’s football, right? It has to be an edge for us, here in Florida. And knowing that, shoot, last year, we had a delay in Week 1. We’ve got to get that working … You’re concerned, guys anchoring and slipping out. But it’s football. I mean, stuff happens.” Most of Duval County has heard by now that Coen considers the running game to be one of the Jaguars’ few “stinks” from last year. When asked what specifically the team is working on to improve in that area, Coen focused on double-team blocks. “Yeah, just being thicker on combinations a little bit. Sometimes, based on the scheme, the O-Line will think they have to maybe get on an angle because of where the ball’s going. Say it’s outside zone, they feel like they just have to run because it’s outside. Well, no, let’s take care of the down [block] first, and be a little bit thicker through combinations so that we’re moving the line of scrimmage.” Another way that Coen is looking to improve is by experimenting with plays from other teams. “When we watch all of our wide zones, we watch, let’s call it 100 of them. Directly underneath are the top, let’s call it, three to five teams around the league that we felt ran wide zone the best … you get to see you, and you get to see the best that are doing that exact concept. So, whether it’s scheme, truly the concept, or a fundamental of how they’re doing it, ‘Well, hey, does that fit us?’ And we’re trying some of those things now, yeah.” Jaguars fans, let us know your thoughts in the comments below!

Five Observations from Saturday’s Practice | Chiefs Training Camp 8/1 | Chiefs.com 2. Defensive back Chris Roland-Wallace hauled in an interception during 11-on-11 drills. Roland-Wallace made one of the defensive plays of the morning when he corralled an interception during an 11-on-11 period. Fellow rookie defensive back Zelmar Vedder also recorded an impressive play with a diving pass-breakup during an 11-on-11 period. ‘He’s as strong as an Ox and has feet like a Ballerina’ — Josh Simmons looks like KC Chiefs’ most improved player at training camp | A to Z Sports “Josh (Simmons) is a great player,” Karlaftis said. “You know, obviously had a great season last year, so that was out a few games and stuff like that. No. 1 on the list is host Joe Rogan with his Spotify show “The Joe Rogan Experience.” That program brings in $82 million a year. So, yes, that’s more than many professional athletes make in a year. As for Travis and Jason, they ranked No. 7 on Forbes’ tally with an estimated earnings of $35 million. They actually have Swift to thank too, at least partially. Around the NFL A.J. Brown on injury: ‘Thumb out of place, you keep going’ | ESPN “It was tough. I tried to get back into that flow-state zone really quickly because obviously you’re going through some pain,” Brown said in an interview with Mike Garafolo and Brian Baldinger, who were broadcasting from practice. “The game is what it is, you’re going to get bumps and bruises, and you have to keep going. I know it’s practice, but I’m not coming out of practice. Thumb out of place? You keep going.” Mike McCarthy wants Aaron Rodgers to play in Steelers’ preseason games | NFL.com “He (wants me out there for) 30 or 40 plays,” Rodgers told Silver. “I said, ‘Mike, if you want me to play, I’ll play.’ I’m not saying I want to do it. But if he wants me to, I will.” McCarthy clarified his expectations on Monday. “Those decisions are really gonna be made once we get up to it,” the Steelers coach said. “Trust me, I have a lot of ideas. … We have plans, but being a healthy system, let’s see what happens. A lot can happen between now and [then]. Sean Payton: Broncos in ‘no hurry’ with possible pursuit of Taysom Hill | The Athletic On Monday, though, Payton said the Broncos are in “no hurry right now” to get Hill into their building. Payton, who coached the multi-position Hill for five seasons in New Orleans, noted that he would visit with the 35-year-old this weekend in Canton, Ohio, where both will be attending the Hall of Fame induction of former Saints quarterback Drew Brees. “We’ll see where he’s at and kind of go from there,” Payton said. “The key thing is his health and where he’s at mentally. I don’t want to assume that he still wants to play. I haven’t had a chance to talk with him.” In case you missed it on Arrowhead Pride Chiefs training camp: 3 players with the most to lose Kansas City’s tight end depth has been poor for multiple seasons now, and it is not looking much better, and that is precisely why Gray could be a loser once camp and the preseason conclude. If any player behind him in the depth chart can make any sort of immediate impact, or show that they can surpass him, the addition would be welcome by Chiefs Kingdom. Gray has not been bad for Kansas City, but being a below-average run blocker and scheme-dependent pass catcher has not allowed the Chiefs to have much diversity from the primary backup for Travis Kelce. title: Monday Musings: The most impressive player at Chiefs camp so far
summary: We are five days into Kansas City Chiefs training camp this year and have only seen one full practice with the team in pads. As I drove back from St. Joe to Kansas City on Monday afternoon, a thought came to mind: who has been the single-most impressive performer, the MVP so to speak, of […]
full_text: KANSAS CITY, MISSOURI - JUNE 08: Drue Tranquill #23 of the Kansas City Chiefs on set during a production shoot at The University of Kansas Health System Training Complex on June 08, 2026 in Kansas City, Missouri. (Photo by Aaron M. Sprecher/Getty Images) | Getty Images We are five days into Kansas City Chiefs training camp this year and have only seen one full practice with the team in pads. As I drove back from St. Joe to Kansas City on Monday afternoon, a thought came to mind: who has been the single-most impressive performer, the MVP so to speak, of Chiefs camp so far? Drue Tranquill sneaky camp MVP through five practices. He’s been super active, especially picking up downfield routes. He’s stuck to WRs and taken away some throws — Ron Kopp Jr (@RonOnChiefs) August 3, 2026 From Day 1 to Day 5, it sort of blew me away how easily I settled on linebacker Drue Tranquill to answer that question. Tranquill has shown off his ability to anticipate run plays and knife into the backfield from the weak-side linebacker position, but he has also played on the edge in a few looks that featured three down linemen and three linebackers; Tranquill was the fourth player on the edge, in a similar role to former Chiefs linebacker Leo Chenal during his time. He has looked stout against the run, but Tranquill feels like the answer because of his effort and energy to make plays in coverage. On Saturday, he seemingly baited quarterback Patrick Mahomes into throwing over the middle, watching his eyes and driving from the back side to make the interception in a seven-on-seven period. Throughout practices, Tranquill has played with urgency when dropping into coverage, sticking to pass catchers entering his zone and denying passes regardless of how far down the field the route goes. On one play Monday, Mahomes looked for wide receiver Jimmy Holiday down the field towards the sideline, but Tranquill back-handed the ball away, looking like a defensive back in the process. He seems to be having a complete camp, with high energy included. He’ll get animated after making a big play and bring fire out of teammates, like when running back Kenneth Walker beamed Tranquill with the ball after Tranquill finished a play aggressively in shells. It’s not a bad thing to stir the pot at camp, but that play — along with the interception mentioned before — symbolizes Tranquill’s mentality as one of the defense’s veteran leaders. “[We’re] trying to make an emphasis this year on getting the ball out,” Tranquill told the media after Friday’s practice. “We need to get the ball out more on defense.” Who has stood out to you the most from your intake of camp coverage, or your own in-person observations? Let us know in the comments.

title: Chiefs training camp notebook Day 5: Peter Woods pops in pads
summary: It was a sunny, warmer day in St. Joe for Kansas City Chiefs training camp practice, the fifth of camp and the first in full pads. The team came into Monday’s practice fresh off the first off day since the full team arrived on the campus of Missouri Western State University. Here’s the recap of […]
full_text: ST JOSEPH, MISSOURI - JULY 25: Peter Woods #99 walks toward the practice field during Kansas City Chiefs Training Camp at Missouri Western State University on July 25, 2026 in St Joseph, Missouri. (Photo by Jamie Squire/Getty Images) | Getty Images It was a sunny, warmer day in St. Joe for Kansas City Chiefs training camp practice, the fifth of camp and the first in full pads. The team came into Monday’s practice fresh off the first off day since the full team arrived on the campus of Missouri Western State University. Here’s the recap of Monday’s practice: Attendance report Head coach Andy Reid spoke to the media after practice and provided details on the three active Chiefs who were unavailable on Monday : wide receivers Cyrus Allen and Xavier Worthy, and defensive end Ashton Gillotte. As they have each day of practice, cornerback L’Jarius Sneed and wide receiver Rashee Rice took the field with the team in full uniform. Each participated with pads on, although Rice seemed to be held out of 11-on-11, full-team period work against the defense. Sneed seemed to be in the same boat, although I have noted his movement as closer to 100% comparatively to Rice. Peter Woods properly introduces himself While observing the full-team periods, star defensive tackle Chris Jones reminded fans of his dominance with a few disruptive, blow-by snaps. However, rookie defensive tackle Peter Woods also stood out by disengaging from blocks ferociously or leveraging himself to plug a gap while fighting with an offensive lineman. Peter Woods was very pleased after these two 1-on-1 reps. #Chiefs pic.twitter.com/lI2mEZp71m — Harold R. Kuntz (@HaroldRKuntz3) August 3, 2026 I didn’t get a good look at his performance in the one-on-one pass-rush drills, but Harold Kuntz of FOX4 highlights a couple of notable reps that show off the skill Andy Reid pointed out when asked about Woods after practice. “I like what I’ve seen. He’s an explosive kid,” Reid said. “He’s learning; he’s smart, and he’s trying to hone in on some of these techniques we’re asking him to do. [I] like his effort. He’s got a ways to go, but you sure like the tools, the effort and how smart he is. I appreciate that.” On one particular one-on-one rep in the lineman drills, right guard Trey Smith stonewalled Woods, who tapped him on the helmet with respect after the rep. It was truly iron sharpening iron; Smith sounded excited about his new teammates across the line of scrimmage when talking to reporters on Monday. “Peter’s really talented,” Smith said. “The sky is the limit for him. In terms of his hand utilization, speed, power, he’s really sort of a full-package guy. He’s young, and he’s figuring out the game, but he has a willingness to learn. I’ve really, really enjoyed the way he has stepped into this program, this organization and how he’s trying to turn himself into a great player,“ Smith emphasized. ”Definitely has an outstanding future ahead of him, just really excited to help with his development where I can.” Who is catching passes from Patrick Mahomes? Without Worthy and Allen running routes for the Chiefs’ offense, the three starting receivers when running plays on air were wide receivers Rashee Rice, Tyquan Thornton and Andrew Armstrong. Rice wasn’t playing much during full-team periods, so players like Jalen Royals, Nikko Remigio and Jimmy Holiday saw more time in the mix with the starting offense. Similar to the way Allen was seemingly Mahomes’ favorite target for an early stretch of camp, Armstrong stepped up on Monday. Reid can see it. “Armstrong… he went through the rookie camp, and pushed through that. I thought he did a nice job there, and he has transferred that over,” Reid shared. “It looks like Pat has trust in him. So I think that’s a plus; he’s getting better every day. Big target, strong… I like that part of it.” On second-year wideout Jalen Royals, who hasn’t made the same pop as Allen or Armstrong in camp, Reid kept the praise simple. “I think Royals has kind of gotten better playing faster every day that he has been here.” What Andy Reid is looking for at right tackle On the first day of full pads, rookie Kahlil Benson got the nod as the starting right tackle for the fourth consecutive practice. However, veteran Jaylon Moore quickly rotated in with the starters in practice; the two seemingly split time between the first and second teams on the right side. “Let them compete, and just see where it goes,” Reid said of the position battle after practice. “Both of them can play, I think. We just have a young guy we haven’t seen much of, but he has some talent. Let’s see where that goes. “Moore keeps battling; he has had a couple good days, too,” Reid noted. “We’ll need all of them, that’s how it goes.” When asked about the inevitable mistakes Benson will make as a first-year player, Reid made his stance on the learning curve clear. “Not to make the same mistake twice, right? That’s what I’m looking for,” Reid said. “We’ll give you a chance here to learn, but if you start making it consistently, then we have a problem. But he has been doing a good job. There’s a hiccup here or there, but he fixes it, normally.” Andy points to pass-pro improvement for Brashard Smith In the early stages of camp, second-year running back Brashard Smith has seemingly been the most immediate backup to Kenneth Walker in the Chiefs’ starting backfield. He has been an outlet for quarterback Patrick Mahomes on screen passes and in the flat during practice, but he has also received plenty of handoffs in run-game work. If he is to continue seeing the ball with the first team, he will need to be effective in all facets of a pass down. “I know he can run the football; I know he’s good with the ball in his hands, catching the ball,” Reid said of Smith. “Can you do all the small things that a running back has to do with protection, the intricacies of the different routes we have for him? We’ll see how we’ve improved, protection being the big one.”
