title: Patriots 2026 scouting report for TE Tanner Arkin
summary: The New England Patriots made some significant investments in their tight end group this offseason. However, at the end of the day, it might not be a surprise if the most impactful player of the bunch ends up being one who flew largely under the radar: undrafted rookie Tanner Arkin. One of the pleasant surprises […]
full_text: Jul 28, 2026; Foxborough, MA, USA; New England Patriots tight end Tanner Arkin (84) dose a drill during training camp at Gillette Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Eric Canha-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect The New England Patriots made some significant investments in their tight end group this offseason. However, at the end of the day, it might not be a surprise if the most impactful player of the bunch ends up being one who flew largely under the radar: undrafted rookie Tanner Arkin. One of the pleasant surprises of this year’s training camp, Arkin currently looks like the Patriots’ top blocking tight end. It is a role he is well-suited to fill. Hard facts Name: Tanner Arkin Position: Tight end Jersey number: 84 Opening day age: 23 (7/7/2003) Measurements : 6’3 5/8”, 262 lbs, 10 1/8” hand size, 32 1/4” arm length, 77 5/8” wingspan, 4.88s 40-yard dash, 7.44s 3-cone drill, 4.50s short shuttle, 33 1/2” vertical jump, 9’5” broad jump, 21 bench press reps, 5.45 Relative Athletic Score Experience NFL: New England Patriots (2026-) | College: Colorado State (2021-22), Illinois (2023-25) A three-star recruit coming out of Fossil Ridge in Fort Collins, CO, Arkin started his college career less than six miles from his high school field: he joined Colorado State in 2021, and in two season as a Ram played 15 games with eight starts. Catching 15 passes for 125 yards along the way, he decided to enter the transfer portal shortly after his redshirt freshman campaign. Arkin took his talents to Illinois, where he saw prominent action right out of the gate before becoming a fixture in 2024 and 2025. A team captain both seasons, he finished his tenure in Champaign with the second-most career starts by a tight end in school history (29 of 38 games). He also hauled in 30 catches for 226 yards and six touchdowns before leaving school in 2026. Primarily a blocking tight end in college, Arkin received limited hype entering the NFL. He eventually went undrafted and joined the Patriots as a rookie free agent. Scouting report Strengths: From his build to his tenacity and physical play style, Arkin is a blocking tight end through and through. Checking in at just under 6-foot-4 and 262 pounds, he is able to hunker down as a pass protector and take the battle to the defense as a run blocker. He uses his big hands and natural grip strength well to latch onto defenders, and keeps his feet churning to drive them off the ball. He also has the core strength and raw power to hold his own 1-on-1 against defensive edges, as well as a natural feel for leverage and balance. In addition, he operates well when asked to block on the move and can execute down and reach blocks from his alignment on the edge. #Patriots TE Tanner Arkin (#85) run blocking pic.twitter.com/HmbZyOKI35 — Taylor Kyles (@tkyles39) April 27, 2026 Weaknesses: Arkin catching only 45 passes during his college career did not happen by accident. He simply lacks the foot speed and agility to function as anything but a rudimentary part of a passing game, while also not having the length to be used as a consistent contested-catch target. Even when he was thrown the ball, he has been unable to do a lot with it as far as picking up yards after the catch or breaking tackles is concerned. Even as a blocker, he is not a finished product. He oftentimes forces his way to success, winning by brute strength rather than an advanced technical setup particularly in regards to his hand usage. 2025 review Stats : 13 games (13 starts) | 684 offensive snaps, 156 special teams snaps | 17 targets, 13 catches (76.5%), 114 receiving yards (8.8/catch), 2 TDs, 1 drop | 8 QB pressures surrendered (2 sacks, 2 hits, 4 hurries) | 2 penalties (incl. 0 declined/offsetting) Season recap: Arkin earned a starting role in the Illinois offense in 2024, and he retained it heading into his final season in college. That was not the only continuation between those two years: he also was once again voted a team captain and ended up seeing a majority of his snaps as a blocker: either run blocking or pass protecting on 72.5% of his offensive snaps, he set new career highs in terms of usage in both categories. Arkin blocked the run on 368 snaps, and the pass on 128. He was at his best in the running game and helped Illinois average 4.6 yards per carry and score 11 touchdowns when running outside the tackles. Those numbers are naturally not only a byproduct of his presence on the field. That said, his steady usage is an illustration of his success and the trust head coach Bret Bielema and his staff had in him. As a pass protector, meanwhile, Arkin surrendered a career-worst eight pressures, including two sacks. His 6.6% pressure rate allowed, however, on par with his 2024 season. In the receiving department, Arkin was again somewhat quiet and went catch-less in five of 13 games. The others saw him post career-highs in yards (114) and yards per catch (8.8), but his impact was still relatively inconsequential — a result of both his role as well as his comparatively uninspiring abilities as a receiver. After the season, Arkin did participate in the American Bowl. He was neither invited to any of the premier college showcases nor the Scouting Combine. 2026 preview Position: Y-tight end | Ability: Depth player/Role player | Contract: Signed through 2028 (2029 RFA) What will be his role? Arkin is the prototypical blocking tight end and will be used accordingly as a Patriot. His first eight training camp practices already show what this means: he mostly lines up inline as a Y-tight end to help create a push in the run game and occasionally provide an extra body in pass protection. Unsurprisingly, he has been employed in a limited fashion as a receiver. The 23-year-old projects as a second or third tight end. What is his growth potential? It would be easy to say that Arkin has room for growth as a receiver, but the expectations in that regard should still be tempered; his abilities and athletic skill are simply not at the level of a regular pass game contributor outside of helping shore up the protection. When it comes to his blocking, he already is looking like an NFL player but should still improve with more time and experience. He therefore has the potential to become a starter-level TE2 and one of the league’s better blocking specialists at the position. Does he have positional versatility? Arkin’s versatility manifests itself differently that for other players. He won’t move all around the formation as a receiver, even though he does have some experience in that regard. He also should not be expected to see a high number of snaps as a receiving outlet. He is mostly a blocker, but one who can perform his duties from various alignments inline or in the backfield. He additionally brings extensive special teams experience to New England, having seen most of his action on kickoff return as well as a protector on punts, field goals and extra points. What is his salary cap situation? Arkin’s salary cap number of $890,833 consists of an $885,000 base salary as well as a fully-guaranteed signing bonus proration of $5,833. In addition, the deal includes $145,000 in salary guarantees. At the moment and with the NFL’s Top 51 rule in place, only the signing bonus counts against New England’s cap. How safe is his roster spot? Typically, undrafted rookies are longshots to make a team’s roster. Arkin, however, does not look like your typical UDFA. He did not particularly stand out during open offseason workouts, but has regularly repped with the starters since the beginning of training camp and at this point can be regarded the team’s top run-blocking tight end. If there is one rookie free agent to make the team this year, it very well could be him. Summary: The season-ending injury suffered by free agency acquisition Julian Hill changed the Patriots’ tight end room and robbed them of their designated blocking tight end. Arkin, however, appears to have picked up the slack and…

title: What signing Casey Rogers means for the Patriots
summary: After releasing linebacker Otis Reese, the New England Patriots headed into the weekend with one open spot on their roster. They filled it on Monday: the team of head coach Mike Vrabel signed defensive tackle Casey Rogers following a successful workout. Let’s asses what the move means. Defensive line TBD Besides filling out their 90-man […]
full_text: EAST RUTHERFORD, NJ - AUGUST 08: Casey Rogers #91 of the New York Giants warms up prior to an NFL football game against the Detroit Lions at MetLife Stadium on August 8, 2024 in East Rutherford, NJ. (Photo by Perry Knotts/Getty Images) | Getty Images After releasing linebacker Otis Reese , the New England Patriots headed into the weekend with one open spot on their roster. They filled it on Monday: the team of head coach Mike Vrabel signed defensive tackle Casey Rogers following a successful workout. Let’s asses what the move means. Defensive line TBD Besides filling out their 90-man roster, the Patriots now also have 10 defensive tackles on their roster; the team effectively replaced Otis Reese’s roster spot with an interior defensive lineman. However, as a seemingly trivial look at the jersey numbers shows, more change might be afoot: Interior defensive line (10): Milton Williams (97), Christian Barmore (90), Cory Durden (94), Joshua Farmer (92), Leonard Taylor III (93), Eric Gregory (95), Jeremiah Pharms Jr. (98), Isaiah Iton (62), David Blay Jr. (96), Casey Rogers (96) At the moment, the team has assigned both Rogers and undrafted rookie David Blay Jr. the No. 96 jersey. That might in itself not mean much, but with the latter ominously absent from practice on Monday , it appears another move could very well be on the horizon. For now, all we know is that Rogers is on the team and that Blay Jr’s status is unclear. Immense athleticism Rogers projects as a rotational member of the Patriots’ interior defensive line who is best suited to attack from a 3-technique position. More of a pass rusher than a run stopper, he brings an intriguing athletic profile to the table: his 9.82 Relative Athletic Score had him ranked 34th out of 1,809 DTs coming out of college between 1987 and 2024, the year he entered the league as a rookie free agent. The Patriots signed an impressive athlete today. — Bernd Buchmasser (@berndbuchmasser.bsky.social) 2026-08-03T22:01:21.852Z So far in his career, Rogers has not been able to make use of his athletic skills. He has played just 35 defensive snaps over three career games and has no statistics to his name. Maybe another change of scenery — he also had a brief stint in Buffalo last summer — will help him properly get his career started. Familiarity The Patriots coaching staff has some familiarity with Rogers. Defensive coordinator Zak Kuhr, for example, was a defensive assistant with the Giants when they signed the Oregon product as a UDFA in 2024. Also part of the New York staff were Shane Bowen, the former Giants DC who came to New England as a defensive analyst earlier this offseason, as well as vice president of player personnel Ryan Cowden. That familiarity might not have been the ultimate deciding factor in hiring Rogers over fellow workout participant Jared Penning, but it certainly did not hurt either. The 27-year-old having some experience in a similar system should make for an easier transition. No cap changes Rogers is entering his third season in the NFL, but his addition as the 91st player on the team — including roster-exempt offensive tackle Lorenz Metz — does not have an impact on New England’s salary cap. His expected $960,000 minimum salary pact does not qualify for Top 51 status, and no guarantees will be part of the pact he signed to come to Foxborough. As of Monday afternoon, cap expert Miguel Benzan’s calculations have the Patriots $33.7 million under the salary cap.
author: Bernd Buchmasser

title: 6 performances of note from the Patriots’ eighth training camp practice
summary: The New England Patriots practiced behind semi-closed doors on Monday, moving their session into their Field House due to inclement weather. The conditions may have prevented fans from attending, but they did nothing to stop the competitiveness. To recap the eighth practice of the summer, please visit our Patriots training camp notebook. In the meantime, […]
full_text: Jul 28, 2026; Foxborough, MA, USA; New England Patriots wide receiver Mack Hollins (13) catches the ball during training camp at Gillette Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Eric Canha-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect The New England Patriots practiced behind semi-closed doors on Monday, moving their session into their Field House due to inclement weather. The conditions may have prevented fans from attending, but they did nothing to stop the competitiveness. To recap the eighth practice of the summer, please visit our Patriots training camp notebook . In the meantime, here is who caught our eye during the two-hour session. Standout of the day WR Mack Hollins: With other wide receivers drawing most of the attention early in training camp, Hollins had a relatively quiet start to his second summer in Foxborough. That changed on Monday, with the veteran taking center stage and leading all receivers in catches and touchdowns during 11-on-11s. Working as a second-string option behind the starting trio of A.J. Brown, Romeo Doubs and DeMario Douglas, he hauled in five passes including three scores. It wasn’t just the numbers but more so the fashion in which the ever-flamboyant wideout produced: he caught the pass all over the field and won his matchups regardless of the route he was asked to run. He failed to haul in his lone end zone target from Drake Maye, but that was the only blemish on an otherwise solid day. Other performances of note WR Efton Chism III: Mack Hollins’ workout buddy made the most of his opportunities on Monday, including seeing some time with Drake Maye and the top offense in lieu of an injured Kyle Williams. He finished with three receptions in team drills, including an impressive high-point touchdown over Marcellas Dial, and also was part of the first kickoff returners duo alongside Terrell Jennings. LB Chad Muma: With undrafted rookie Khalil Jacobs putting some pressure on veteran backups K.J. Britt and Chad Muma, the latter delivered a good performance on Monday. Not only did he see some action with the starters, he also had a pass breakup against Rhamondre Stevenson and looked good as a run defender, including on one quick stuff. CB Channing Canada & CB Karon Prunty: With Carlton Davis remaining sidelined, the Patriots opted to give a pair of rookie cornerbacks some opportunities with the starters. Canada was particularly impressive, allowing just one catch on three targets and also winning a 1-on-1 against Romeo Doubs. Prunty, meanwhile, provided some good coverage on a fade intended for A.J. Brown. CB Kindle Vildor: Entering training camp, Vildor looked like a candidate to challenge for the CB4 spot. However, not only does Charles Woods seem fairly secure in that position, the youngsters have also started taking some reps from him. To make matters worse, he also was beat by Mack Hollins on a fade touchdown. Not the best day for the veteran. Other players worth mentioning include A.J. Brown, who was competitive despite dislocating his thumb during a 1-on-1 drill. Furthermore, Kayshon Boutte had some positive moments again, as did rookies Dametrious Crownover and Quintayvious Hutchins. The Patriots will hold their ninth practice of training camp on Tuesday. If the conditions allow for spectators, the gates will open at 9:15 p.m. ET. Practice is scheduled to kick off at 10:15.

title: Will Campbell entering Year 2 with confidence after strong start to camp
summary: One year into his NFL career, Patriots left tackle Will Campbell no longer feels like a rookie. After starting 17 games, making a run to Super Bowl 60 and playing through a knee injury late in the season, Campbell entered Year 2 with a much better understanding of what it takes to succeed in the […]
full_text: Jul 28, 2026; Foxborough, MA, USA; New England Patriots offensive tackle Will Campbell (66) works with a member of the coaching staff during training camp at Gillette Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Eric Canha-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect One year into his NFL career, Patriots left tackle Will Campbell no longer feels like a rookie. After starting 17 games, making a run to Super Bowl 60 and playing through a knee injury late in the season, Campbell entered Year 2 with a much better understanding of what it takes to succeed in the NFL. “I know what to expect now. I know what it takes to win and play at a high level in this league, and then what stuff can get you hurt,” Campbell said. “Just trying to be more consistent, not make rookie mistakes… Try to be a guy up front that they can count on and help lead the team.” Through the first several padded practices of training camp, Campbell has backed up those words. The offensive tackle has protected Drake Maye’s blindside at a high level and added two more wins to his impressive 1-on-1 record Monday. Campbell has also looked fully healthy after last year’s knee injury and appears to have expanded his pass-set toolbox. “I feel good. My body feels good,” Campbell said. “I’m just trying to be consistent as I possibly can be every single day and get better. And find something that I might not being doing well out at practice and try to attack that the next day. “Getting some great opportunities to go against really good guys. Dre’[Mont Jones] is a guy I played in a game and he’s a really good player. It’s good work for both of us because we’re familiar with each other. It’s kind of like a little chess match out there. So, it’s been fun and I’m excited to keep going.” After being selected fourth overall in the 2025 NFL Draft, Campbell started the Patriots’ first 12 games at left tackle before suffering an MCL injury. He returned for the regular-season finale and remained on Drake Maye’s blindside throughout the Patriots’ four-game playoff run, but struggled as he was not 100 percent healthy. Now healthy entering his second season, Campbell believes the continuity around him has allowed him to play faster and with more confidence. “I think the confidence comes knowing that the guys that we have on this team, everybody believes in each other. Also we’re in the same system for the second year,” Campbell said. “It’s a lot less thinking. OTAs last year when I got here was a lot of installing and taking more time. This year, we were kind of just able to hit the ground running from where we left off. “We added a few new guys, so we had to teach them, but for the most part, we just hit the ground. That’s how we’ve been doing it and that gives you a sense of confidence, just the familiarity and what we’re trying to get done.” Campbell’s new left guard, Alijah Vera-Tucker, believes the differences can help the 22-year old take the next step. “I think that he’s a very smart two-year guy,” Vera-Tucker said. “And I can see him making that very big two-year jump. But I only say that because he is a competitor. I know what kind of talent he has.”

title: Patriots training camp recap: Gabe Jacas increases participation level
summary: After a day off on Sunday the New England Patriots were back to work on Monday. While the rain pushed the team inside the FieldHouse, the pads stayed on as work was inside the red zone with a focus on the run game. Here’s what went down throughout the competitive session. Attendance Absent: CB Carlton […]
full_text: Foxborough, MA - August 1: New England Patriots linebacker Gabe Jacas arrives for training camp at Gillette Stadium on August 1, 2026. (Photo by Jonathan Wiggs/The Boston Globe via Getty Images) | Boston Globe via Getty Images After a day off on Sunday the New England Patriots were back to work on Monday. While the rain pushed the team inside the FieldHouse, the pads stayed on as work was inside the red zone with a focus on the run game. Here’s what went down throughout the competitive session. Attendance Absent: CB Carlton Davis III, OL Caedan Wallace (new), DT David Blay Jr. (new) Returnee: RB Terrell Jennings (NFI) Limited: WR Kyle Williams PUP/NFI: TE C.J. Dippre, ED Harold Landry III, S Brenden Schooler Patriots second-year wide receiver Kyle Williams joined practice late on Monday and did not participate after appearing to be banged up on Saturday. Offensive guard Caedan Wallace, who also suffered an injury on Saturday, was then a new absence. The Patriots did activate running back Terrell Jennings off the NFI list. Jennings took a handful of reps in full-team work and worked as a kick returner in his first practice of the summer. Meanwhile, newly-signed defensive tackle Casey Rogers was present. Undrafted rookie David Blay Jr, on the other hand, was not. Takeaways Jacas’ participation: After making his practice debut on Saturday, rookie pass rusher Gabe Jacas upped his participation level on Monday. Jacas took a handful of reps in full-team work and a lone 1-on-1 rep — where he beat depth tackle Lorenz Metz along the edge. OLB coach Mike Smith did get his revenge, however, after Jacas bullrushed the coach over in drills last practice. Smith pretended to give his group instruction with Jacas next in line before tackling him down onto a pad before added some playful punches. Best friends: With Kyle Williams sidelined, best friends Mack Hollins and Efton Chism III were active throughout the day. Hollins hauled in five passes from Tommy DeVito including three touchdowns on a slant, play-action crosser and goal line fade. The big bodied receiver was not able to pull in his lone target from Drake Maye in the end zone. As for Chism, the slot receiver took a handful of reps with Maye’s offense in run packages but caught three passes from DeVito — including another high-point touchdown grab over Marcellas Dial in the back of the end zone. For the rest of the wide receivers, A.J. Brown suffered a dislocated thumb after getting pressed by Christian Gonzalez in a 1-on-1 rep. Brown spent time with the trainers and put on a brace but did not miss any time as he caught three passes from Maye in full-team work. Kayshon Boutte then added two touchdown receptions from DeVito, including a fade in the end zone to end practice. Depth corners: As veteran Carlton Davis remained sidelined, cornerback Charles Woods continued to serve as the top option opposite of Christian Gonzalez and had an impressive breakup along the goal line guarding Romeo Doubs. New England then got a pair of younger cornerbacks increased reps as UDFA Channing Canada received a late first-team rep after a competitive day that featured a pass breakup on Hollins, while rookie Karon Prunty continued to stack positive days by forcing an incompletion on a go-ball against A.J. Brown and nearly hauling in an interception on Behren Morton. 1-on-1s: Work transitioning inside the bubble gave a good look at the offensive and defensive lines for 1-on-1 work. Rookie tackle Caleb Lomu appeared to split his six reps, but overset and was beat inside by both Quintayvious Hutchins and Bradyn Swinson. Hutchins also had an impressive victory over Marcus Bryant as the seventh-round speed rush continues to impress. It was also a strong day for rookie offensive tackle Dametrious Crownover, who used his length to beat Elijah Ponder while also recording a win over Swinson. Other notes: After a slow start to the summer, the Patriots run game had their most competitive day of training camp on Monday. The group also had a pair of positive plays off screens. With the focus on the ground, Drake Maye threw just 14 passes with plenty of play-action and screen work. On 3rd-and-short situations, the Patriots introduced loud sirens on the speakers instead of the usual music to amplify noise. Rookie tight ends Eli Raridon and Tanner Arkin continued to be used with the first-team offense. Raridon had a drop in the end zone on his lone target from DeVito, but appeared to help pave the way in-line next to Morgan Moses for a long touchdown run by Rhamondre Stevenson. Veteran offensive lineman James Hudson got some work at guard on Monday. He won a 1-on-1 rep there with an impressive anchor vs. Jeremiah Pharms. Chad Muma had an impressive pass breakup while guarding Stevenson out of the backfield and was active on run defense with a quick stuff. Kick returners: Terrell Jennings and Efton Chism was the first duo up followed by Lan Larison, Channing Canada, Kobe Prentice, Jam Miller, and Myles Montgomery. The Patriots will be back on the practice fields on Tuesday, which is set to begin at 10:15 a.m. ET where the expectation is to be back in full pads.

Anthony Nesmith/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images A.J. Brown was actively involved during the New England Patriots’ eighth training camp practice on Monday. Along the defensive line, new free agent signing Casey Rogers was present to take the place — and jersey number — of David Blay Jr. Meanwhile, running back Terrell Jennings […]
full_text: FOXBOROUGH, MA- JUNE 11: Terrell Jennings #26 of the New England Patriots with the ball in a drill during New England Patriots Minicamp on June 11, 2026, at Gillette Stadium in Foxborough, Massachusetts. (Photo by Summer Lamont/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The New England Patriots returned to practice on Monday for their eighth session of training camp, and they did so with a slightly different-looking roster. Along the defensive line, new free agent signing Casey Rogers was present to take the place — and jersey number — of David Blay Jr. Meanwhile, running back Terrell Jennings made his practice debut in a limited capacity after being activated from the non-football injury list. Rogers, 27, originally entered the NFL as a rookie free agent in 2024. The Oregon product started his career with the Giants, for whom he appeared in three games over two separate stints. He also spent time with the Bills. Most recently, the 6-foot-4, 294-pound defensive tackle was with the UFL’s DC Defenders. Blay Jr, 23, spent his college career at West Chester, Louisiana Tech and Miami. He was signed by the Patriots as an undrafted free agent in early May, following a successful workout at the team’s rookie minicamp. Jennings, 25, arrived in New England as an undrafted free agent in 2024. He has since appeared in 10 games, registering a combined 37 carries and receptions for 115 yards and a touchdown. The 6-foot-0, 222-pound back was one of three Patriots to begin training camp on injured reserve, joining safety Brenden Schooler and since-activated edge defender Gabe Jacas. The Patriots held their eighth practice of training camp on Monday. Due to inclement weather, the session was moved indoors and therefore unable to accommodate any fans. The next practice is scheduled for Tuesday, Aug. 4, at 10:15 a.m. ET .

summary: Coming off their second off-day of training camp, the New England Patriots are in for an intense stretch of work. Starting Monday, the team of head coach Mike Vrabel will practice on five consecutive days. Here is what you need to know about the first of those sessions. Schedule Business as usual is over at […]
full_text: Jul 28, 2026; Foxborough, MA, USA; New England Patriots safety Mike Brown (33) does a drill with safety Dell Pettus (24) during training camp at Gillette Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Eric Canha-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect Coming off their second off-day of training camp, the New England Patriots are in for an intense stretch of work. Starting Monday, the team of head coach Mike Vrabel will practice on five consecutive days. Here is what you need to know about the first of those sessions. Schedule Business as usual is over at Patriots camp on Monday. The eighth practice of this year’s training camp will not be open to the public: while originally scheduled as such, it has been moved indoors due to inclement weather and therefore can no longer accommodate fans. 10:15 a.m. ET: Practice ca. 12:15 p.m. ET: Player availability (RB Lan Larison, WR Romeo Doubs, LT Will Campbell, DT Milton Williams, S Kevin Byard III, S Dell Pettus) As always, of course, the schedule is tentative and subject to change. For more information, please visit our Pats Pulpit Training Camp Guide . Story of the day Will there be any changes on the injury front? Coming off their second off-day, the Patriots will be hoping for reinforcements either through the non-football injury or physically unable to perform list, or in the form of some other absentees returning to action. Meanwhile, another question is if any of the players who were limited participants on Saturday — RB Rhamondre Stevenson, WR A.J. Brown, RT Morgan Moses, ED Gabe Jacas, CB Christian Gonzalez, CB Marcus Jones — will see an uptick in reps. Injuries to monitor NFI: RB Terrell Jennings, S Brenden Schooler PUP: TE C.J. Dippre, ED Harold Landry III Injured: OT James Hudson III, OL Caedan Wallace, CB Carlton Davis III Absent: FB Reggie Gilliam, LG Alijah Vera-Tucker The Patriots’ NFI list saw a change since the most recent practice on Saturday, with second-round rookie Gabe Jacas making his practice debut. However, the session also saw offensive linemen James Hudson and Caedan Wallace get banged up, while fullback Reggie Gilliam was absent for a second day this camp. Players to watch RB Lan Larison: The second-year runner had a challenging practice on Saturday, including losing a fumble during 11-on-11s. With fellow roster bubble back Jam Miller having started to string solid practices together lately, Larison needs to show a short memory and begin making some of the plays that Miller has recently made. ED Elijah Ponder: With Gabe Jacas looming (and Harold Landry as well), Ponder’s time as a starter-level edge might be nearing its end. He better makes most of the high-level opportunities still awarded to him, something he was unable to do on Saturday. CB Karon Prunty: Consistency is one of the biggest problems for rookie players in the NFL, which means that Prunty will be tasked with keeping his foot on the pedal on Monday. The fifth-round draft pick, after all, had a good practice on Saturday but needs to keep stacking days in order to separate himself from the bunch in the race for a backup cornerback job. S Dell Pettus and S Mike Brown: Pettus, like Karon Prunty, managed to snatch an interception on Saturday. He seemingly finds himself ahead of Brown in the competition for the third safety spot at the moment, but the tides can change quickly in training camp. Any dip in performance, and that particular battle might be turned on its head. Pats Pulpit will have you covered throughout the day, so please make sure to regularly check back to patspulpit.com for all the latest news from camp. Credentialed Patriots beat writers Brian Hines ( @iambrianhines ), Andrew Guindon ( @NestPgs ) Taylor Kyles ( @tkyles39 ) will bring you live updates from camp on their Twitter/X feeds, so please make sure to give them a follow.

title: Saints’ new guard explains why the run game is coming together early in camp
summary: The New Orleans Saints are still in the early stages of training camp, but one of the team’s newest additions, former Buffalo Bills guard David Edwards, believes the offense is already beginning to establish its identity on the ground. Speaking with the media after practice, the veteran offensive lineman said the biggest strength of the […]
full_text: Jul 30, 2026; Metairie, LA, USA; New Orleans Saints guard David Edwards (76) during training camp at Ochsner Sports Performance Center. Mandatory Credit: Stephen Lew-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect The New Orleans Saints are still in the early stages of training camp, but one of the team’s newest additions, former Buffalo Bills guard David Edwards, believes the offense is already beginning to establish its identity on the ground. Speaking with the media after practice, the veteran offensive lineman said the biggest strength of the Saints’ backfield is that every running back brings something different, giving the coaching staff plenty of options when building the rushing attack. He pointed to new Saints running back Travis Etienne Jr. as a player whose patience separates him. “I think the beauty of Travis is his ability to start and stop and kind of have this patience behind the line of scrimmage as well as at the line of scrimmage,” he said. “Then make a decision and go is really special and unique.” He also praised Alvin Kamara’s ability to change a game with one touch. “What’s really special and unique about AK is I feel like that guy can hit a home run at any second,” he said. “His twitchiness, athleticism and burst is really unique.” Rather than asking every running back to do the same thing, Kellen Moore and the coaching staff are working to put each player in positions that fit his skill set. “You’ve got to find a certain balance between, ‘This guy does this well. This guy does that well,’ and then ultimately letting the guy cut it loose and play free and have fun,” he said. That approach also refers to the blocking schemes up front. The veteran said New Orleans has been installing both zone and gap concepts throughout camp, giving the offense multiple ways to attack defenses while emphasizing the details behind every play. “I think there’s been some great zone schemes that we’ve been activating, there’s great gap stuff,” he said. “It’s all the same stuff that I’ve kind of been accustomed to, but it’s been really cool to have the nuance and the detail.” He added that the Saints’ coaching staff has done a good job making sure everyone on offense understands not only their own job, but how every position works together. “I really believe our coaches have done a great job of incorporating the entire unit, 11 players working as one, to accomplish a great play. The best part is we’re still installing,” he said. “Once that full package is in, and you can activate a gap scheme, a zone scheme, a keeper, a play action, out of all these different formations, I just feel like that’s going to serve you well as an offense.” Like every offensive line around the league this time of year, much of the focus has been on fundamentals. The emphasis has been on technique, footwork and building good habits before the physical work ramps up as the Saints had their first practice in pads on Monday. “There are certainly clips and reps that we’ve had where you can reference and say, ‘Hey guys, this is exactly how we want to do it,'” he said. “There’s a lot of good things that we’ve done so far, and there’s a lot of stuff that we’ve got to clean up and be better at, but there are a lot of things we can point to right now and say, ‘Hey guys, this is what we’re hunting up.'” The Saints still have plenty of work ahead before their season opener against the Detroit Lions on the road, but the early signs indicate the offensive line and running backs are beginning to develop the chemistry needed to make the ground game a reliable part of the offense.

title: Offense wins the day, but defense is winning Saints training camp
summary: With the second week of training camp underway, the New Orleans Saints offense finally found its rhythm. The defense has looked very good, and that’s a positive for a unit that finished last season strong under first-year defensive coordinator Brandon Staley. The addition of LB Kaden Elliss following the departure of Demario Davis is already […]
full_text: METAIRIE, LOUISIANA - JULY 30: Tyler Shough #6 of the New Orleans Saints participates in drills during training camp at Ochsner Sports Performance Center on July 30, 2026 in Metairie, Louisiana. (Photo by Tyler Kaufman/Getty Images) | Getty Images With the second week of training camp underway, the New Orleans Saints offense finally found its rhythm. The defense has looked very good, and that’s a positive for a unit that finished last season strong under first-year defensive coordinator Brandon Staley. The addition of LB Kaden Elliss following the departure of Demario Davis is already paying dividends. Staley has been moving Elliss all over the defense, utilizing him in multiple roles within the scheme. The pass rush has also been effective early in camp. It’s not as if the offensive line has been struggling in one particular area—the defense has simply been making the right plays. The coverage on the back end has been very strong as well. Jonas Sanker is making significant strides at the star position, and it’s helping elevate the entire defense. This is how the flow of camp should go. A defense with a great deal of returning experience should naturally be a little ahead of an offense that is young and breaking in several new players at key positions. Today, however, belonged to the offense. Nick Underhill of NewOrleans.Football reported that the offense had a huge bounce-back performance . This was the first padded practice of camp, and that proved to be a major benefit for the offensive line. With pads on, the line of scrimmage can finally play the way it’s intended to—with maximum physicality. The offensive line was able to establish true run fits and lean on that physicality to help slow down an aggressive pass rush. That, in turn, opened things up for Tyler Shough, who put together his best practice of training camp so far. Underhill noted that Shough finished team periods completing 11 of 14 passes, with one throwaway and no turnovers. It’s also important to note that Shough’s average depth of target was more than 10 yards, meaning the offense was pushing the ball downfield rather than relying on short, safe throws. It was an outstanding response considering how uncomfortable both Shough and the offense looked on Sunday, when he reportedly finished team periods just 3 of 13. A practice like this is one the team can build upon. The defense now has some film to evaluate and make adjustments, while a young offense can gain confidence, continue to develop chemistry, and grow together.

summary: There may be an unsuspecting star rising for the New Orleans Saints as the first day of pads ended. Rookie wide receiver Barion Brown has been stacking good days and performed well again on Monday. Brown, a sixth-round pick by the Saints, was making plays left and right. Despite being announced as a return specialist […]
full_text: Aug 02, 2026; Metairie, LA, USA; New Orleans Saints wide receiver Barion Brown (19) during training camp at Ochsner Sports Performance Center. Mandatory Credit: Stephen Lew-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect There may be an unsuspecting star rising for the New Orleans Saints as the first day of pads ended. Rookie wide receiver Barion Brown has been stacking good days and performed well again on Monday. Brown, a sixth-round pick by the Saints, was making plays left and right. Despite being announced as a return specialist during the draft, Brown has been a favorite target among quarterbacks through the first week of camp. Ironically, the first comment by the commentators when the LSU wideout was drafted was “Look how they announced it…so don’t come in here thinking you gonna be catching a whole bunch of passes.” At 5-foot-11, Brown has game-breaking speed, but his ability to make contested catches is better than many expect. He won’t be the same red zone target as Devaughn Vele, but he is a willing playmaker and has a wide catch radius. Barion Brown 🔥 pic.twitter.com/Oq1zNQ6bvK — New Orleans Saints (@Saints) August 3, 2026 The Saints wide receiver room is a lot different than what it was just a year ago. From entering the season saying “who’s going to help Chris Olave” to wondering how New Orleans will get all their playmakers on the field at the same time. With Olave, Vele, and first-round pick Jordyn Tyson, Tyler Shough will have plenty of weapons to spread the ball to. Brown was also the third and last wide receiver the Saints drafted in the 2026 NFL Draft, making his road to seeing playing time with the offense even further. Despite this, he has taken advantage of his opportunities and shown the ability to make plays. Monday saints training camp 1-on-1 Barion Brown making the catch deep down the sideline @wdsu https://t.co/pH3cV0GrPd pic.twitter.com/pmdfqlct4y — Sharief Ishaq (@ShariefWDSU) August 3, 2026 Brown’s versatility as a kick returner already made his chances of making the roster high, but the display of his speed and effort during training camp has only elevated his chances. This is only emphasized with the recent and surprise retirement of wideout Ja’Lynn Polk, who was placed on the reserve/retired list on Saturday. With his continuous playmaking and one less player to beat out, Brown is looking like a lock to be on the Saints’ 2026-27 roster.

title: NY Giants training camp, practice No. 5: Arvell Reese dominates
summary: WHITE SULPHUR SPRINGS, W.Va. — The New York Giants held their first padded practice of 2026 training camp on Monday, a sloppy, one-hour, 45-minute that began in a sprinkle, went for about an hour in a torrential downpour, and finished in heat and bright sunshine. “(Former) college (football) coach Tom Reed used to always tell […]
full_text: WHITE SULPHUR SPRINGS, W.Va. — The New York Giants held their first padded practice of 2026 training camp on Monday, a sloppy, one-hour, 45-minute that began in a sprinkle, went for about an hour in a torrential downpour, and finished in heat and bright sunshine. “(Former) college (football) coach Tom Reed used to always tell us every single day, rain, sleet, snow, hot, it’s a great day for football. Every day.,” said head coach John Harbaugh. “We’d look at each other, really not that great a day, but he would say every day is a great day for football. “And that was kind of a little bit of the theme out here. I mean, it’s raining pretty good. And the guys are out there dealing with the elements, obviously impactful, but we’ll have to play in that at some point in time. So, we got a good day in the rain, and that was positive.” There were at least a dozen penalties, perhaps as many as 14, during the 11-on-11 portions of practice. Moat of those were false starts, though there were offside penalties, defensive pass interference, and offensive and defensive holding calls, as well. Harbaugh was surprisingly non-plussed by the sloppiness. “I think two things. I mean, I think you’ve got the elements a little bit and you’ve got the first day in pads,” Harbaugh said after practice, when it was sunny outside. “So, it’s not really unexpected, but we’ll be working on it.” False start penalties have been prevalent through the first five practices. Harbaugh said that might be due to the “absolutely designed” cadences the Giants are working into their offense. “Part of the offense has a lot of elements of cadence. I mean, that’s part of it. Cadence is something that we hope to use as a weapon, so to speak. It slows the defense down and keeps them honest a little bit, but you have to work at it. There’s got to be growing pains with that,” Harbaugh said. “If you don’t work through it, then you’re not going to get good at it. So yeah, it’s kind of tough on the offense, too. They have to get used to it in a lot of different circumstances. Play clock’s running down, we’ve got motions and shifts. They’ve got to remember a lot of things at the line of scrimmage in terms of calls and which linebacker we’re going to or whatever it might be. And then you’ve got play count or cadence, things that you have to execute. So, all that stuff going together is stuff that you’re working on. “It’s, what, the fifth day in camp right now? We’ll just keep working on that stuff. The goal is to get really good at it, and that’s what we’ll have to do. So, it’s not unexpected this early for that to be the case.” Winners The defense overall — The defense has had the better of the offense throughout most of the early part of training camp. That was the case again Monday. The offense had moments, but on a play-to-play basis the defense was clearly better than the offense. “I thought the defense probably got the better of the offense today up front,” Harbaugh said. “We’ll see it on tape, probably going to be the case. But we got a few plays out in the run game on offense, too, so I’m really looking forward to seeing it. “Everybody always says the defense is ahead of the offense early in camp. Probably found that to be true over the years, so it seems to be the case.” Arvell Reese — Somebody forgot to give the rookie linebacker the memo that there was no live tackling in practice. Reese dumped Cam Skattebo and Tyrone Tracy at the line of scrimmage. He had a sack of Jaxson Dart, where he fortunately remembered not to hit the red jersey. Impressively, that sack came on a blitz with Andrew Thomas the nearest offensive lineman. Reese also had a couple of nice plays in coverage. Harbaugh said he was “very encouraged” by the play of the team’s No. 5 pick in the 2026 NFL Draft. “I think he looked good today from what I could see.,” Harbaugh said. “I can’t wait to see the tape, but he’s playing really well. He’s been playing well the whole camp since he got here. “You see the talent, obviously. I think he’s very sharp for a first-year guy. He gets things right pretty much all the time, makes very few mistakes. He’s a very serious-minded guy, and he’s very determined.” Micah McFadden — After missing all but a dozen snaps last season due to a foot injury, McFadden is no longer a starter at inside linebacker. He reminded everyone on Monday, though, that he is a useful player. McFadden had an interception off a tipped ball, at least one tackle for loss, and a couple of other good plays in coverage. Calvin Austin — The dimimutive slot receiver has made plays every day thus far in camp, with Monday being more of the same. “Calvin’s had a heck of a camp,” Harbaugh said. “He runs the routes really well. He gets open. He makes catches. He deserves some attention, no doubt. He’s having a good camp so far.” Dalen Cambre — The second-year wide receiver had the play of the day for the offense. In the driving rain, Cambre leaped to take a deep 50-50 ball away from cornerback Korie Black. When the ball popped into the air, a stumbling Cambre grabbed it for a long catch before falling out of bounds. Losers My notebook — There was no protecting my notebook from the pouring rain. It is now in tatters, with some pages having simply disingtegrated, others being completely illegible, and me now questioning whether this notebook will dry sufficiently for me to use it again this week. Oh, one other thing. I am big fan of nice pens, especially gel pens. I knew this already, but gel pens are disastrous in the rain. There will be a basic stick pen in my pocket the rest of the week. Tae Banks’ hands — Toward the end of practice, as the sun had come out and things began to dry out a bit, a jotted a few potential winners and losers in my notebook. Banks was in the ‘winners’ column. He had a tipped ball that led to McFadden’s interception early in practice, then a nice play in run support that ened with a tackle for loss. Then, Jameis Winston lofted a pass toward the left pylon. The ball was at least 5 yards off target and Banks, looking like a centerfielder waiting for a fly ball, was alone waiting for the catch. Only, he didn’t make the catch. The ball fell through his fingers to the grass. The amount of time the mortified Banks, who has struggled with ball skills throughout his career, took to get back to the huddle showed he knew how bad that drop was. An important week The Giants have five more practices before leaving West Virginia to return to East Rutherford, N.J. Harbaugh said the Giants will be in pads for “most of them.” “This is a big week. The second week is the big week of camp. This is your opportunity to really grow as a football team,” Harbaugh said. “We always say the second everything. The second day, the second game, the second week of camp. You build your foundation in training camp for your team. The second week should be where you cover the most miles, gain the most ground. We want to put the most miles behind us as far as developing the foundation of our team this week. “This is just a go-to-work week. Just get to work and get better. That’s really what we’re focusing on this week. Not too much evaluating, just more really trying to build this week. You really have to build this week, and that’s what this week is for.” Remaining Greenbrier practice schedule Tuesday, August 4 — 1:30-3:30 p.m. Wednesday, August 5 — 1:30-4 p.m. (Open to the public) Thursday, August 6 — 1:30-4 p.m. (Open to the public) Friday, August 7 — 1:30-4 p.m. (Open to the public) Saturday, August 8 — 10 a.m. – 12:30 p.m.

summary: The New York Giants are hard at work in their 2026 training camp, which is currently being hosted by The Greenbrier Resort. So far, the returns have been positive, starting with wide receiver Malik Nabers returning to the practice field. Jaxson Dart has produced highlight plays throwing to free agent tight end Isaiah Likely, rookie […]
full_text: Jaxson Dart (6) with Darius Slayton during training camp. | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect The New York Giants are hard at work in their 2026 training camp, which is currently being hosted by The Greenbrier Resort. So far, the returns have been positive, starting with wide receiver Malik Nabers returning to the practice field. Jaxson Dart has produced highlight plays throwing to free agent tight end Isaiah Likely, rookie receiver Malachi Fields, and veteran Odell Beckham Jr. On the flip side, the Giants’ defense has been incredibly disruptive after a slow start on the first day of camp that featured multiple dropped interceptions — of course, you can’t drop interceptions if you aren’t getting your hands on the ball. Since then, the Giants’ pass rush has been all but dominant and the secondary has been disruptive, preventing the offense from finding much of a rhythm at all. We’re moving into a new phase of camp as the players don their pads on Monday, which will doubtless ratchet up the intensity. We’ll see how the defense responds when the offensive line is in pads and able to play more roughly. So we wanted to use the opportunity to take the temperature of the fanbase: How are you feeling about the Giants after the first week of camp? Are you hyped up and believe the Giants are ready to compete with the Cowboys and Rams to start the year? Are you cautiously optimistic? Encouraged by the news coming out of camp but not ready to buy in yet? Are you cautiously pessimistic? Guarding your heart after having been hurt by promising off-seasons before? Or are you out completely? Do you believe that the Giants lack the talent and no coaching can speed up what needs to be multi-year rebuild? full_text: Odell Beckham | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Instead of doing a pure 53-man roster projection ahead of New York Giants training camp, we are looking at the Giants’ 91-man roster a different way Below is an updated position-by-position look at who I consider to be locks to make the 53-man roster, bubble players, and long shots after the first four days of practice. The intent is to look at where the most interesting competitions are and the chances of individual players. Quarterback Locks (2) — Jaxson Dart, Jameis Winston Bubble players (0) — None Long shot (1) — Brandon Allen [No change] Allen received few reps over the first four days. The Giants did one 7-on-7 session in each of those practices, and Dart often took Allen’s reps with the third team. As coach John Harbaugh said in the spring, whatever reps Dart wants, Dart will get. Running back Locks (4) — Cam Skattebo, Tyrone Tracy, Devin Singletary, Patrick Ricard Bubble players (1) — Dante Miller Long shots (3) — Eric Gray, Damon Bankston [ Change: Miller moves from long shot to bubble] At the risk of getting the ‘Turbo-maniacs’ fired up, only to once again end up disappointed, it has been clear through the early practices that the Giants see Miller as being ahead of Gray or Bankston. I still won’t believe Miller will make the roster until I see it happen. Tight end Locks (3) — Isaiah Likely, Theo Johnson, Chris Manhertz Bubble players (1) — Tanner Conner Long shot (1) — Thomas Fidone [ Change: Conner and Fidone switch places] Conner has made plays every day. Fidone, coming back from foot issues, has been mostly invisible. Wide receiver Locks (5) — Malik Nabers, Darius Slayton, Calvin Austin, Darnell Mooney, Malachi Fields Bubble players (4) — Odell Beckham Jr., JuJu Smith-Schuster, Braxton Berrios, Dalen Cambre Long shots (5) — Ryan Miller, Jalin Hyatt, Xavier Gipson, Beaux Collins, Isaiah Hodgins [ Change: Cambre and Hodgins switch places] I still don’t have a good handle on who leads the competition for the last roster spot or two at this position. title: Scouting Jets wide receiver Quincy Skinner
summary: The Jets’ first personnel move of training camp was to sign wide receiver Quincy Skinner to replace the injured Jalen Walthall. Today, we break Skinner down in detail. The 23-year old Skinner is listed at 6’2” and 205 pounds and caught 66 passes for 809 yards and eight touchdowns in four seasons at Vanderbilt. He […]
full_text: FLOWERY BRANCH, GA - JULY 26: Atlanta Falcons wide receiver Quincy Skinner Jr. #36 runs a route during Atlanta Falcons training camp on July 26, 2025 at IBM Performance Field in Flowery Branch, GA. (Photo by Jeff Robinson/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The Jets’ first personnel move of training camp was to sign wide receiver Quincy Skinner to replace the injured Jalen Walthall. Today, we break Skinner down in detail. The 23-year old Skinner is listed at 6’2” and 205 pounds and caught 66 passes for 809 yards and eight touchdowns in four seasons at Vanderbilt. He spent time with the Falcons as an undrafted rookie last year. Background Skinner – who is not to be confused with Quentin Skinner, another wide receiver who until last month was with the Jets but is now in Buffalo – was a three-star high school recruit. He headed to Vanderbilt, where he made eight appearances in his freshman season but only played two offensive snaps. His second season, in 2022, saw him start contributing as a rotational receiver. He had 17 catches for 238 yards and two scores. His role continued to increase in 2023 and he caught 20 passes for 204 yards and three scores. 2024 saw him start 12 of 13 games and post career-best numbers with 29 receptions and 367 yards. He added another three touchdowns. The Falcons picked Skinner up as an undrafted free agent after the 2025 draft and he caught three passes for 29 yards in preseason but did not make the team. Skinner was signed by the Jets on the second day of training camp, following an injury to Walthall. Let’s move onto some more in-depth analysis of what Skinner brings to the table, based on in-depth research and film study. Measurables/Athleticism Skinner’s workout numbers at his pro day were disappointing. He ran just 4.59 in the 40-yard dash, and posted a poor vertical and disappointing agility numbers. His broad jump (123 inches) and bench press (17 reps) were solid, though. Usage Skinner has primarily played on the outside both at Vanderbilt and in his preseason action with the Falcons. He played in the slot about 10 percent of the time in college, but it was less than that in his final year. He carried once in his college career, gaining 22 yards on an end around. Deep threat Skinner only had two plays of longer than 40 yards during his college career, but did make several downfield catches as he showed a good ability to track and locate the ball. He was targeted down the field more often in his final season but his success rate on such throws was lower. Hands Skinner caught 71 percent of his targets in 2022 but his catch rate dropped to 64 percent in 2023 and 60 in 2024. To some extent the 2024 drop can be explained by the fact he was targeted downfield more often than in 2022 but that wasn’t the case in 2023 when he was targeted on more shorter routes. His drop rate was solid in his first two seasons, as he had just one drop in each season. However, he had five in 2024. Skinner has a big catch radius and can use this to go up and get high throws and has shown a good ability to lay out for diving catches, and concentration on low throws. Routes Skinner shows some decent raw route running skills, as he looks smooth on his release and shows good deception and change of direction abilities. As alluded to earlier, he had more of a possession role in 2023 but was targeted more on downfield throws in 2024. His success rate doing the latter was not that high, but some of this was down to the quarterback play as he did show the ability to get open. Red zone Although he only had eight touchdown catches in his college career, Skinner did make a few nice plays in the red zone and has shown that he can be someone you can throw it up to (even though he will have to adjust to getting two feet down under the NFL’s rules). In addition to those eight touchdowns, he also scored on two two-point conversions. After the catch Skinner’s numbers after the catch are nothing special and he doesn’t break many tackles. However, he does have a few highlights of this nature. He wasn’t particularly successful on screen passes during his college career, averaging less than four yards per play when targeted behind the line. Skinner had one fumble during his college career. Run Blocking Skinner’s performance grades as a run blocker on sites such as Pro Football Focus were generally pretty good and the film backs this up as he is an effective contributor who gives a good effort, uses his size well and gets after it. He was called for offensive holding downfield on a quarterback scramble in his final season of college. Physicality Skinner had mixed results on contested catches during his career, with his success rate dropping off in his final season but did make some good plays when tightly covered. He had a 79-yard touchdown catch in college that was called back because he was flagged for offensive pass interference. Special Teams Skinner saw some action in his freshman year as a blocker on the kick return unit and in kick coverage, but didn’t generate any production and then barely played on special teams after that during his college career. With Atlanta, he blocked on the kick return unit and played as a vice and rusher on the punt return unit. He had one play where the gunner beat him cleanly on a punt return (although he missed the tackle), but impressed with his physicality on the kickoff return unit here. Instincts and Intelligence Skinner displays the ability to read coverages and time his route to find the soft spot in the zone. He also typically executed his blocking assignments well. In addition, it is also impressive how early he tracks and locates the ball when it is in the air. He was flagged for two pre-snap penalties in 2024, though. Attitude Skinner was someone whose coaching staff at Vanderbilt praised him for growing into a role as a vocal leader in the wide receiver room over the course of his career. His on-field discipline was solid as he had just five penalties in his career, although four were in 2024. Injuries Skinner played in 41 games in college and doesn’t seem to have had any issues with missing time for injury related reasons. Scheme Fit Skinner will look to get in the mix on the outside and should see time there in preseason, if he lasts that long. During his time with the Falcons, Skinner was a teammate of current Jets defensive lineman David Onyemata. Conclusions Skinner will be a long-shot to make the Jets’ roster, of course. However, he’s a player they worked out a while back and obviously kept on their watchlist so they will be keen to get a longer look. If he can impress in preseason, Skinner might have a shot at sticking around so he can try to compete for a role next season. His measurables, production and lack of any elite traits would tend to suggest this is unlikely, but there were a few impressive moments on film that show he might be capable of making some things happen.

In addition, preseason games have been cut from four to three, and starters who used to see a good deal of action in the preseason now barely make occasional cameo appearances. The pads go on this week and the hitting starts, inevitably putting the players at an elevated risk level. There’s a balancing act here between health and preparation. title: Eagles Training Camp Practice Notes: Jalen Hurts strikes back
summary: Today marked the fourth Philadelphia Eagles training camp practice ahead of the 2026 NFL season. The players were in pads for the first time this summer while practicing indoors due to heavy rain outside. Here’s what I observed at the Jefferson Health Training Complex. EAGLES PRACTICE NOTES UP NEXT: The Eagles practice again tomorrow starting […]
full_text: PHILADELPHIA, PENNSYLVANIA - JULY 30: Jalen Hurts #1 of the Philadelphia Eagles reacts during training camp at Jefferson Health Training Complex on July 30, 2026 in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Mitchell Leff/Getty Images) | Getty Images Today marked the fourth Philadelphia Eagles training camp practice ahead of the 2026 NFL season. The players were in pads for the first time this summer while practicing indoors due to heavy rain outside. Here’s what I observed at the Jefferson Health Training Complex. EAGLES PRACTICE NOTES JALEN HURTS UPDATE: Monday was a bounce back performance from Hurts and the offense after they were bested by Vic Fangio’s defense in the previous two practices. Encouraging to see. THE GOOD: The first-team offense was aided by going up against the second-team defense during the first 11-on-11 series. Hurts found Dontayvion Wicks crossing to the left downfield for a chunk gain. Hurts hit DeVonta Smith on an out to beat Mac McWilliams along the right sideline. Hurts’ success wasn’t limited to facing the Eagles’ backup defenders. During 7-on-7, Hurts made his flashiest completion of camp thus far by throwing with anticipation over the middle into the end zone to split the safeties and connect with Elijah Moore for a touchdown. Hurts found Darius Cooper for multiple completions over the middle. During a red zone sequence, Hurts hit DeVonta on another out route for a touchdown. The Eagles lined up to go for a two-point conversion and Hurts rolled to his right only to throw across his body to find DeVonta again, who made the grab despite being tightly covered by Riq Woolen. During another red zone sequence, Hurts took a shotgun snap and pretended to drop back before taking off running to the end zone untouched for a score. This wasn’t a case where the quarterback benefited from wearing the red jersey that reminds defenders not to get close to him. This was about Hurts correctly identifying a weakness in the defense and exposing it with his legs. Hurts and his offense teammates were fired up to celebrate this score. THE BAD: Hurts did throw a pick six to Quinyon Mitchell in 7-on-7 … but it looked like there was a miscommunication with Moore stopping his route earlier than the quarterback expected. Hurts held the ball for a long time and got “sacked” by either Jalen Carter or Jordan Davis (unclear which) at one point. Hurts sailed a downfield pass to Tank Bigsby, who had a step on Zack Baun (but not by much), over the running back’s head and out of bounds. The wheel route is no longer undefeated. Hurts had a pass deflected at the line by Jalen Carter. Fortunately for the offense, the ball landed in Hollywood Brown’s hands for a short gain. EAGLES INJURY UPDATES: DID NOT PARTICIPATE: OT Lane Johnson (excused absence/not injury related) Johnson also missed Saturday’s practice. It’s unclear what’s been keeping him away. OG Micah Morris (shoulder) S Cole Wisniewski (hamstring) EDGE Keyshawn James-Newby (ankle) OG Jaedan Roberts (calf contusion) Roberts was carted off the field on Saturday but he reportedly avoided a major injury . Good news. LIMITED PARTICIPATION: WR Makai Lemon (?) Lemon was not listed on the team-issued injury report but he didn’t appear to participate in team drills. I couldn’t find him again after seeing him take part in some individual drills early in practice. Something to monitor. UPDATE: The Inquirer’s Jeff McLane says that “whatever it was that limited Makai Lemon at practice, I’m told it wasn’t significant.” OT Cameron Williams (knee contusion) Williams was able to partake in some team drill activity. RETURNED TO PRACTICE: WR Elijah Moore and LB Jihaad Campbell were back in action after being excused from Saturday’s practice. Fred Johnson saw the first first-team reps at right tackle with Lane Johnson not practicing but Markell Bell also rotated in. Bell previously saw first-team right tackle action during spring practices but these were his first reps with the starters this summer. Good practice for the Eagles’ roster bubble wide receivers. Elijah Moore ran a sharp route to get open in the middle of the field for a completion of at least 15 yards. He later caught a touchdown from Hurts, as previously mentioned. Darius Cooper caught everything thrown his way, including when he made a diving grab on a Hurts throw over the middle. Johnny Wilson made a couple catches over the middle on passes from Andy Dalton. Wilson did fail to secure a Tanner McKee pass to him that was a little low but still catchable. BACKUP QUARTERBACK BATTLE UPDATE: Dalton was first up as the Eagles’ QB2 in 11-on-11 but the Eagles rotated him and Tanner McKee. Dalton looked sharper than McKee on Monday; the 38-year-old veteran quarterback ripped the ball over the middle to Wilson for multiple first downs. Dalton’s red zone sequence resulted in a touchdown pass to a wiiide open Will Shipley in the flat before he found Hollywood Brown on an out route for the successful two-point conversion. McKee seemed guilty of holding the ball too long at times and he wasn’t able to cash in during his red zone opportunity. Dalton has the edge over McKee early in camp. I like what I’ve seen from A.J. Epenesa in camp thus far; he’s been active. Epenesa “sacked” McKee while rotating in as a first-team edge rusher. Seems like he might be a nice rotational player. (RELATED READING — Eagles Film Review: A.J. Epenesa signing is very sensible.) Chance Campbell was in good position to stop a Saquon Barkley stretch run to the right side early in practice. Nolan Smith had tight coverage on Stone Smartt to force a short incompletion during 7-on-7. He celebrated with an exuberant incompletion motion right in front of Smartt after the play. Moro Ojomo totally blew up a run in the backfield while going up against the second-team offense. I wrote down Eli Stowers’ name twice in my notes today. The first time was when he made a short catch on a play where McKee rolled right and threw a short pass to him. Stowers immediately got shoved out of bounds by Zack Baun. Later, Stowers couldn’t make a catch with edge rusher Arnold Ebiketie covering him. Stowers wanted a flag on the defense but the practice refs did not throw one. Cole Payton continues to be fearless. The rookie quarterback took a downfield shot to Erik Ezukanma, who got his hands on the ball but couldn’t control it to the ground with three defenders very close to him. Payton connected with Dae’Quan Wright for a catch-and-run touchdown. Wright wasn’t shy to initiate contact to power his way into the end zone. The undrafted rookie tight end’s desire to bulldoze through defenders is apparent from his college highlights. Tariq Castro-Fields got his hands on a Payton pass that Ezukanma was able to stay with and make the grab on a bouncing ball. Payton more cleanly hit Smartt for a two-point conversion. Quez Watkins almost made a sick one-handed catch in the back of the end zone via a McKee pass but it was ruled that he did not get both feet in. Yes, Quez Watkins is still on the team and has been since he returned to Philly on the practice squad last season. Veteran cornerback Jonathan Jones was flagged for defensive holding in the end zone while going up against Hollywood Brown in a red zone sequence. Not the best practice for Jones, who also gave up a touchdown to DeVonta. Undrafted rookie free agent safety Maximus Pulley made a diving grab that was ruled incomplete for not getting both feet in. McKee forced the pass into the end zone during a two-point conversion try. Good effort by Pulley. UAR BERNARD UPDATE: I’ve seen some BGN commenters ask about how the Eagles’ intriguing seventh-round defensive tackle is doing. So, here’s what I’ve got. Bernard’s not getting many reps, which is typical for third/fourth string defensive linemen. I only saw one of his 1-on-1 offensive line versus defensive line reps since that action was happening on the opposite side of the field while 7-on-7 was concurrently taking place…

title: Eagles veterans explain why the new scheme is offensive line-friendly
summary: The Eagles offensive line has been a dominant staple for the team for more than a decade, but heading into the 2026 season, the group was forced to make a lot of changes — both to the coaching staff and to the overall offensive scheme. As the guys get more reps in the new system […]
full_text: PHILADELPHIA, PENNSYLVANIA - NOVEMBER 16: Lane Johnson #65, Fred Johnson #74, Tyler Steen #56, Cam Jurgens #51, Saquon Barkley #26, Landon Dickerson #69, and Jordan Mailata #68 of the Philadelphia Eagles huddle against the Detroit Lions at Lincoln Financial Field on November 16, 2025 in Philadelphia, United States. (Photo by Mitchell Leff/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Eagles offensive line has been a dominant staple for the team for more than a decade, but heading into the 2026 season, the group was forced to make a lot of changes — both to the coaching staff and to the overall offensive scheme. As the guys get more reps in the new system through the first few days of training camp, veterans like Lane Johnson and Jordan Mailata talked about how their job as tackles should actually be easier this year. All-Pro right tackle Lane Johnson explained that some of the new things they’re doing should open up the passing game and get more guys, more touches. But that wasn’t his favorite part about the changes. JOHNSON: “What I like about this, though, is that everything looks very complex to the defense, to the offense it’s pretty simplified. So, obviously, we have to pick up on communication and cadence, and stuff, but it’s very o-line friendly compared to maybe some past years I’ve been involved in.” Johnson went on to explain that there’s a lot more under center plays which makes it more difficult for defense’s to make reads pre-snap. JOHNSON: “For me, it’s like I always have a presence of a guard in pass protection where I have inside help, where I’ve never had help in my entire career in pass protection here, so it’s been a lot of games are different for me and Jordan [Mailata] as far as other offenses.” Jordan Mailata spoke with reporters the following day and very quickly agreed to Johnson’s assessment of things being easier for the tackles. He also elaborated on how the scheme overall will look different and make things more confusing for opposing defenses. MAILATA: “Stretching the defense a lot more than we did in the past — this is not a knock to our past schemes or our past coaches, but we get to stretch the defense and kind of stress them out a little more. They don’t know if it’s a pass or run and the play-action game being married is pretty key to the scheme. It’s been fun so far, but still early days, so we just gotta keep stacking days and go from there.” Mailata went on to explain that it’s fun to play a different style and it’s a little more aggressive than they’ve been in the past. He noted that it also is super fun to see the defense so tired, because they’re engaging the defensive line a lot more — like running to the left and then passing over the middle. By convincing the d-line that they’re running, it confuses the linebackers and then opens up the middle of the field for a pass. As far as technique, Mailata said there’s a bit of a change with regard to their footwork because rather than moving laterally, they’re going across the line of scrimmage — being more aggressive and meeting them across the line rather than at the line. MAILATA: “When we’re being taught the scheme, just the explanation of how the defense is going to see it and the plan, in those meetings you just see like — ‘Oh wow, that’s pretty smart. Why didn’t I think of that?‘ Mailata has repeatedly expressed how impressed he’s been with new OC Sean Mannion this offseason, and the offensive coordinator, on Saturday, described how he and new OL coach Chris Kuper are trying to prioritize assignment commitment for the guys up front. MANNION: “We want these guys to go out there, know exactly where to go, and play fast. So, throughout all of our teaching, we want to make as many things as black and white for them as possible, so we’re all on the same page and we’re off and running. At least we all know where we’re going, and we’re going with total assignment commitment to attack our aiming points, attack our targets, and that will ultimately allow us to play fast, play physical, have the play style that we want. But, we want to make everything as cut and dry, and black and white for the offensive line so they can fire off.“ Landon Dickerson also reiterated the groups new priority of having things be as simple as possible and being able to play a lot faster as a result. DICKERSON: “I think for the o-line as a whole, a big emphasis is eliminating the slow play, not having a lot of time on the clock, just getting up there, being able to make a call, stick with it, and run the play. So, I think just for us, it’s about getting to the ball and playing fast, which can help a lot.” The LG said that a lot of it is trying not to overthink things. Dickerson explained that in their last system, a lot of it was problem solving and identifying things at the line of scrimmage, but the new system is all about playing fast. It’ll be awhile before we see the offense at full speed, but that so many veteran offensive lineman are excited about doing something new this season — and something they can believe in — is encouraging if nothing else with just over a month until Week 1.

full_text: PHILADELPHIA, PENNSYLVANIA - OCTOBER 26: Jalyx Hunt #58, Jordan Davis #90 and Jalen Carter #98 of the Philadelphia Eagles look on against the New York Giants at Lincoln Financial Field on October 26, 2025 in Philadelphia, United States.
