Edge – Jonathan Greenard/Nolan Smith Jr.. IDL – Jordan Davis/Moro Ojomo. IDL – Jalen Carter. Edge – Jalyx Hunt. Philadelphia already had a top-half pass rush last season, with all meaningful contributors returning, before dealing a pair of third-round picks for Vikings standout edge rusher Jonathan Greenard. This unit is led by elite interior rusher Jalen Carter, with Greenard’s elite length and get-off giving Philadelphia a very good No. 2 in the hierarchy and a stable of solid to above-average pieces behind them. Jalyx Hunt projects as the third-best option, while Moro Ojomo offers pocket-pushing power that helped him finish 11th among interior rushers in TPR in 2025. This is one of the deepest units in the NFL and firmly a top-five group entering 2026. Sean Mannion sets Eagles training camp expectations, talks Jalen Hurts, and more – BGN The Eagles were back on the practice field on Saturday, but before taking the field, new offensive coordinator Sean Mannion spoke to reporters — in just his second time speaking to Philly media since being hired. He explained his training camp expectations, why he’s enjoyed working with Jalen Hurts, and their approaches to installing a new offensive scheme. Five Eagles Training Camp Thoughts With BLG! – The Ringer’s Philly Special Sheil is joined by Brandon Lee Gowton of Bleeding Green Nation to discuss his biggest takeaways from the first week of training camp. One of the biggest questions this upcoming season will be the offense in its entirety. How has it looked so far in camp? What are the biggest concerns? Which defensive player does BLG think is ready to make a major leap next season? Eagles mailbag: Is Makai Lemon’s slow start to camp cause for concern? – PhillyVoice Makai Lemon hasn’t done much so far, but as noted in the first paragraph, we’re only three days into camp. Would it be a lot cooler if he was lighting it up? Sure! But it’s pretty normal for rookie receivers to take a little time to get their sea legs in camp. In DeVonta Smith’s first training camp, he sprained his MCL in the fourth practice, and then missed the next eight practices. Before the injury, he had probably shown a little more than Lemon has so far, but he too was mostly quiet. Lemon has talent. He’ll make some plays. If after the first 10 or so practices he’s still just not making catches then it would be a much more reasonable cause for concern. Newcomer Dontayvion Wicks already earning trust from Jalen Hurts – NBCSP After just a few days of training camp, the biggest highlight play belongs to receiver Dontayvion Wicks. It wouldn’t have happened without trust. On Day 2 of camp, Jalen Hurts rolled to his left and never set his feet before tossing up a 50-50 ball to Wicks, who had to climb the ladder and secure the catch through double coverage from Jakorian Bennett and Cole Wisniewski. “Just trust. Building that chemistry and trust,” Wicks said. “[Hurts] just coming out, he don’t see nobody, just throw it up and trusting me to go get that and that’s what I did.” Eagles’ 53-man roster projection: How the picture looks entering training camp Week 2 – Inquirer Wide receivers (6): DeVonta Smith, Dontayvion Wicks, Makai Lemon, Hollywood Brown, Darius Cooper, Elijah Moore. Cut: Johnny Wilson, Danny Gray, Britain Covey, Quez Watkins, Erik Ezukanma, Samori Toure. The top four players should be considered locks. Cooper is competing with Wilson for a role that Nick Sirianni described as doing the “dirty work.” Keeping both seems redundant. Cooper currently has the edge in that competition. Moore is a wild card. If the Eagles decide to go with just five here, he likely would be the odd man out. Gray had the play of the day Saturday, but there’s a lot of traffic ahead of him. 2026 NFL training camp: Position battles on each depth chart – ESPN The departure of Reed Blankenship in free agency left a starting spot open in defensive coordinator Vic Fangio’s secondary. Cooper DeJean will move from nickel to safety in base packages and probably will be paired with second-year player Andrew Mukuba. Marcus Epps and Michael Carter II are vying for starting spots when the Eagles are in sub packages, which is most of the time. In the early stages of camp, Epps and Mukuba have been paired the most frequently, but Fangio has been rotating players to get different looks. Spadaro: The joy has returned for Hollywood Brown – PhiladelphiaEagles.com Hollywood Brown feels it. He is running free and has his explosiveness. The burst he displays on the football field is special, and that’s part of the joy Brown has in this 2026 Eagles Training Camp. “I’m faster than I’ve ever been. I feel like I’m playing that way, for sure,” he said. “It’s an awesome feeling. I had a Lis Franc injury in my rookie year and that is the kind of injury that is a career-ender, they say. It’s cleaned out, I took some time to rest in this offseason and I’m seeing the benefits of that. “I’m playing more freely. I’m having fun. Enjoying what we’re doing out here.” Brown, signed in the offseason during the free agency process, is part of a diverse and talented receiving room. It is early, far too early for a hot take, so we will leave that for a larger sample size, but Brown is moving around at receiver in the Eagles’ offense. We’re still in a bit of a discovery period and that’s the way it is in every NFL Training Camp. Who’s Eagles best rookie (so far) in camp? Why it’s not Makai Lemon – Delaware Online There was always going to be a learning curve for Eagles wide receiver Makai Lemon, their first-round draft pick. And that’s even more the case for tight end Eli Stowers, the Eagles’ second-round draft pick. Neither has stood out during the Eagles’ first three training camp practices. So far, it seems like the Eagles’ best rookie has been third-round pick Markel Bell, the massive 6-foot-9, 346-pound offensive tackle. Best NFL team fits for notable remaining free agents: Stefon Diggs to NFC East? – NFL.com MEKHI BECTON. Right guard has been a problem spot for the Seahawks for some time. Seattle is expected to run it back with returning starter Anthony Bradford, who is likely to be pushed by fifth-rounder Beau Stephens. Becton has the experience to be an instant upgrade as a stop-gap until Stephens can find his way to bona fide starter status or another year goes by with a better chance to find a suitable starter in the draft. Other options: 49ers, Cardinals, Eagles. 49ers sign RB Khalil Herbert and former Colts 6th-round edge rusher; waive Eli Apple – Niners Nation The San Francisco 49ers have signed running back Khalil Herbert to a one-year deal. They’ve also added Titus Leo, a 6’3”, 245-pounder who was drafted in the sixth round by the Colts in the 2023 NFL Draft. Leo has only appeared in four games during his tenure, most recently appearing on the Eagles’ practice squad in October 2025. We knew the 49ers were working out various defensive linemen. It was reported the team had a tryout with Ogbo Okonkwo, but ultimately went younger. Leo tested well at his Pro Day back in 2023, running a 4.69 40-yard dash, with a 129” vertical jump — an elite number. [BLG Note: Okoronkwo was on the Eagles last year. And Herbert participated in the Eagles’ 2026 rookie minicamp on a tryout basis.] 3 biggest surprises so far at training camp – Blogging The Boys Cowboys linked to trade for All-Pro LB Jordyn Brooks. The Cowboys selected Jaishawn Barham in the third round, and he’s been flashing so far at camp. Plus, they added Dee Winters during the offseason. They will battle it out at middle linebacker,…

title: Steelers training camp: Young cornerback shines, Drew Allar makes another big throw
summary: LATROBE – The Pittsburgh Steelers put the pads on for the first time on Monday, taking another step toward their first game action of the year when they host the Green Bay Packers next Thursday. As always, there is much to discuss – including a breakout day from an under-the-radar quarterback, another big throw from […]
full_text: Jul 30, 2026; Latrobe, PA, USA; Pittsburgh Steelers quarterback Drew Allar (186) participates in training camp drills at Saint Vincent College. Mandatory Credit: Charles LeClaire-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect LATROBE – The Pittsburgh Steelers put the pads on for the first time on Monday, taking another step toward their first game action of the year when they host the Green Bay Packers next Thursday. As always, there is much to discuss – including a breakout day from an under-the-radar quarterback, another big throw from Drew Allar, and Jaquan Brisker’s best day. Let’s get into it. Doneiko Slaughter throws his name in the mix While Asante Samuel has been the story of training camp, No. 19 Doneiko Slaughter made several plays to stand out on Monday. For starters, he picked off Will Howard on a deep throw to the left sideline. He also broke up a deep pass from Will Howard to Max Hurleman. With such a deep cornerback room, it’s understandable that the young Slaughter isn’t a name many were focused on, but he’s becoming a name to circle once preseason play begins for the Steelers next week. Drew Allar throws another splash touchdown It was a good day for Allar, who made the splash throw of the day – a 55-yard touchdown to Cole Burgess during seven-on-sevens. He also ripped a completion over the middle to Max Hurleman on fourth down during team period. Allar has played very well through the first week of practices – better than anticipated. Especially when the overwhelming expectation was how raw he would be as a talent. However, he’s looking more comfortable with each practice and continuing to impress. Aaron Rodgers is dialed in At this time last year, the offense was rocky, as was Rodgers. Through nearly a full week of practices, he has been absolutely dialed in. He and DK Metcalf connected on a total of four passes. Metcalf made an incredible one-handed grab over Jamel Dean. He also went up and over Dean for a nice chunk play before Rodgers fit a seed to the star receiver down the sideline for a big gain. Additionally, his connection with Pat Freiermuth has been one to watch. The two connected for a touchdown on Saturday, and Rodgers found No. 88 for another big gain during team period. Jaquan Brisker has best day of camp The first-year Steeler nearly made a big splash play. He read a pass from Rodgers and had the pass hit him in the stomach, nearly picking it off. Later on in team period, he came untouched off the edge for what would have been a sack in-game. Brisker’s versatility is what makes him such a good piece to have on the defense. He continues to flash. Other notes Brandin Echols picked off a pass that looked like a miscommunication between Rodgers and Roman Wilson. Couldn’t tell if he trapped it on the grass, but it appears it was ruled a pick Asante Samuel continued his streak of impressive pass breakups, batting down a pass intended for Michael Pittman Will Howard connected with Brandon Smith on the left side of the field off a play action pass in team period Esezi Otomewo nearly picked off a short pass on the same play Brisker would have had a sack. He also batted down a pass in team period Let us know what you think in the comments . Be sure to bookmark Behind the Steel Curtain for all the latest news, breakdowns, and more! title: Pittsburgh Steelers roster 2026: Zach Frazier, Jamel Dean, Eli Heidenreich are underrated
summary: Reunions can be splashy things, but they don’t always work out. For every Led Zeppelin, Soundgarden, or Eagles, there’s a Van Hagar, Sex Pistols, or Velvet Underground. Just because you worked well together once upon a time doesn’t mean that you can recreate the magic. Obviously, Mike McCarthy and Aaron Rodgers are hoping to wind […]
full_text: PITTSBURGH, PENNSYLVANIA - JANUARY 4: Zach Frazier #54 of the Pittsburgh Steelers in action during the game against the Baltimore Ravens at Acrisure Stadium on January 4, 2026 in Pittsburgh, United States. (Photo by Joe Sargent/Getty Images) | Getty Images Reunions can be splashy things, but they don’t always work out. For every Led Zeppelin, Soundgarden, or Eagles, there’s a Van Hagar, Sex Pistols, or Velvet Underground. Just because you worked well together once upon a time doesn’t mean that you can recreate the magic. Obviously, Mike McCarthy and Aaron Rodgers are hoping to wind up on the positive side of the ledger in their own reunion. They worked together in Green Bay from 2006 through 2018, and while McCarthy helped develop Rodgers as an NFL quarterback, he also benefited from Rodgers at his best in the early 2010s, when Rodgers may have been the best pure thrower of the football we’ve ever seen. Now, as Rodgers winds his career down, the whole thing is about getting the Steelers past the recent spate of mediocre seasons we’ve seen as of late. Mike Tomlin will have a bust in Canton someday, and the fact that he never had a losing record over 19 years is ridiculous, but stringing together a bunch of 10-7 seasons with Wild Card playoff losses isn’t really the point in the Steel City. “ I felt last year might be it ,” Rodgers recently said of his future. “And then Mike [McCarthy] got hired. I talked to the wife, and she said, ‘You can do one more year.’” If Rodgers is to go out on a high note, and if McCarthy is to match the successes of his predecessors, everybody on the roster will want to step up — especially the guys whose names aren’t as familiar to the nation. To that end, I’ve identified three Hidden Gems for the 2026 Steelers — one underrated veteran, one underrated free-agent signing, and one underrated draft pick. Underrated veteran: Center Zach Frazier The Steelers already have more than their share of Pro Football Hall of Famers, and former center Maurkice Pouncey could find himself on that list someday. The nine-time Pro Bowler, two-time First-Team All-Pro, and member of the Hall of Fame All-2010s team retired after the 2020 season, and for a while, the center position was in flux without him. But in 2024, the team was smart enough to select West Virginia’s Zach Frazier with the 51st overall pick in the second round of the draft. Since then, center has not been a problem, no matter the quarterback. Over his two NFL seasons, Frazier has allowed two sacks and 23 total pressures in 1,258 pass-blocking snaps, he’s become a true force as a run-blocker at 6’3” and 310 pounds, and he’s perfectly capable of sorting out line calls and protections pre-snap. Something that impressed a certain Aaron Rodgers right away. “Well, it starts with Zach,” Rodgers said before the 2025 season. “Zach is a highly intelligent player. It helps, because as much as I have a good feel for the offense, I’m not what I would call an expert yet. I become an expert when you break the huddle, and you can see the picture in your mind. Every now and then the picture’s a little fuzzy still, so I’m still working some things out, but Zach is so freaking smart. He’s making some calls for me. I told him, ‘Don’t get used to that.’ I said, ‘At some point, I’m going to be making the calls for you.’ He’s got a real good disposition for a center. He’s obviously a talented player, and I think his leadership is what I’d like to see most continue to grow, because the leadership often grows at the same rate as a performance, and everybody knows what kind of player he is. He’s going to have more opportunities to lead.” Those leadership opportunities will continue as the Steelers’ offensive line shuffles everywhere but Frazier’s position in 2026. Tackle Troy Fautanu and guard Mason McCormick are moving to the left side from the right, and that right side is up for grabs with any number of options (including rookie guard Gennings Dunker and rookie tackle Max Iheanachor) in play. However that shakes out, the Steelers have the right man in the middle, and you should expect Frazier to continue his ascent as one of the NFL’s best centers… because he’s there already. 2025 was Year 2 for Zach Frazier. He has all the technique and protection smarts in the world, but what I love is the instinct to dominate. Get ready to see "First-Team All-Pro" before his name. @steelers pic.twitter.com/yusgxgZZYg — Doug Farrar ✍ (@NFL_DougFarrar) August 2, 2026 Underrated free agent: CB Jamel Dean Last season, the Steelers’ defenders lined up at either slot or outside cornerback allowed 140 completions on 249 attempts for 1,792 yards, 16 touchdowns, seven interceptions, 39 pass deflections, and an opponent passer rating of 88.6. Not one of the worst situations in the NFL, but not in the top five, either — and certainly not what Steelers fans are used to expecting when it comes to defensive excellence. New defensive coordinator Patrick Graham is in charge of making things better in 2026, and the front office helped Graham out by signing former Tampa Bay Buccaneers cornerback Jamel Dean to a three-year, $36.75 million contract with $12 million guaranteed. That puts Dean pretty far down the list of average annual salaries for the position , and it could turn out to be an amazing bargain. Because when he’s allowed to do what he does, both in press and off coverage, the 30-year-old Dean still has it all together when it comes to coverage. Last season for the Bucs, Dean allowed 25 catches on 54 targets for 311 yards, 105 yards after the catch, one touchdown, three interceptions, five pass breakups, and an opponent passer rating of 47.7 — the NFL’s lowest among corners who played at least 50% of their teams’ snaps. “You guys know this better than I do, but first it starts with your division,” Graham recently said when asked what it means to have two cornerbacks in Dean and Joey Porter Jr. who can be physical players and press corners as well. “If you’re talking about a division where teams run the ball and have big receivers, it’s good business. Whether you’re talking about Cincinnati, you’re talking about Baltimore, or you’re talking about Cleveland, in terms of whether I’m talking about the receivers, the run game, that’s what our division is all about. So, I think it’s good business. “It’s a highway-speed league. So, if you’ve got length, you’ve got speed, and then the fact that there’s some physicality to it, that’s always going to be good for us. Because no matter what we talk about, the spread, run game, the spread pass game, when it gets down to January, and in this division every week, it comes down to the physicality of the game, and you have to establish that. “So, when you have corners that can tackle, that’s a bonus.” Well, Dean also had 38 solo tackles, 10 stops, and two forced fumbles last season, so the 6’1”, 206-pound veteran has no issue getting grimy in the paint. Most importantly though, Dean’s tape shows a player conversant with breaking down any passing game concepts, and blowing it up. Dean’s value to the Steelers will be the perfect blend of acumen and athleticism, and that will show up right away. Jamel Dean is the NFL's best cornerback nobody talks about nearly enough. @steelers pic.twitter.com/KvTjmnKuGs — Doug Farrar ✍ (@NFL_DougFarrar) August 2, 2026 Underrated draft pick: RB/FB/WR Eli Heidenreich When we talk about versatile players in football, we are generally focusing on defensive linemen who can win from multiple gaps, linebackers who can also rush the passer at the line of scrimmage, or defensive backs who can credibly play multiple positions without embarrassing themselves. In this case, we’re talking about a running back and a receiver in the person of Navy’s Eli Heidenreich, who was one of the more interesting prospects in this class, regardless of position. Frankly, I was shocked that the Steelers were able to steal him with the 230th overall pick in the seventh round.…

title: Seahawks star Devon Witherspoon snubbed from NFL Top 100 list
summary: A Pro Bowl, All-Pro votes, 72 tackles, 0.5 sacks and an interception. These are all statistics that Seattle Seahawks star cornerback Devon Witherspoon totaled in the 2025 season while leading a defense to a Super Bowl victory. However, he is not one of the NFL’s Top 100 players, at least not according to a survey […]
full_text: A Pro Bowl, All-Pro votes, 72 tackles, 0.5 sacks and an interception. These are all statistics that Seattle Seahawks star cornerback Devon Witherspoon totaled in the 2025 season while leading a defense to a Super Bowl victory. However, he is not one of the NFL’s Top 100 players, at least not according to a survey completed by his peers. No, the third-year man out of Illinois narrowly missed making the list, being ranked at 107 behind several stars, according to the NFL. Witherspoon fell behind players like Detroit Lions wide receiver Jameson Williams, Houston Texans quarterback CJ Stroud and new San Francisco 49ers wideout Mike Evans. Not to mention the players who actually made the list, like Seahawks’ legend Bobby Wagner (81), who is currently a free agent, and Eagles corner Quinyon Mitchell (47). Players who just missed the NFL Top 100… 110: Tyler Warren 109: Tee Higgins 108: Brian Branch 107: Devon Witherspoon 106: Jameson Williams 105: Dexter Lawrence 104: Chris Lindstrom 103: CJ Stroud 102: Lane Johnson 101: Mike Evans pic.twitter.com/bjfSYLDg0V — NFL (@NFL) August 3, 2026 For whatever reason, NFL Top 100 survey ballots start after Thanksgiving of the previous season and players often submit them after the Super Bowl . Witherspoon has proven to be an x-factor in Mike Macdonald’s defense, with his speed and tackling ability elevating the Seahawks anytime he’s on the field. This game-changing ability was on full display in the Seahawks’ Super Bowl against the New England Patriots, in which he recorded one sack, one pass defensed, four tackles and a strip of Drake Maye, which was caught by Uchenna Nwosu for the game-sealing touchdown in the fourth. With Witherspoon’s snub, there remains only one Seahawks player on the NFL Top 100 list after over half the list has been revealed. Ernest Jones IV, the team’s impeccable linebacker, just barely cracked the list at No. 97 after a 126-tackle and five-interception season There are only 39 players on the list yet to be revealed, and it’s safe to assume at least a few more of Seattle’s stars will make the list, including Leonard Williams and Jaxon Smith-Njigba. The list will continue to be revealed weekly until Sept. 4, when undoubtedly we will have far more to complain about than this list.

title: Seahawks 2026 training camp: 3 things we’re looking for during Week 2 of practice
summary: The Seattle Seahawks resume training camp practice on Monday. It’s their last full week of practice before preseason begins on Aug. 15 versus the Dallas Cowboys. full_text: The Seattle Seahawks resume training camp practice on Monday. It’s their last full week of practice before preseason begins on Aug. 15 versus the Dallas Cowboys. There will be more padded practices than non-padded practices, and the competition for roster spots will really start to heat up in the days to come. Field Gulls will once again be at Seahawks this week, providing written and video content over the next several days. Yours truly and Bryce Coutts are set to attend Aug. 5 and Aug. 7 practices at VMAC, and on Aug. 8 we’ll be joined by Josh Hite to make it a Field Gulls trio for Football Fan Fest at Lumen Field. All of this, of course, is pending the air quality not being completely unhealthy due to the incoming smoke from the horrifying Spokane wildfires . To get prepped for camp, the three of us each listed three things we’ll be paying attention to throughout the practices. Have a look below! Mookie Alexander First thing I’ll be paying attention to is the straight dropback passing game. Obviously, you don’t show your whole playbook in camp, but last year when Klint Kubiak was spamming under-center play-action and getting Tory Horton increased work with the first-team offense, that proved relevant when the games actually happened. An area where I think Brian Fleury can and arguably must improve from Kubiak’s offense is the passing attack without play-action. Seattle’s efficiency wasn’t terrible in non-PA but it wasn’t amazing, and less so when Jaxon Smith-Njigba wasn’t targeted. I’m curious to see if we’ll get a glimpse of more running back targets, three-step quick game, slants, and shallow crossers with YAC potential. Second on my “What/Who to watch for” list is the young’uns in the secondary, more specifically Julian Neal (who’s injured, so it may be moot on his part), Andre Fuller, Michael Dansby, and Bud Clark. Dansby has been heralded throughout camp, so I’m intrigued to see if he can go from afterthought to a real roster candidate. Clark has had a few splash plays and worked with the starters over the weekend, and he has that nose for the ball that will make him an intriguing and exciting watch. The last thing I’m looking forward to seeing is how Rylie Mills performs. He excited everyone with his sack in the Super Bowl, and he’s drawn rave reviews in camp already. Mills could be a major part of Seattle’s interior pass rush. I’m curious to see how often he lines up as a 3-tech vs. 5-tech. Josh Hite The Seahawks generally keep five cornerbacks on the roster, and Devon Witherspoon and Josh Jobe are solidly locked in, but the remaining three spots are open for grabs. Will the rookies step up and claim them, or will the veterans like Noah Igbinoghene fight off the rookies? Another area I will be watching is the pass rushers. With the rumors that the Seahawks have interest in another veteran pass rusher, I believe a lot of that will depend on how the younger pass rushers are producing in camp and the preseason games. Can these younger players show the coaching staff that they can take that next step? Finally, I will be watching the interior offensive line. The Seahawks generally keep 10 offensive linemen on the active roster, Grey Zabel, Jalen Sundell, and Anthony Bradford seem to have the staring gigs locked up, but the backup spots remain in contention. Will Olu Oluwatimi and Christian Haynes make the team once again, or will Mason Richman, Bryce Cabeldue, and Beau Stephens show the coaches that they can step up? These are things I will be looking out for while I am there. Bryce Coutts When I’m on location at Seahawks training camp this week, there are three things I’ll be watching especially closely through my coaching lens. The first is the continued evolution of Seattle’s offense and what it looks like with Sam Darnold running the show. We talk about this constantly: quarterback play is about much more than completion percentage or whether a throw ends up on a highlight reel. I want to watch Darnold’s feet, timing, eye discipline, command of the offense and how quickly he is processing when the picture changes after the snap. I’ll also be paying close attention to how Brian Fleury is putting this offense together the formations, motions, play-action concepts, RPO elements and how Seattle is creating answers for the quarterback before the ball is even snapped. Connected to all of that is my second major focus: the offensive line and protection. I want to see communication, how they handle movement and pressure, whether the run game is creating displacement and how consistently the five-man unit is giving Darnold a clean platform. The Seahawks can have all the weapons they want, but everything offensively still starts with winning up front. The third thing I’ll be studying is Mike Macdonald’s defense and how much further Seattle can take what has already become one of the defining identities of this team. I’m going to be watching the details that don’t always show up on a camp highlight: pre-snap disguise, safety rotations, communication, leverage, how defenders pass routes off in coverage and whether Seattle can create pressure with its front without constantly having to add bodies to the rush. I’ll also be watching the competition throughout the roster because camp isn’t simply about which player makes the biggest play on a given afternoon it’s about consistency. As a coach, I want to see what happens on the rep after a mistake. Does the player correct it? Does his technique hold up when he gets tired? Does he understand the assignment or is he simply relying on athletic ability? Those are the details I try to bring to my analysis, and being on the ground in Seattle this week gives me the opportunity to evaluate this team beyond the highlights and really see how ready the Seahawks are for what comes next. And as a final reminder… The Seahawks Syndicate quartet of myself, Bryce Coutts, Dan Viens, and Brandon Cain (who will be joining our podcasts virtually this year) are back for more training camp podcasts! Our live shows will broadcast from our special recording area at Fast Fashion Brewing in SoDo! Emerald City Spectrum ’s Corbin Smith will be a special guest on Aug. 5 at 7:30 pm PT . You’re all invited to all three recordings, but especially our Town Hall style show on Aug. 7 at 7:30 pm, in which there will be a ticket giveaway by Dan for the Seahawks-Cowboys preseason game. Our last show is 2:30 pm PT before Fan Fest on Saturday. Come hang with us at Fast Fashion and/or meet us at the berm on those two VMAC days. There’s a lot of guys that have good skill sets. It’s a matter of, can they make the right decisions? Can they block a gunner when they’re supposed to? Can they let a ball hit the ground when they’re supposed to? Can they go up and catch a fair catch when they’re supposed to? There’s a lot more that goes into it than just returning the ball. We’re trying to find the guy that has the whole package, that we can count on every week, that can catch the ball and make great decisions.” 49ers Camp Notes: I’m all in on Romello Height (paywall) “[Height’s] arms are short, though, which raises a question about whether he actually finishes plays himself. He might end up being more of a guy who creates sacks for someone else than one who racks them up personally — more pressures than finishes. What I’m confident of is his ability as a disruptor, even if it’s a bit role. I do know I saw him cook Colton McKivitz at least once on Monday. Another time, I saw him spin inside violently, forcing Dominick Puni to help. He and McKivitz ultimately drove Height into the ground, but it also meant Puni had to account for him. It was a proactive double team on a rookie. If people are having to double-team Height the way they double Nick Bosa or Osa Odighizuwa, that’s going to result in sacks and meaningful pressure elsewhere on the line. I’m legitimately all in on this kid as a pass rusher. He has a four-move bag I outlined in the draft guide that’s predicated on converting speed and hesitation……Good day for both starting corners. Deommodore Lenoir had at least a couple of breakups, including one on Jake Tonges. Renardo Green looked pretty good. I loved that he, Marques Sigle, and Dre Brown were all communicating together. That communication is fundamental to raising the defense’s ceiling. Green had a full clamp on Jordan Watkins in the red zone….. Tonges looks really good. I think he’s a great No. 2 receiving tight end I’d expect production from him regardless of George Kittle’s status. Jordan Watkins showed up from time to time and looked alright. There was one incredible catch from Brayden Willis: a back-shoulder, one-handed grab, defended by (I think) Patrick McMorris. That was the only time I really noticed Willis. Good stuff from Junior Bergen. Popped up in a lot of different places. Demarcus Robinson also had at least one nice grab early on….Keep an eye on Bryson Eason. He’s a hefty guy who packs some real punch with his hands. I think he has a route to make the team, especially with Gracen Halton not practicing.“ Mike Evans joins 49ers’ growing list of injuries despite team’s dialed-back camp (paywall) “Jaden Dugger was drafted in the fifth round to play linebacker. His versatility, however, was notable after he played linebacker, edge and safety at different points in his college career. Monday was the first time Dugger worked with the defensive line group, which was particularly shorthanded due to injury. Dugger recorded what would’ve been a sack in a live setting from a defensive end’s alignment.” Matt Maiocco’s 53-man 49ers roster projection 1.0 ahead of the 2026 NFL season “Cowing looks the most comfortable among all the candidates when he is fielding punts. Winning that job in the return game will lock him into one of those spots.….The last couple spots [on the defensive line] are wide open, and such players as Sample, Sebastian Valdez, Bryson Eason and James Thompson still have plenty of time to win their spots….There is good competition among the cornerbacks. Veteran Nate Hobbs is definitely right there for one of these spots, as is fourth-round draft pick Ephesians Prysock. Depending on how he looks in the two joint practices and three preseason games, Prysock could be a no-brainer to win a spot on the team. The 49ers might feel that way, anyway, because he was selected in the fourth round and has a lot of promise. But, right now, Luter is looking good as one of the backups behind the top four guys: Lenoir, Green, Stout and Jones.” Do the 49ers finally have a Trent Williams heir? Enrique Cruz Jr. is off to a good start (paywall) “Instead, the least experienced of them all, rookie Enrique Cruz Jr., bounded into the huddle like an eager golden retriever, and the second-team offense didn’t skip a beat. “Coach, who goes in?” Cruz recalled excitedly asking Chris Foerster. The offensive line coach’s quick response: “You! You go in!” The sequence ended up being a good way to get rid of Day 1 jitters, Cruz said. And it offered a glimpse at one of the rookie’s top qualities: He isn’t shy. “He has an infectious personality,” Cruz’s high school coach, Nick Hildreth, said. “He’s fun, he’s so outgoing, he’s so happy to be there. I’ve never seen him where he’s negative toward anybody, ever.”….. and though the two hit it off right away, there were some early obstacles. The first was Cruz fancied himself a basketball player. Even after Hildreth convinced him to give football a try, he informed his coach he was a wideout. “And I’m like, ‘You’re not a wideout,’” Hildreth told Cruz, who grew to 6 feet 5, 252 pounds before his senior season. “We did throw him the ball his senior year. He got the ball in his hands once.” Another problem was Cruz’s GPA, which fell as low as 1.4. His worst subject? Cruz laughs and admits it was Spanish — funny because his family’s from Puerto Rico and he speaks the language. “It was a different version of Spanish,” he said. “I’d be at my grandma’s house doing it, and my grandma would tell me it’s wrong, it’s the wrong term because it’s Puerto Rican Spanish and not Spanish Spanish. So it was pretty hard for me to learn.”….Hildreth also convinced Cruz to drop his beloved basketball for wrestling, a sport he’d never tried before but one that would make him a better offensive lineman. “It’s hard on the ego to be the biggest, baddest kid in the building and then go to the wrestling room and get beat up,” Hildreth said. Cruz truly took off as a junior. He was tall, powerful, long-limbed, and he could pull and wreak havoc on opposing linebackers. During the playoffs that year, Cruz caused a riot of euphoria on the Willowbrook sideline when he blocked a highly touted opponent out of the back of the end zone and into a snowbank. “That was the beginning of his coming-out party,” Hildreth said. By the time he graduated, his GPA was up to 3.0, and he’d gotten a scholarship from Syracuse. When I came off of the one in 2020, it forced me to..I don’t know how to…

And while he’s currently on the Active/PUP List, […]
full_text: LAS VEGAS, NEVADA - FEBRUARY 08: George Kittle #85 and tight ends coach Brian Fleury during San Francisco 49ers practice ahead of Super Bowl LVIII at Fertitta Football Complex on February 08, 2024 in Las Vegas, Nevada. (Photo by Chris Unger/Getty Images) | Getty Images George Kittle continues to progress from his January surgery that repaired a torn right Achilles tendon. The San Francisco 49ers are kind of caught in limbo with what to do with Kittle, as it sounds like there is uncertainty whether Kittle will be ready for Week 1. And while he’s currently on the Active/PUP List, using the same designation once the season begins would mean Kittle couldn’t play for the first four games of the season. Decisions, decisions. My guess is the team doesn’t rush one of the most important players on the roster, and they start Kittle on the PUP list. See ya in October, George. Mykel Williams is also a candidate to begin the season on the PUP. John Lynch didn’t sound like somebody who was confident in Williams being ready to play by Week 1, despite the second-year pro’s best efforts . According to our weekly FanDuel Sportsbook survey, 49ers fans are convinced we’ll see Kittle on the field before Williams. If that’s the case, how long until we see Mykel? He’s the queen on the chessboard for this 49ers defense. He’s the player — if Mykel is as good as the Niners believe him to be — who can unlock the pass rush and raise the run defense’s floor dramatically. That’s under the assumption he takes a jump in his second season and remains healthy — a dangerous assumption to make.

title: 49ers WR Mike Evans’ quad strain believed to be ‘not too serious’
summary: The hits keep coming for the San Francisco 49ers. Wide receiver Mike Evans isn’t practicing on Monday due to a quad strain. Rookie running back Kaelon Black has an adductor injury and will also miss Monday’s session. Depending on the grade of the strain, Evans could miss anywhere from one week to multiple months. If […]
full_text: SANTA CLARA, CA - JUNE 03: Mike Evans #5 of the San Francisco 49ers speaks with the media after a team OTA practice at SAP Performance Facility on June 3, 2026 in Santa Clara, CA. (Photo by Matthew Huang/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The hits keep coming for the San Francisco 49ers. Wide receiver Mike Evans isn’t practicing on Monday due to a quad strain. Rookie running back Kaelon Black has an adductor injury and will also miss Monday’s session. Depending on the grade of the strain, Evans could miss anywhere from one week to multiple months. If it’s a Grade 1 strain, Evans would be sidelined anywhere from 1-to-3 weeks. The problem there is a strain could feel fine early, but a re-tear of the fibers is possible, just as they begin to knit together. It’s how these kinds of injuries can go from two weeks to two months. Needless to say, expect the 49ers to be overly cautious with Evans. Kyle’s update, 12:32 p.m. PT: Ian Rapoport said Evans’ injury wasn’t serious and that he could return to practice sooner rather than later: Black is the second player in as many practices to suffer a groin injury. Again, depending on the grade, Black could miss anywhere from a week or two to a couple of months, depending on whether it’s a mild strain or a complete rupture. The 49ers have suffered injuries to three of their top four running backs before they made it to the third window of the practice blocks. That explains why they went out and signed Khalil Herbert this weekend. Wide receiver De’Zhaun Stribling will continue to sit out with hamstring tightness. He’s day-to-day. Mikail Kamara suffered a torn ACL. He was waived/injured over the weekend. CJ West and Romello Height will practice on Monday.

title: Do the 49ers still need to improve their defense ahead of the season?
summary: The San Francisco 49ers took multiple steps to improve their defense this offseason, adding key players both via free agency and the draft. San Francisco signed linebacker Dre Greenlaw back to pair with Fred Warner. They traded for Osa Odighizuwa to add a veteran at defensive tackle alongside second-year pros C.J. West and Alfred Collins. […]
full_text: The San Francisco 49ers took multiple steps to improve their defense this offseason, adding key players both via free agency and the draft. San Francisco signed linebacker Dre Greenlaw back to pair with Fred Warner. They traded for Osa Odighizuwa to add a veteran at defensive tackle alongside second-year pros C.J. West and Alfred Collins. They drafted Romello Height to provide more juice for the pass rush from a speed perspective. But are the moves enough to improve a pass rush that ranked 32nd in the NFL last year in sacks? Or do the 49ers need to add more to their defense to return to a top unit this season? Speaking to reporters last week, general manager John Lynch acknowledged the defense wasn’t good enough last year. But he feels confident that they’ve made considerable progress this offseason. “I think when we’ve been successful here, our defensive line has wreaked havoc,” Lynch said. “And I think that’s pretty consistent around the league. We weren’t good enough last year. And there’s a lot of reasons for that. But ultimately, all those reasons are just excuses. So you have to address it. I feel confident with the way that we addressed it. “Yes, Nick [Bosa] being back is a difference maker, but it was bigger than that. And so we’ll do some things schematically without changing. Raheem [Morris]’s background comes from Monte Kiffin, so very similar to what [Robert] Saleh has done for us and who we’ve been. But there will be some expanded things, some more versatility. In addition to the schematic changes, San Francisco is going to trust on its young core to develop and produce. “We’ve kind of turned over this defensive line over the last couple of years with players like Alfred Collins and CJ West and this year, Gracen Halton, Romello Height, Keion White who came in last year. I’m really excited to see that group together and see what they can do because that certainly is a priority. “When we’ve been at our best, we’ve made life miserable on the opposing offense from the defensive front. Everything starts there. I agree. I knew that as a player. I was a better player when I played with Warren Sapp than when I went to Denver and didn’t have that. So I get that, believe me. And we’ve made a concerted effort to improve that. Now we’ve got to go show that we have.” San Francisco’s defense has been dealing with a few injuries and recoveries. Nick Bosa, Mykel Williams, Alfred Collins, and C.J. West are all recovering from offseason procedures or last year’s injuries. In addition, Height has missed some of the early practices as he works through an injury sustained in camp. Collins and West will be crucial for the 49ers, not only in stopping the run, but also in the passing game, as they’ll need to take another step. The big key is obviously Bosa, who is trending well ahead of the season and has even shared he’s felt faster this offseason. Now, the 49ers secondary hasn’t made changes, and that wasn’t necessarily a strong point last season. But San Francisco will hope for another jump from both Upton Stout, who was quite good as a rookie, and Renardo Green, who had his inconsistent moments in 2025. San Francisco hasn’t been against a midseason trade, but we’ll see if they make a veteran addition, potentially even on the defensive line, ahead of the season.

title: 49ers star Nick Bosa shares why he feels faster after his 3rd ACL injury
summary: Sports’s Illustrated’s Albert Breer caught up with San Francisco 49ers edge rusher Nick Bosa, where they discussed surgery, rehab, and why Bosa jokingly could play for a handful more years at an elite level. Bosa said, “I had a little tendinitis from my high school ACL, and he cleaned that up while he fixed my […]
full_text: NEW ORLEANS, LOUISIANA - SEPTEMBER 14: Nick Bosa #97 of the San Francisco 49ers celebrates a sack against the New Orleans Saints during the second half in the game at Caesars Superdome on September 14, 2025 in New Orleans, Louisiana. (Photo by Sean Gardner/Getty Images) | Getty Images Sports’s Illustrated’s Albert Breer caught up with San Francisco 49ers edge rusher Nick Bosa, where they discussed surgery, rehab, and why Bosa jokingly could play for a handful more years at an elite level. Bosa said, “I had a little tendinitis from my high school ACL, and he cleaned that up while he fixed my ACL. That’s gone. So it’s like an improvement. So once I’m through this rehab, I feel like my right knee — because that was kind of a chronic issue that I had a little bit, and he cleaned that up in my quad tendon, and that hasn’t been an issue at all — could feel better when I’m done with this recovery.” Bosa explained why he feels faster after his third ACL injury: “You learn something every time you do it, every year really, injury or not, you kind of learn how to prepare a certain way to be your best. When I came off of the one in 2020, it forced me to..I don’t know how to explain it. Honestly, my legs get so big when I have years built up of training them. And it’s not like I trained to bodybuild my legs. They get big. And I feel like it’s just an observation that I’ve made: coming off that injury in 2020, I was moving better with less mass on my legs.” If you’ve ever seen Bosa in person, he has tree trunks for legs. It’s almost as if he’s waddling from side to side when he’s walking because of it. Good on Bosa for evolving and understanding what his body is telling him. He continued: “This is a speed game. I’m a power rusher, but speed creates power, and the way you can move is everything. So I think there’s something to, ‘I move better when my legs aren’t quite as massive.’ I kind of have that feeling right now.” We’ll see how long it takes until the 49ers clear Bosa to return to practice as a full participant. I bet the offensive line is content doing 11-on-11 drills without Bosa. Bosa also told Breer, “I should play four more years because I tear my ACL every five years.” The 49ers would welcome Bosa with open arms if he could play for another contract.
author: Kyle Posey

title: 3 questions for the 49ers at running back
summary: Running back was a revolving door for the San Francisco 49ers in the first few years of the Kyle Shanahan era. But that all changed when the 49ers acquired Christian McCaffrey in the 2022 season. Now, it’s hard for any running back not named McCaffrey to get consistent carries, and for good reason, with McCaffrey […]
full_text: SANTA CLARA, CALIFORNIA - JULY 27: Christian McCaffrey #23 of the San Francisco 49ers works out during training camp practice at SAP Performance Facility on July 27, 2026 in Santa Clara, California. (Photo by Thearon W. Henderson/Getty Images) | Getty Images Running back was a revolving door for the San Francisco 49ers in the first few years of the Kyle Shanahan era. But that all changed when the 49ers acquired Christian McCaffrey in the 2022 season. Now, it’s hard for any running back not named McCaffrey to get consistent carries, and for good reason, with McCaffrey being one of the best offensive weapons in the league. But with McCaffrey coming off one of his least productive seasons in terms of yards per attempt and him starting to get a little bit longer in the tooth, there might be some serious questions surrounding the position group. Here are three questions that will be answered over the next six months for the 49ers running backs: What does Christian McCaffrey look like as a running back in 2026? Christian McCaffrey was easily the Offensive Player of the Year and the likely MVP for the 49ers during the 2025 season, but that wasn’t because of his effectiveness on the ground but his role as an offensive weapon. But if you take Christian McCaffrey and remove the receiving numbers and look at him just as a running back, it was one of the least productive seasons as a pro. Yes, he surpassed 1,200 yards, but that was more of a product of quantity over quality. McCaffrey eclipsed 300 rushing attempts for the first time in his career. But that number of rushes didn’t produce the results you’d expect from what McCaffrey had shown in his previous seasons with the 49ers. For just the third time in his career, McCaffrey averaged fewer than four yards per rush, the first two instances coming in an injury-riddled 2020 when he averaged 3.8 yards per rush attempt in just three games, and his rookie season in 2017 when he averaged 3.7 yards per attempt on 117 carries. To give some context to McCaffrey’s 2025 production on the ground, he became the 41st running back since 2010 to eclipse 300 rushing attempts in a season. Of those 41 running backs, McCaffrey’s 1,202 rushing yards ranked 39th , only beating out 2021 Najee Harris who had 1,200 yards on 307 attempts and 2010 Cedric Benson who finished 1,111 yards on 321 attempts. McCaffrey was the most important piece to the 49ers’ offense in 2025, but the 49ers would probably prefer him to give more production than a Najee Harris or a Cedric Benson, especially with that heavy of a workload. Will Christian McCaffrey have as heavy of a workload? Now, this is three questions for the running back position, but we will cheat a bit and include McCaffrey as a pass catcher in this next section. Due to injuries and Brandon Aiyuk falling off the face of the earth, McCaffrey stepped into a larger role than expected and not only led the 49ers in rushing, but also receptions and receiving yards. Due to that, McCaffrey finished with a career-high 413 touches, just the second time he’s eclipsed the 400-touch plateau in his career. Not only was the 413 touches the most in his career, but McCaffrey led the league in touches by a healthy margin. Jonathan Taylor finished second in the league with his 369 touches, with Bijan Robinson third at 366 touches (although Robinson finished with 172 more total yards than McCaffrey despite the 47 fewer touches). Now, with the additions of Mike Evans, De’Zhaun Stribling, and now Deebo Samuel, and George Kittle ideally staying healthy, McCaffrey’s role as a pass catcher will likely drop to closer to the 65-70 receptions per season he averaged entering the 2025 season, and in theory, that helps save his legs to improve on his 2025 season as a running back. But all of that doesn’t even factor in that McCaffrey hit the dreaded age of 30 for running backs, which likely won’t affect his workload, but if the production on the ground is like it was in 2025, that ugly word regression might rear its head. How will the other running backs be used? For the third consecutive year, the 49ers used a draft pick to add a running back, using the 90th overall selection in April’s draft on Indiana’s Kaelon Black. Drafting running backs, however, hasn’t meant much usage, with Isaac Guerendo and Jordan James combining for just 84 rush attempts over their combined tenures with San Francisco. The 49ers were so confident in Guerendo and James entering training camp last year, they went out and sent a sixth-round pick to Washington for one season of Brian Robinson, who finished second on the team in rushes with his 92 rushing attempts. I think the short answer to this question is that it really doesn’t matter how the non-McCaffrey running backs will be used, as they will likely only see the field when McCaffrey needs a breather. Since the 49ers acquired McCaffrey, he has been far and away the most used running back on the team. With 2023 being McCaffrey’s first full season with the 49ers, here’s the breakdown year-to-year since 2023 of McCaffrey’s carries versus the other running backs (which removes Deebo Samuel and QB scrambles), throwing out the 2024 season since McCaffrey missed 13 games: 2023: McCaffrey – 272 carries Elijah Mitchell, Jordan Mason, Tyrion Davis-Price combined – 121 carries 2025: McCaffrey – 311 carries Brian Robinson – 92 carries In his two full healthy seasons, McCaffrey has taken 74.5 percent of all carries taken by 49ers running backs. It’s hard to imagine that any of Black, Guerendo, or James will change that in 2026. Maybe the addition of Samuel throws a wrench in things, but even then, it’s hard to imagine McCaffrey not getting around that 75 percent share of the carries we have seen.

title: 49ers News: Welcome to the Bay, Khalil Herbert

The 28-year-old was once viewed as a promising, big-play threat. He entered the NFL with 4.48 speed, but injuries have since zapped some of that explosive ability. Herbert will likely spell Kaelon Black and […]
full_text: CHICAGO, IL - SEPTEMBER 11: Talanoa Hufanga #29 of the San Francisco 49ers tackles Khalil Herbert #24 of the Chicago Bears during the game at Soldier Field on September 11, 2022 in Chicago, Illinois. The Bears defeated the 49ers 19-10. (Photo by Michael Zagaris/San Francisco 49ers/Getty Images) | Getty Images 49ers sign RB Khalil Herbert and former Colts 6th-round edge rusher; waive Eli Apple “Herbert played sparingly in 2025 with the Jets. The 28-year-old was once viewed as a promising, big-play threat. He entered the NFL with 4.48 speed, but injuries have since zapped some of that explosive ability. Herbert will likely spell Kaelon Black and Patrick Taylor in the preseason, assuming we don’t see much of Christian McCaffrey. ” This week, Herbert referred to his vision as a running back as “God’s gift.” It’s how he explains his ability to find running lanes and more on the field. The Bears have enhanced it. “We work on those things throughout the week, too,” Herbert said. “(Running backs coach David Walker) says, ‘A lot of people say you can’t teach vision.’ But he works on it to help us get our eyes right in the right place and help the O-line put them in a place to succeed.” ….His ability to identify landmarks on the defense, plant his foot and get upfield are part of that. Getsy describes Herbert as having a “cool patience about him.” “That’s as much as anything,” Getsy said. “I think Coach ‘Walk’ does a great job with those guys and training their eyes where they’re supposed to be. But I think Khalil’s got a really cool patience about him, that he’s able to kind of let things happen and make it feel like he’s not necessarily going full speed but he is, which then allows him to make cuts and read off the blocks of guys really well.” ….“When you start getting into rhythm, you start feeling the game more, feeling how the defense is playing, feeling how the O-line is blocking,” Herbert said. “And as that starts building up, you kind of just feel it. You’re able to feel how the game’s going and feel where there’s empty space once you get in rhythm.” Khalil Herbert and Virginia Tech found what they were looking for in each other (paywall) “When he did make weight, he lined up on the offensive line, later moving to defensive line and linebacker as he moved through middle school. It wasn’t until high school that his athleticism started to shine and the seeds of a future at running back were planted….. Like when he was younger, getting past those pudgier days, he works at it. [QB Hendon] Hooker, who is Herbert’s roommate, was heading in to watch film last weekend, as quarterbacks do, so the running back decided to join him. “His work ethic is just incredible,” Hooker said. “The way he can break down defenses while watching film and then implement it in the game is incredible.” “Those times kind of waiting and having to sit behind, I kind of learned a lot just about myself and about the game studying those guys and learning different moves, techniques, different things they do kind of helped me out, helped me to be where I am right now,” Herbert said. “So, everything works out in perfect timing, I think. This is just working out how everything’s supposed to work out.” That studiousness was forged by his parents, who stressed education and hard work throughout his life. Khari Sr. is an engineer who specializes in power generation and diesel mechanics. Khalil, who got a degree in business administration at Kansas, is pursuing a Masters of Information Technology at Virginia Tech. “He’s one of them types of people that when he gets serious about something, he’s all in,” Khari Sr. said. “He dissects and he studies, because he just always wants to be ahead of the game, more or less. But that’s with everything, not just football.” 49ers’ Dre Greenlaw details brutal road that included depression, 2 games in 614 days (paywall) “I don’t have to go out there and do more,” Greenlaw said. “I don’t have to go prove it to nobody. … I have to go play football still. But I don’t have to go out there and overdo and prove to them that I’m a football player, or who I am as a person. I think that’s going to help a lot.” Greenlaw tore his Achilles during the 49ers’ overtime Super Bowl loss to the Chiefs after the 2023 season. After a 10-month rehab, he played in two late-season games during the 2024 season before his quadriceps travails delayed his Denver debut last year to mid-October. “Going to Broncos, I’m thinking ‘This is the year I’m finally going to make it happen,’” he said. Greenlaw is confident this will be the year he finally makes it happen. It nearly has to be. He knows a third consecutive injury-plagued season could leave him with limited options in free agency in 2027, when he will turn 30. For now, Greenlaw said he has not felt this good physically since January 2024, when his Achilles began bothering him in the weeks before the Super Bowl. “It’s been one (injury) after another, one after another, and I’ve just been playing catch-up the whole time,” Greenlaw said. “But I just feel like I’m where I need to be now.” Report: 49ers work out veteran edge rusher Ogbo Okoronkwo “The veteran pass rusher has 17.5 sacks over his eight-year NFL career, including 7.5 sacks during his two seasons with the Browns. He recorded 4.5 sacks in 2023 and another three in 2024. His best season was in 2022 when he had five sacks with the Texans. Okoronkwo had no sacks last season, but only appeared in one game for the Eagles.” 49ers work out two more defensive players, including former Cardinals draft pick “Carter has spent time with the Minnesota Vikings, Las Vegas Raiders, and Washington Commanders. He originally entered the NFL as an undrafted free agent out of Army following the 2023 NFL Draft and has experience playing as an edge rusher. Thomas is a former Arizona Cardinals edge rusher who entered the NFL as a fifth-round draft pick out of Clemson in 2024. He spent his college career as a productive pass rusher and was viewed as an intriguing developmental prospect coming out of Clemson.”

title: Titans need to break passing yards curse in 2026
summary: The Tennessee Titans have not fielded an effective passing offense in five seasons. That’s an extremely sad sentence to write, but it’s true. This past campaign, they ranked 30th as an offense in passing yards, averaging 166.1 per contest. They finished the 2024 campaign ranked 26th in passing yards under Brian Callahan and Will Levis, […]
full_text: Tennessee Titans Offensive Coordinator Brian Daboll addresses the media during his first press conference at Ascension Saint Thomas Sports Park in Nashville, Tenn., Wednesday, Feb. 18, 2026. | DENNY SIMMONS / THE TENNESSEAN / USA TODAY NETWORK via Imagn Images The Tennessee Titans have not fielded an effective passing offense in five seasons. That’s an extremely sad sentence to write, but it’s true. This past campaign, they ranked 30th as an offense in passing yards, averaging 166.1 per contest. They finished the 2024 campaign ranked 26th in passing yards under Brian Callahan and Will Levis, averaging 195.1 per game. They were 29th in 2023 (180.4/game), 30th in 2022 (171.4), 24th in 2021 (201.1), and 23rd in 2020 (228.3). That’s an unfathomable streak of consistently being a bottom-10 passing offense. The Titans invested significant offseason resources to hopefully change that in 2026. After hiring a defensive minded head coach in Robert Saleh, the Titans hired one of the most sought-after offensive coordinator candidates in Brian Daboll. Coach Daboll loved Cam Ward as a prospect and is legitimately excited to develop him this year. The Titans also invested big at wide receiver. They drafted Carnell Tate with the fourth overall pick and paid Wan’Dale Robinson $70 million in free agency. Both additions were improved by Daboll, and he’s expected to make them the focal point of his passing offense. The Titans are arguably deeper at wide receiver than they’ve ever been. They kept Calvin Ridley via a restructured contract as opposed to making him a salary cap casualty. They also have sophomores Chimere Dike and Elic Ayomanor. At tight end, they have the developing Gunnar Helm, and paid Daniel Bellinger $8 million per year in free agency. The Titans need to field a significantly more impactful aerial attack in 2026 than they have in several seasons. A lot of that will be decided by how Ward develops as a sophomore quarterback. Adding supporting pieces like Daboll, Tate, and Robinson should have a monumental impact. The Titans have the pieces in place to effectively pass the ball in 2026.

full_text: Tennessee Titans Coach Robert Saleh speaks before mandatory minicamp at Vanderbilt Health Football Center in Nashville, Tenn., Wednesday, June 17, 2026. | ANDREW NELLES / THE TENNESSEAN / USA TODAY NETWORK via Imagn Images The Tennessee Titans totally revamped their defensive line this offseason. They hired Robert Saleh to be the new head coach. Saleh came in and reimagined the defensive line in his vision. It started when the Titans traded for Jermaine Johnson II. They signed John Franklin-Myers , Jordan Elliott, and Jacob Martin in free agency. Mike Borgonzi also traded for Solomon Thomas. Saleh coached all five of these players in New York and San Francisco. Of course, they’re joining Jeffery Simmons, who inked a historic extension with the Titans earlier this offseason. Saleh will attempt to develop sophomore Femi Oladejo. The Titans also drafted Keldric Faulk with a first-round pick. Faulk was another Saleh-approved addition, given his similar length and build to Arik Armstead. The aforementioned eight players will essentially be the Titans’ defensive line rotation this season. Coach Saleh is expected to field an aggressive, attacking-style defense. That’s the focal point of his defense. It should lead to impressive sack numbers for the Titans’ defense. Expectations are high. Given the Titans’ lack of talent at EDGE last season, defensive coordinator Dennard Wilson actually did an excellent job manufacturing pressure. An All-Pro season from Simmons helped. The Titans ranked 12th (tied) in the league in sacks with 42. That exceeded preseason expectations. Interestingly enough, Saleh’s 49ers defense ranked last in the NFL in sacks with 20. Remember they lost Nick Bosa and Mykel Williams to season-ending ACL injuries. It’s a reminder that even the greatest defensive coaches need talented players to produce results. The Titans have an elite talent in Simmons, and Franklin-Myers should be very productive too. The EDGE spot is mysterious. Johnson is coming off a disappointing 2025 season and 2024 Achilles injury, and Oladejo disappointed as a rookie. Coach Saleh needs to elevate this defense to produce another 40+ sacks in 2026.

Sometimes after the whistle. “Yeah, definitely like even after the whistle they’re going at the ball,” said tight end Chig Okonkwo. “I mean one time today, you know, [K’Lavon Chaisson] got me after the whistle. Them boys are coming and it’s just nice to, you know, have that competition that just raises up, raises up another level of competition.” To read more of this article, CLICK HERE Washington Post (paywall) Commanders’ offense gets cooking and other observations from Monday’s practice Overall, it was easily the best practice the offense has had in camp thus far. Daniels was on the money, and the pass catchers did a better job of creating separation. The downside: The offensive line continued to have issues both in pass protection and the run game. As has been the case throughout training camp, the defensive line outperformed its counterpart. The run defense was stout throughout practice, and the running backs didn’t have much room to create. The defensive line did a good job of maintaining gap integrity, while the linebackers were quick to trigger and make plays close to the line of scrimmage. In the passing game, the defensive line was able to win frequently off the edge while also creating a consistent push up the middle of the pocket. Oweh credited defensive coordinator Daronte Jones for making it clear when players can go all-in on the pass rush and giving them freedom to improvise along the way. To read more of this article, CLICK HERE Commanders Roundtable Daronte Jones’ brought constant heat, but Jayden Daniels and new-look offense flashed high-end creativity on Day 1 in pads David Blough’s hands-on energy: Offensive Coordinator David Blough is an active, hands-on coach. Throughout practice, you could see him engaged in drills, dropping back into coverage, or pulling a player aside to talk one-on-one. To begin practice, the WRs engaged in light pass-and-catch drills. Blough used what looked like a padded pole to punch at the ball and try to provoke a fumble. He seems like a guy with real attention to detail. Defense wins Day 1: If I were to declare a winner today, I would give it to the defense. On many occasions, they penetrated the gaps and took away any potential for positive yardage on runs. In this same Red Zone series, Javon Kinlaw broke through the line and “sacked” Daniels. The defense provided sticky coverage, and while Daniels tried to buy time, it was to no avail. Personnel wrinkles: The offense will provide fans (and opposing defenses) a lot of eye candy with pre-snap motion. The Commanders ran a lot of 12-personnel sets today and moved both tight ends in pre-snap motion. It’s an interesting wrinkle that wasn’t present last year. On defense, I was surprised to see Frankie Luvu at the Mike position. He spent a good amount of time there, which allowed other LBs, including Styles, to blitz off the edge. Sinnott’s versatile role: Sinnott will be used creatively this season. Today, we saw him as an H-Back and a true fullback in I-formation. I can see why he is excited for a fresh start under Blough. title: Commanders EDGE Odafe Oweh details underrated part of his game
summary: Odafe Oweh has built a reputation as an excellent pass rusher. Collecting 17.5 sacks over the last two seasons will establish that. His quarterback pressure rate is way up there, hovering near 16%, illustrating how ferocious he can be getting after the passer.   His usage suggests that as well, with the Baltimore Ravens using […]
full_text: Odafe Oweh has built a reputation as an excellent pass rusher. Collecting 17.5 sacks over the last two seasons will establish that. His quarterback pressure rate is way up there , hovering near 16%, illustrating how ferocious he can be getting after the passer. His usage suggests that as well, with the Baltimore Ravens using him primarily as a situational pass rusher. The Commanders edge rusher would like to remind you that wasn’t always the case. He had zero sacks in his final season at Penn State , even with all the physical tools required to be an excellent NFL pass rusher. Without the pass-rush stats, Oweh had to be a force in another aspect of his game that has gotten a bit lost as he enters his fifth professional season. “My run game,” Oweh said in a press conference following Monday’s training camp practice . “I came in as a run defender. I had zero sacks (his last year at Penn State), and some people forget that. I worked hard, and by the grace of God, he has helped get better as a pass rusher. The run game is what I hung my hat on at first. People forget that, because I was a designated pass rusher in some defenses. I’m really trying to get back to that playing style against the run, attacking the edges and getting TFLs.” He’s right. Go back to his NFL.com draft profile and you’ll find this assessment of his run defense: “He has dominant potential as a run defender with burst and range to upend back-side and play-side runs, turning them into short gains or losses.” Opportunity plays a part in how much run defending Oweh gets to do. He was more of a situational guy in Baltimore, where he was drafted No. 31 overall back in 2021. While pass rushing was key to the Commanders giving him a four-year, $96-million contract in free agency, he’ll be more of a three-down presence in Washington. That will give Oweh a chance to prove he’s a complete player. He’s proud of his development as a pass rusher, which involved refining the technique required to accentuate his elite physical skills. His motivation stems from doubters, from those projecting what he can’t do. “Each obstacle, each moment of adversity is like a test,” Oweh said. “That’s when you’ve got to work. That’s the universe telling you that’s where you’ve got to get better. Even if you’re listening to the fans, you can compartmentalize it and use it as motivation. I think, ‘Alright, I’m going to show you guys.’ That’s why I celebrate so much and point to the naysayers. You have to use that. “We play sports. You can’t hang your hat on the bad reps. You have to work hard for the good ones. I feel like that was the best part for me. I’m glad I went through (tough times), because now y’all know me as a pass rusher, but y’all gonna remember that I’m a run defender, too. That’s a testament to how hard I work and my ability to close out the naysayers and do my job well.” Oweh believes Daronte Jones will give him great opportunities to do that. He has generally been a secondary pass rusher, behind Kyle Van Noy or Justin Houston in Baltimore and Khalil Mack with the Chargers. Washington brought in some serious talent off the edge, Oweh’s the alpha here. New coordinator Daronte Jones is given Oweh some freedom on when to stay disciplined in rush lanes and when to take a big shot. He’ll have plenty, but isn’t putting everything on his shoulders to sack the quarterback. “Rushing well as a group is key,” Oweh said. “I’d rather have that than one dominant pass rusher. A group of pass rushers who know how to play and work well together. That’s what these first few days of training camp are all about…having chemistry with the guys and understanding what they like to do.” A quick reader poll:

title: Commanders News: Did GM Adam Peters miss by not extending Daron Payne?
summary: The Daily Slop – 3 August 2026 Editor’s note: Each day, Hogs Haven compiles a collection of articles, podcasts & tweets from around the web to keep you in touch with the Commanders, the NFC East, the NFL and sports in general, with a sprinkling of other stuff. full_text: Freelance photographer | Instagram: @scott_taetsch: Daron Payne signs autographs at Commanders training camp on Monday, August 3, 2026 | @scott_taetsch The Daily Slop – 3 August 2026 Editor’s note: Each day, Hogs Haven compiles a collection of articles, podcasts & tweets from around the web to keep you in touch with the Commanders, the NFC East, the NFL and sports in general, with a sprinkling of other stuff. Enjoy! Commanders links Today’s sked: ⛅️: temps in mid to upper 70s; 🎤: Dan Quinn before practice 🏈: 8:30 am. 1st day in pads 🎤: Chig Okonkwo/Odafe Oweh after practice 👨🏻‍💻: camp nuggets to https://t.co/1YYxI4NQrS 🎥: video to https://t.co/1YYxI4NQrS 🗣️🎙️: podcast later today — John Keim (@john_keim) August 3, 2026 Articles Bleacher Report Most Important Contract Decision for Every NFL Team Ahead of 2026 Season Washington Commanders DT Daron Payne Commanders general manager Adam Peters said there’s no huge hurry to extend the 29-year-old after a down 2025. “I don’t think we’re gonna explore that at this time,” he said. “Really excited to have Daron with us next year, and can probably address that later, maybe after the year. But, and I’ve talked with his agent about that, what I can say is I got a ton of respect for Daron. His toughness, his physicality, his leadership, his ability to play and be available all the time. And there’s nobody tougher than him, and I think he’s going to really have a chance to flourish in this new defense, which will be a little bit multiple and allow him to move around a little bit.” It’s a decision that could come back to haunt the Commanders. The last time Payne was in a contract year, he exploded for a career-high 11 sacks. If that happens again, Peters is going to have a difficult choice to make, especially with multiple edge-rushers also set to hit the open market next spring. The Big Dawg on the D-Line Daron Payne #DAWGWORK 🐕 #RaiseHail Photo credit( @scott_taetsch ) pic.twitter.com/2vuNosIUVz — B&G Soulja 🪖 (@FLYSHit_Period) August 3, 2026 To read more of this article, CLICK HERE Bullock’s Film Room (subscription) What CB Rasul Douglas brings to the Washington Commanders When the signing was first announced, I thought it was just a camp body to fill in while Amos recovered from his injury, but reports out of camp so far suggest Douglas has been one of the better corners on the roster in the opening few days of camp, having already recorded at least one interception and reportedly been close to quite a few more. Due to those positive reports, I thought I’d go back and watch some of his film from last year to see what he has to offer. He’s listed at 6-foot-2, 209 pounds and has long arms. With that size and length, you might think Douglas is a press-man corner. But actually he’s better suited to playing zone and match coverages, which fits what we’re expecting from new Commanders defensive coordinator Daronte Jones. When he’s playing off and with vision while keeping the play in front of him, he’s quick to react and close on receivers, where he can then use his length to get his hands in at the catch point and break up passes. Douglas also shows great instincts for coverage and awareness of game situations. Rasul Douglas was signed by the Commanders just before training camp. He's caught the eye on a number of occasions already, so what exactly are the Commanders getting in the veteran CB? I took a closer look: https://t.co/hsj2ujO68u pic.twitter.com/vuUoOSOyPL — Mark Bullock (@MarkBullockNFL) August 3, 2026 Commanders Roundtable Commanders add depth with signing of free agent center Julian Good-Jones, who served on the practice squad last season, was spotted taking reps with the ones as rookie Matt Gulbin rounded out the two-deep. Brandon Coleman is also entrenched in the starting competition at left guard, but he was also seen taking snaps at center following Saturday’s practice where he could become another candidate to reinforce depth while adding to his value to the unit. Yet Hill, 26, arrives back in the NFC where he will look to battle through training camp into the preseason. A former sixth round pick out of Georgia in the 2021 NFL Draft, Hill began his career with the Cincinnati Bengals where he started in three games and appeared in 24 through his first two seasons with the organization. He then fell out of the rotation after not appearing in any game during the 2023 season while being a healthy scratch in several games. Hill was then waived ahead of the 2024 season before joining Cincinnati’s practice squad. Hill then signed a reserve/futures contract with the Green Bay Packers in Jan. 2025 before being part of the final roster cuts, allowing him to land on the practice squad with the Chicago Bears exactly one month later. His most recent stint materialized with the Tennessee Titans after signing a reserve/future contract in January before being waived on June 16. To read more of this article, CLICK HERE A quick reader poll: Sports Illustrated 4 Things We’ll Learn From the Commanders’ First Padded Practice at Training Camp How the Offensive Line Holds Up Monday will give the team a chance to gauge whether its current options pass the sniff test presented by Washington’s defensive interior. The featured trench matchups to keep an eye on should be easily identified between Laremy Tunsil and Josh Conerly Jr against Odafe Oweh, K’Lavon Chaisson, Charles Omenihu, and Washington’s other edge rushers. The Commanders have a lot riding on Conerly’s ability to anchor against power and hold that edge from collapsing. They already know how he can move on the next level and as a mobile blocker, but they need to see how much raw power he added this offseason. The line has a lot to prove before anyone is going to fully trust Jayden Daniels behind what they have seen in the past. With the new system will come a new blocking structure. While we do not know the complete layout of that yet, it will likely be associated with the zone blocking scheme in some form, based on new OC David Blough’s lineage. Monday will also give the chance to see if the early camp dominance and pressure from the defense came mainly from the limitations you put on a group without contact in a contact-driven sport. To read more of this article, CLICK HERE Riggo’s Rag Odafe Oweh is turning heads at training camp Oweh’s quickness has been easy to notice through the first week of training camp. He has reportedly generated multiple sack opportunities, something Washington is going to need to do a much better job of in 2026. The Commanders just didn’t make plays on defense last year. They only turned their opponents over 10 times, which ranked ahead of only the lowly interception-less New York Jets. Their 42 team sacks ranked slightly above league average, but they never seemed to come in defining situations. Five of the team’s projected starting front seven in the new 3-4 base unit — Oweh, K’Lavon Chaisson, Leo Chenal, Tim Settle Jr., and No. 7 overall pick Sonny Styles — are fresh faces, including both edge rushers and interior linebackers. Oweh has the scope to completely transform Washington’s defensive unit for the better. Styles will be the most important player on the Commanders’ defense in the long run , but it’s the former Baltimore Ravens and Los Angeles Chargers pass-rusher who needs to set the tone in the here and now. To read more of this article, CLICK HERE Riggo’s Rag 5 standouts from Commanders 2026 training camp Day 4 Van Jefferson Jr. – Commanders WR Jefferson is a curious case. He looked well on course for a highly productive NFL journey during the early stages of his career with the Los Angeles Rams, but things tailed off dramatically. The Tennessee Titans also tasked him with too much last season , continuing his downward trend. It’s still early days, but things are looking up for Jefferson. If he keeps up this sort of consistency, the Commanders will have no choice but to take him through onto their 53-man roster. Rasul…
